# Capabilities — what this engine does, what it does not, and what holds that true

**True against engine 4.1.1**, container format 1.17, 760 test files and 7152 tests passing.

The single map. Anything else claiming to list what is missing is either older than this file or
is a plan for closing one of its rows. Established by reading the tree rather than the release
notes: every `absent` row below names a sentinel symbol, and `scripts/docs.test.mjs` asserts each
one is still missing, so the commit that builds a capability is the commit that has to correct
this document. What the native host has that a page does not is guarded the other way round (§2a).

---

| Backends                              | WebGL2 and WebGPU behind one surface, selected and reported by `createRenderer`, which **prefers WebGPU by default as of 2.6.0** and falls back silently; GPU frame timing on both. **A device is accepted by drawing with it as of 2.7.0** — `probeDevice` compiles what it is given and reads back a known pixel, and a refusal falls back to WebGL2 carrying the device's own words. **`renderer.frameBudget` reports what a frame asked for against every ceiling a backend imposes**: fourteen on WebGPU — draws, material changes, two kinds of shadow draw, water bodies, light volumes, four kinds of effect batch, four kinds of overlay — each carrying what was _asked for_ rather than what fit, because 1,267 of 1,024 says how much to cut where 1,024 of 1,024 only says a frame is full. **The draw and material rings grow to fit the scene as of 3.32.0**, at the start of the frame after one that ran out and to the next power of two above what it asked for, bounded at 64 MiB of staging each — so a frame over the line loses geometry once instead of for as long as the scene stays that size, measured on an AMD card at 1,200 material changes: the frame that discovers the ceiling puts 165,527 lit pixels on screen and the third puts 194,650, which is what WebGL2 draws having no ceiling at all. Growing replaces the buffer, so every flat bind group over it is rebuilt, the blank one with the material maps forced null. The other twelve ceilings are feature counts rather than measures of world in frame and still skip, which is deliberate and stated at `UniformRing.allocate`; what was not deliberate is that the only signal was one `console.warn` per renderer lifetime, which no check can read. **WebGL2 reports the same fifteen lines with a `null` ceiling** because it imposes none, **counted by the same rules** — each verb after the same guards, and a material change by `materialChanges.ts`, which both backends call — and `webgpu/renderer.test.ts` runs one scene through both and compares every line. That is true as of 2026-09-19; before it WebGL2 declared three of the fifteen, and this row said otherwise. Because it imposes none, so a scene over a WebGPU ceiling draws in full there and loses geometry here with nothing failing — and a consumer developing on the fallback can now see that coming rather than hearing about it from a player | Lighting                              | Directional with cascaded shadows (rotated Poisson, receiver-plane compensation); ten point lights with cube shadows; ray-marched light volumes with a dust field, a sun-shadow cut, and — a medium the beam answers to: `medium` on the draw scales the volume by the haze at the _volume's own_ height against the density it was authored for, so a headlight cone fades as the air clears and is skipped entirely in clear air. The shader's own header had said since it was written that a beam is more visible in fog and nothing implemented it; the same cone was drawn in soup and on a clear night, which a consumer reported as fog filtering the frame rather than changing what could be seen through it. A multiplier on the CPU in `lightVolumeDraw.ts` rather than a uniform, because the shader clamps strength to one and the value is per draw, so both backends read the one function and no shader changed. Driven by `demo/dev/volume.html?fog=` **Environment probes stand on a grid, 3.49.0.** `ProbeGrid` places them on a lattice and `nearestProbes` returns the eight around a point with trilinear weights; a single baked probe is a grid of one, so there is one path and every scene that bakes an environment keeps the picture it had — measured against `main` on the same GPU, within about one level of 255 on every figure `ibl-check.mjs` publishes, with the no-probe control identical. **It costs no texture unit.** Fifteen of WebGL2's guaranteed sixteen are spent and one is left, so the `samplerCube` became a `TEXTURE_2D_ARRAY` of octahedral maps at the same binding: levels 0 to 4 are the GGX chain and level 5 is a cosine convolution, so one sampler carries the reflection and the diffuse ambient both and unit 15 stays free. That retired the spherical-harmonic path outright — `irradianceSh.ts`, `probeReadback.ts`, the synchronous `readPixels` in the bake, and the second gate uniform that existed because one backend's ambient landed a frame or two after its reflection. **A filtered octahedral map needs a gutter**, which the point-shadow array never did at one level and `NEAREST`: the square's border is a fold, and a texel filled by that rule matches the one it is folded against to 3.3e-16 against 4.6e-2 without it. Probes cost layers rather than units, capped at `MAX_ENV_PROBES` of 64 — 683 KB a layer, 43.7 MB for the lot, against the point-shadow array's 92.3 MB. **21,495 gzipped bytes on `core-only`, 3.33%**, of which the generated WGSL is 16,502. Checked by `scripts/probegrid-check.mjs`: fifteen assertions on both backends agreeing to 0.23 levels, with a repeat-measurement floor of 0.00, and both distinguishing claims written from mutations that passed the version before them — a nearest-probe switch and a grid bound to one layer everywhere | Post                                  | Bloom, output transform, exposure, **a colour grade as a 3D lookup table**, ambient occlusion, camera motion blur, speed rush, MSAA, frame veil **Refraction ships and completes Track D**: a copy of the frame's colour, latched at the first refracting draw, sampled at an offset along the surface normal and absorbed by Beer-Lambert. **9.05 KB gzipped over core** against the 19.8 KB the census had priced it at — a uniform and a branch in `flatFrag`, not a permutation, so the fragment stage stays at sixteen. A frame that refracts nothing takes no copy, breaks no pass and binds an empty texel, which is what keeps it off the bill of a consumer who never wants glass. **Neither backend can read what it is writing and they answer differently**: WebGL2 blits, which _resolves_ a multisampled source and so works where `colorAttachment` returns null; WebGPU ends the pass, copies the resolved `post.sceneColor` and reopens with `loadOp: 'load'`, a fourth instance of a boundary already run for the mirror, the volume depth and text. **The absorption is stated as what survives one metre** rather than as a coefficient, so clear glass is `(1, 1, 1)` with no special case, and the path length divides by `dot(N, V)` — which is the whole difference from a tint, and is why a glass edge goes green while its middle stays clear. Thickness rides the per-vertex channel's `.w` lane, reserved by 3.42.0 and spent here, so it cost a varying and no attribute. **Texture unit 14 of the two that were free**, leaving one. Measured by `scripts/refraction-check.mjs` on both backends agreeing to the digit: the pattern behind a pane shifts 11 px at one strength and 23 at double, a tinted pane reads 9.7,88.4,18.6 against a clear 108.9, an edge-on pane absorbs to 32.03 where face-on holds 38.55, and the thickness lane separates 85.21 from 39.44. It replaces the surface's own shading rather than mixing, so glass carries no specular of its own; a caller wanting a glint draws a second, non-refracting pass | Reconstruction                        | **DriftTR, the analytic tier, ships on WebGPU and is off by default.** `quality.reconstruction` takes a ratio from 1.3 to 2.0, and anything outside it is off: the world draws at the output size divided by it, jittered along a Halton sequence of eight phases for every output pixel a render pixel covers, and a compute resolve accumulates it into the output — history read bicubically where the surface was, clipped to its neighbourhood's variance box in YCoCg, refused where depth, motion or normals say it is another surface, and sharpened inside the range of its neighbours. Camera motion comes from the frame's depth; a draw that states its previous transform or skin palette is drawn again into a motion target. A contributed pass is handed the frame's jitter (`PrepareContext.jitter`, applied with `jitterClip`), and the GPU-driven pipeline and splats draw with it. **Measured on the gilded chamber at 1280 by 607, three runs each: 3.08–3.15 ms of GPU off, 2.62–2.69 at 1.3, 2.42–2.49 at 1.5 and 2.16 at 2.** `recon-parity.mjs` holds the resolve's WGSL to its reference over seven frames, `ghost-check.mjs` measures a moving object under a still camera and `pan-check.mjs` a moving camera over a still world, and a replay fingerprints the same with it on at every ratio as with it off (`webgpu/renderer.test.ts`). A multisampled frame is not reconstructed, and says so once. | Surfaces                              | Gerstner water, caustics, planar reflection, wet film with roughness, reflection probe, procedural sky and atmosphere, fog, grain, relief. **A body of water is a rotated rectangle**: `bounds` was a centre and one half-extent, so the only shape it could take was a square, and the square that contains a 3 by 21 metre channel floods eighteen metres of ground either side. Reported from outside, where the workaround was one _unbounded_ body at the ditches' level with the world's whole ground raised above it — a technically flooded world held up by a rule nobody can see, which had already cost one bug. `halfX` and `halfZ` are the body's own axes and `forwardX`/`forwardZ` say which way they point, a direction and not an angle because a consumer bounding a ditch arrives holding the run's direction; `halfM` stays as the square shorthand. What it cannot do is bend, so a canal that turns is one body per straight run. **And a frame can draw more than one body, which on WebGPU it could not**: every body's uniforms lived in one buffer rewritten before each draw, and a queue write does not interleave with the draws it sits between, so four bodies all wore the fourth's extents, level and colours — 387,837 pixels of one frame, measured. A slot each now, from a `UniformRing`, which is the rule in `AGENTS.md` reaching the pass that was still missing it. Driven by `demo/dev/water.html`, four bodies in one frame with one of them turned, at 56 pixels between the backends **A four-lane per-vertex channel, 3.42.0**: `MeshData.channel` carries `sway` in the vertex stage, `skyDirect` for the directional term alone and `alpha` on the draw's opacity, in one `vec4` at attribute location 13 — one location because WebGL2 guarantees sixteen, eleven were spent and an instanced draw spends all of them, so `InstancedMesh` refuses a mesh carrying one rather than reading the absent constant and drawing leaves that never move. Absent is `(0, 1, 1, 0)` through the same disabled-attribute mechanism `grain` and `relief` use, so a mesh that says nothing costs no buffer and is identical to the digest — measured, `f0092361` on both backends. **`skyDirect` multiplies `sunShade` and not `direct`**, because the sun's specular lobe reads `sunShade` on its own and scaling the diffuse alone leaves an enclosed face with no sunlight and a highlight anyway; ambient is untouched, which is the defect it exists to fix — a sky factor folded into `colors` scales ambient and sun together and darkens a cave face twice. **Sway reads the wind `resolveScatterDeform` already produces**, through `setWind` once a frame and bound to the depth pass too, so a canopy and its own shadow bend together; the lane is taken as authored where `scatter.ts` squares its own, because that falloff is derived from height and this one is written by hand. **5.8 KB gzipped over core** and no new permutation on either stage — the vertex stage is 5 variants at 5.2 KB against the fragment stage's 16 at 283.4 KB, which is why a vertex channel is not priced like a fragment branch. Checked by `scripts/vertex-channel-check.mjs`, ten assertions on both backends agreeing to the digit: sway moves the quad 57.343 px one way and 57.105 the other while a `sway = 0` control holds at 0.000, and the sky lane leaves 38.00 luminance where folding the factor into the vertex colour leaves 0.00 **A surface texture can be asked for nearest magnification, 3.43.0** — `filter` on `SurfaceTextureOptions`, defaulting to `linear`, for an image whose pixels are the subject rather than an artefact of resolution. Minification still blends between mip levels, because the option is about magnification and taking the nearest level would trade a smear for a pop; and WebGPU refuses `maxAnisotropy` above 1 unless every filter is linear, so a nearest sampler gets 1 there and an ignored request on WebGL2 | Draws                                 | Instanced scatter, three particle materials, plumes, bolts, flocks, wind streaks, polylines, panels, billboards, bitmap and SDF text, insets. **Rain ships, as streaks rather than sprites**: `RainField` fills a `LineSegments` with a slab of drops that follows the viewer, each drawn from where it is to where it was a shutter-time ago, so the streak runs along the velocity and a gust leans every drop at once with nothing trigonometric. A round sprite stretched by its motion would have wanted a new attribute and a branch in both particle programs; a segment says it with geometry that already ships. It reads no clock and no random number — a drop's column is a hash of its index and how many times it has fallen — so a consumer evaluating instants out of order gets the same rain every time. **Drops land on the ground and do not fall through roofs**, both from the surface seam rather than from anything the rain owns: a roof is the nearest floor under anything above it, and `coveredAbove` asks whether the surface has a face overhead. **A hole is a hole for free** — a gap between pads, a ribbon's `holes`, the edge of a bounded field — because the answer is the geometry's own and cannot disagree with the opening it was cut from. `coveredAbove` is the general query and rain is one caller: a puddle that forms only where the sky reaches, a shaft of sun that should not be indoors, and an agent deciding to take shelter are the same question. **The fall speed moves while the field runs**: `speedMps` and `streakSec` were `private readonly`, so a weather state that changed under a player could not change the rain. Reported from outside by a consumer whose hailstorm — 14 m/s against rain's 9 — had to be expressed as a wider, denser rain and read as heavy rain. Both are plain fields, because nothing is sized by either and nothing caches a value derived from one. Driven by `demo/dev/lines.html`, whose roof has a gap in it and whose `?rainspeed=` is written every frame, so a field reading its speed once at construction draws the wrong streaks **A stroke can say it is light, 3.43.0**: `drawLines` takes a blend, so a glowing outline is one additive pass rather than two alpha-blended ones faking a halo. It is a blend and not a bolt mode, which `AGENTS.md` forbids — what separates a line from a bolt is the path, a bolt jitters because it is lightning, and an additive line still follows the path it was given and is still fogged. Pipeline state on WebGPU, so the additive arm is a second pipeline under its own key | Animation                             | **`@driftengine/animation`**: skeletons, clips sampled as a pure function of a caller-supplied time, poses as three flat arrays, blending and additive layers, a blend tree, a crossfading state machine, two-bone IK, morph targets, retargeting by joint name, **root motion**, and **spring secondary motion** — hair, a coat, an antenna or a chain, evaluated as a pure function of the time asked about rather than advanced, which is what lets a playhead scrub backwards through it. A ragdoll cannot answer that question and was refused in writing by the consumer who asked; a damped spring can, because it forgets, and `springSettleSec` is that forgetting written as a lookback. Each substep is solved in closed form rather than stepped, which is a measurement and not a taste: semi-implicit Euler needed about a thousand substeps a period to hold a hundredth of a four-thousand-step reference march, and the closed form holds 4.0e-4 at thirty-two. A chain remembers longer than any of its links, so `springChainSettleSec` solves the cascade’s own survival function for the lookback, and the whole chain marches on one grid because sampling links independently would cost `steps^depth` anchor calls. **A node of a tree may be sampled on a clock of its own**: `evaluate` walked every node with one time, so the canonical locomotion set — stand, walk, run over one speed parameter — could not be written as one tree, because a stride advances with _distance travelled_ or the foot slides while the body passes over it, while an idle advances with _time_, because somebody standing still is still breathing. A `clip` node names the parameter its own time comes from and the frame clock is what a node without one still gets, so every tree written before this is unchanged. A name is a weight or a time and never both, refused at construction. Reported from outside, where the workaround was two clocks kept by hand and a `blendPoses` per overlay. Driven by the character rig in `demo/dev`, whose gait clips now advance with a distance rather than a frame — 5,899 pixels on both backends, which agree with each other to 4. Skinning and morphing are vertex-shader permutations on both backends; glTF and `.drft` both carry a rig. **This table once had no Animation row at all**, because §2's Animation row grew into a description of what ships and nobody noticed §1 never gained one — the same failure as a sentinel guarding a row that was never written | Chemistry                             | **`@driftengine/chemistry`, CH-0 of Track P**: a closed set of fifteen elements with IUPAC conventional atomic weights, a species registry holding sixty-eight species whose **molar masses are derived from their formulas** rather than stored beside them, the dense species-by-element matrix with an allocation-free scaled-row reduction, `Composition` as mass fractions that must sum to one and are stored sorted by species index so two spellings of a material reduce bit-identically, and `elementTotals` — kilograms of species to moles of elements, into a caller-owned vector, allocating nothing. **A species carries a formation enthalpy and a heat capacity and nothing reads them yet**, which is the correct shape for a foundation: CH-3 derives every reaction's enthalpy from them by Hess's law, so they are checked _here_ instead, by reconstructing eighteen published higher heating values from the stored numbers and holding them to two percent. Pseudo-species — a lumped repeat unit, an average residue, a fuel surrogate — carry an enthalpy **back-derived from a measured heating value**, because nobody has put cellulose in a calorimeter but everybody has measured what a kilogram of it gives off. **CH-1 makes enthalpy the state variable and temperature a reading**: a curve per substance, built once and shared by every parcel made from it, whose **flat regions are the phase changes** — so a kilogram of ice and a kilogram of water at 273.15 K differ by 333,550 J and nothing branches on melting. The curve is exact at its knots, because `cp` is linear in `T` and the trapezoid rule integrates a linear integrand with no error; inverting it is a binary search and a lerp, with no transcendental, no iteration and nothing allocated. `boilingPoint` moves the plateau with pressure by Clausius-Clapeyron, so a stew at 3,000 m is pinned at 90 °C and cannot reach the 140 °C browning needs. `ParcelStore` is structure-of-arrays `Float64Array` columns and `addHeat` is one addition. **CH-2 gives a parcel depth**: nested shells of **equal mass**, so a large object's surface shell is thin and its core is fat, with heat entering shell 0 and conducting inward. The interface conductivity is the **harmonic mean**, because a boundary is a series resistance — measured at a factor of eleven against the arithmetic one where `k` depends on temperature, which is what a char blanket over wet wood will be. The integrator is explicit and sub-stepped **in enthalpy rather than temperature**, because an implicit solve inverts a heat capacity and a phase plateau's is infinite; it conserves a parcel's enthalpy **exactly whatever the step does**, since the same double leaves one shell and enters the next. What it buys is the fact a fire model cannot be wrong about: under 20 kW/m² a 2 mm slab's surface passes 300 °C in 29.2 s and an 80 mm one in 399.6 s — **sub-linear, because a thick slab is thermally thick** — and the 80 mm log's core sits five hundredths of a kelvin above the room while its surface chars. **CH-3 is the reaction network**: every reaction is checked against the element matrix at registration and one that does not balance is **refused naming the element and the size of the gap**, and every enthalpy is **derived by Hess's law** from CH-0's formation enthalpies rather than typed in — methane comes out at −802.6 kJ/mol to steam and −890.6 to liquid water, its published lower and higher heating values, with neither number written down anywhere. Rates are **tabulated at registration** so `exp` never runs on a tick, with knots uniform in `1/T` where `ln k` is exactly linear, measured under 0.5% against the closed form. The solver is **sub-stepped and clamped**: the step is sized from how much of the scarcest reactant a whole step would take, and where demands exceed what is present every reaction drawing on that species is cut **by the same factor** rather than first-come — proven order-independent by registering two competing reactions both ways round and comparing to twelve places. **Elements are conserved over 100,000 ticks** to a relative drift under 1e-12, which is what CH-0 built `elementTotals` for. **CH-4 is the air**: one sparse atmosphere of 8³-cell chunks where empty space costs nothing, carrying oxygen to a fire and smoke away from it. Transport is **flux-form and conservative** — a departure from the design, which chose semi-Lagrangian for its stability: semi-Lagrangian is not conservative, and conservation is what this whole track is asserted on, so upwind flux and a CFL limit handled by the same sub-stepping the reaction solver already uses. Wind comes from the one `WindField`; buoyancy comes from a cell's own lightness; a **blocked cell transports nothing at all**, including to the far field, so a sealed volume is genuinely closed; and a ledger books what crosses an open boundary, including the air a new chunk draws in. **Gas-phase combustion is not a second solver** — a cell is handed to the same `reactShell` a shell is, which is what lets a flame stand off a surface rather than sit on it. **A sealed room runs out of oxygen and the burning stops**, with unburnt fuel left over, because the rate of a reaction with no oxidiser is zero by mass action and nothing had to be told to stop. Reads a game acts on: oxygen fraction, ppm, pressure, density, temperature and visibility. **CH-5 joins the two.** `ChemistryWorld` runs §13's tick, and nothing in it applies a flux: a consumer declares what is radiating and what is touching what, and every parcel works out for itself what reaches it. Radiation is `εσF·A·(T⁴−T⁴)` through a point-source view factor, so **flux falls as 1/r²** — move a log twice as far from a fire and it takes four times as long, which is the one relationship the whole track is built on. A source's range comes from its own power, so a bonfire reaches further than a candle rather than sharing a constant. Convection takes its coefficient from the local gas speed and its heat **out of the cell** rather than from nowhere; contact conduction uses the same harmonic mean a shell boundary does. And a burning parcel **eats the oxygen around it and pushes its smoke into the air**, as one relaxation running both ways, with **enthalpy travelling with the mass**. The pair conserves every element to 1e-11 of the magnitudes involved. **CH-6's opening reversal retired the enthalpy curve.** `§3` built one per substance from its _initial_ composition, so the temperature drifted as reactions ran — about 20% of the rise for cellulose becoming char, which no ignition criterion could be allowed to read. The repair turned out smaller than the thing it repaired: **the latent heat is already in the formation enthalpies**, at 333,611 J/kg for ice against a literature 333,550, so a phase change is a **reaction with a temperature gate** and its plateau emerges from the substep-and-clamp solver rather than from a table. What is left is purely sensible heat, and inverting `h = A·ΔT + B·ΔT²/2` is closed form with **one square root** — one of the two operations ECMAScript specifies exactly. Composition-aware by construction, cheaper than the 256-knot search it replaced, and **231 bytes smaller**: the first time this entry point has gone down. **And ignition is a criterion rather than a flag**: five conditions decide it — surface temperature, volatile mass flux, oxygen above the limiting index, a flammable mixture _at the surface_, and a pilot for the lower of the two temperatures — so `ignite` supplies a pilot and **holding a match to wet wood does nothing**. Extinction is four: fuel gone, oxygen below the index, the surface cooled, or the flame blown off. A smoulder needs no flame and no pilot and survives to about 5% oxygen where a flame stops at 14%, which is why smothering a fire leaves embers. An event buffer of twenty-one kinds is drained per tick. **Char oxidation is transport-limited**, combining its kinetic rate with an oxygen-delivery ceiling as a series resistance, so char glows for an hour rather than vanishing in a minute and an ember brightens when it is blown on. **And `§21`'s log is asserted end to end**: seasoned oak in front of a campfire dries with its surface pinned at the boiling point and its core still at room temperature, then smokes, then catches — and **a green log at the same fire does not**, because steam leaving a wet surface dilutes the mixture above it. **CH-7 is the substance library, and it applies the payload rule to _data_ for the first time in this engine**: thirty-nine substances across **seven separate entry points** — organic, food, fuel, polymer, mineral, metal, biological — because a substance is forty numbers and a composition, so a consumer who wants a campfire imports one family for **953 bytes** rather than seven for five kilobytes, measured by a fixture per entry point against a baseline fixture that is the consumer who wrote three substances of their own. Nine species arrive with the families that need them rather than being carried by everyone. Every number is sourced or back-derived from a measurement, and the derived quantities are asserted against a _second, independent_ one wherever one exists: calcination comes out at +179.2 kJ/mol against a published +178.3, gypsum dehydration at +104.4 against +104, magnesium at 24.75 MJ/kg, aluminium at 31.05 and iron at 7.38 — all three published and none of them stored — aerobic respiration at −2,802.7 kJ/mol against `§8.6`'s quoted 2,803, and fermentation at −68.9 against a textbook −68. Wood tar's formation enthalpy is derived from bio-oil's heating value and levoglucosan's sublimation enthalpy, and the **third** measured quantity then falls out of it: the volatile branch's endotherm at +248 kJ/kg against `§8.3`'s +255. **Arthur's relation is reproduced rather than tabulated** — the two char oxidation paths' activation energies differ by `6240·R` and their pre-exponentials by 2500, so `CO/CO₂ = 2500·exp(−6240/T)` is their ratio identically, and a cool smoulder makes CO₂ where a hot one makes CO. What the library does that nothing in it decides: **a candle** is wax melting, then boiling, then burning, three gated reactions in series with the word appearing nowhere; **a steak cannot brown while it is wet**, because Maillard needs 140 °C and a wet surface is pinned at 100 by the vaporisation plateau, which makes every piece of received wisdom about searing a consequence rather than a rule; **PVC self-extinguishes in air and PMMA does not**, on one limiting oxygen index each; **a hay bale self-heats** out of the mesophilic band in 6.1 adiabatic hours and is picked up by the thermophiles above it; **a submerged parcel makes methane instead of carbon dioxide**, with no gate on either branch, because aerobic decay has oxygen as a reactant and mass action does the rest; and **burning leather gives off hydrogen cyanide**, because collagen carries 1.3 nitrogens per residue. One bias is stated rather than buried: pyrolysis endotherms derived over this species set run high, because the volatile slate stops at C₂ and char is pure carbon — the **total** heat is exact by Hess's law, so what the cap distorts is the split between the gasification and the flame, and it bites the polyolefins hardest and wood barely at all. Two refusals are recorded with their reversal conditions: **wool**, because keratin's sulfur has nowhere to go under pyrolysis in this species set, and **the humidity gate on rusting**, because `ReactionGates` is temperature only. Imports no other engine package, and nothing in core depends on it. **CH-9 is the presentation seam and the installer.** `present/` **imports nothing and names no core type**: every target is described structurally by what it must have, which is the `ragdollFromBones` arrangement, and core's `ParticleInstances` satisfies `SmokeTarget` exactly without either package knowing the other exists. Six mappings, each a physical quantity rather than an art direction — smoke colour from the soot-to-aerosol ratio, flame height from Heskestad's `L ≈ 0.235·Q^(2/5) − 1.02·D`, glow from Planck's law tabulated at three wavelengths, albedo lerped from a substance's own colour to its own char colour by char fraction, roughness from the free surface water, and a scale from the cube root of what is left of the volume — plus three audio scalars, and the package never touches `@driftengine/audio`. **Soot became a species rather than a channel**, so a rich flame blackens its own smoke _through the element ledger_, and with no gate on the equivalence ratio anywhere: soot formation needs no oxygen and oxidation needs plenty, so a rich cell soots and a lean one does not out of mass action. `installChemistry` is three lines with everything after `libraries` optional, matching materials **exactly and reporting what it could not** — `AGENTS.md`'s retargeting decision, and the failure here is worse than a limb that does not move, because a `pine_bark_02` silently matching `pine` is a material with the wrong ignition temperature nobody will notice. A **`SUBS` chunk at container 1.8** pairs material ordinals with substance ids and the baker writes it from a glTF material's `extras.substance`, so an artist labels the oak in Blender and the log burns like oak. `demo/dev/chemistry.html` is `§24`'s hearth and is the track's exit test: the kettle sits at 99 °C, the green log at 100, the ice core at −1, the iron nail reaches 611 °C where the copper coin beside it reaches 75, and the panel reports element drift at **2.6e-10** over the run. **It found two real bugs**, which is what a demo is for: conduction's sub-step cap let a thin, highly conductive parcel ring to 4,000 K and back to 100 with energy conserved the whole way — conservation is not enough when an ignition criterion reads a surface temperature — now clamped at the point a pair would be equal; and the panel's own drift measure divided noise by a near-cancelled net. **Both backends free**, and checked rather than assumed: nothing in `present/` is a shader. **CH-10 closes `§14`, which three phases stood over.** Four level-of-detail tiers — `Hero` at the resolution the substance declared down to one shell every sixteenth tick at `Distant` — and **every tier conserves exactly**: shells are equal-mass by construction, so a fold is a proportional redistribution and mass, every element and enthalpy come through a tier change unchanged, which is what makes one safe to apply mid-burn. What a tier costs is measured rather than asserted: over five hundred seconds of fire `Near` is exact, `Far` drifts 21% and `Distant` 43%, and the coarser tiers char **more**, because a lumped parcel has no cold core to hide behind. **Sleeping**: a parcel still for thirty ticks is skipped, and wakes on heat, water, mass, a contact or a fire coming within range — the last through a coarse scan spread round-robin over four ticks, so a thousand sleepers cost two hundred and fifty range comparisons a tick. A **cadence** integrates the same seconds less often, which is conserving for free. And **`fingerprintChemistry`** — sixteen hexadecimal digits over parcel compositions, enthalpies, the field's elements and the substance registry, order-insensitive over parcels because a handle _is_ spawn order, and covering the registry because two libraries are two worlds. Two logs in different chunks realise them in spawn order, and every walk of the chunk list was then in allocation order — history rather than geometry. The consequence was not confined to the hash, because `sweep` accumulates every face into shared deltas with `+=` and floating-point addition is not associative: measured, two logs eight metres apart spawned the other way round left **1,202 cells differing** after sixty ticks, in their last bit, feeding a stiff exponential rate law. It goes first in every conditions object and needs `customConditions` in the root tsconfig, which is one decision written in two files. **Three defects were found by measuring rather than reasoning.** A devDependency is not a build edge — `drft` declares one on core for a test and core depends on `drft`, so counting it made a cycle out of an acyclic graph and the first build refused to run at all. And **`dist/` is in `.gitignore`, which npm honours**, so every tarball shipped zero built files — the row would have passed every local check and delivered nothing, which is exactly what `npm run cleanroom` exists to catch: it packs, extracts into a real `node_modules` outside the checkout, and imports **25 entry points under plain node**. Nothing is published; these packages stay private, and what changed is that a `file:` consumer can now load them from Node. — `@driftengine/package`, **2.11.0**: a game becomes an installable application through `drift-package`. the person's own browser. **Android ships an APK** around the system WebView, measured on a device: an https origin so it is a secure context, the same bridge injected before the game's own scripts, | Scripting                             | **DriftScript**, an optional strict language for consumer-authored behaviour. `.drs` compiles at the consumer's bundler boundary to JavaScript ESM with source maps, loaded through a runtime that hot-patches a function body while the state it operates on stays alive. Strict types with no implicit null, `Result` and options, `match` with exhaustiveness, defined integer overflow, and units erased to nothing at compile time. Effects are inferred from capability calls and `@deterministic` is checked against the boundary `AGENTS.md` already draws. A `.drs` file may **import another `.drs` file** — a relative specifier is a file, anything else is a capability — and a `data` record may **extend another**, inheriting its fields base-most first and standing in for it wherever it is expected. Module cycles are allowed and inheritance cycles are refused; a capability required through an imported file is refused naming that file. A TextMate grammar generated from the compiler's token table, and a language server whose diagnostics are the build's, resolving imports through open documents so an unsaved edit in one file is what the next file is checked against. **It lives in `driftscript`, which imports no `@driftengine/*` at all** — three mechanisms assert it — and `@driftengine/script` is the only place the two are coupled **Pinned at `driftscript` 1.5.0**, which gave `std/math` and `std/time` a `float` type that does not fix a width — `f32` or `f64`, the same one throughout a call — and the `f32.nearest`/`f64.nearest` conversions a float had never had. Nothing in `drift/*` changed shape: every capability this engine declares is written `f32` and is accepted unchanged, and the bindings go on rounding to single, which the language's own note to hosts Five spellings were compiled against the real registry and every one failed. It came in on the condition `navigation.ts` had itself written down: a route is a function of the graph and two endpoints, `navSearch.ts` breaks ties on the node index so two runs agree, and the `NavPath` written into is simulation state. All three navigation writers are deterministic now. The language had `enum` and `match`'s exhaustiveness all along — its own corpus advertises refusing to compile until every state is handled — and what refused was this engine's component store, so the corpus keeps its `Alertness` in a `data` record, which is not what a system iterates, and a consumer shipped `i32` with three numbers in a comment. `Int32Array` and not a byte: `defineComponent` is | Graph canvas                          | **One editor over three node vocabularies, in `editor/src/graph/`** — `model.ts`, `commands.ts`, `view.ts`, `layout.ts`. Nodes and links with a cycle refused by name and by node; every edit a command, including a node drag, which merges into one undo entry; a canvas that pans and zooms about the pointer. **The hit test is handed no view at all.** `buildGraphGeometry` turns graph space into screen space once, into arrays, and both the draw and the hit test read those arrays — because the commonest defect in a graph editor is a hit test that disagrees with the draw about the pan or the zoom, and the only way to prevent it for good is to leave no second place that could apply a transform. Links are polylines rather than `UiNode`s: a cubic curve is not an axis-aligned box, so they are tessellated once and `strokeGraphLinks` turns the same points into rotated quads through `drawSprite`. Automatic arrangement reads the graph and never the current positions, so tidying is not path-dependent, and it places the nodes on a cycle one column past the rest rather than dropping the broken part of a broken graph. | Behaviour graphs                      | **Emits DriftScript source, and DriftScript's own compiler is what judges it.** The graph gets no semantics, no effect analysis and no hot reload of its own, which is what makes a graph and hand-written code the same artefact and lets a project mix them. `reads` and `writes` come from declaration nodes and nothing derives them from the write nodes — so a graph **can** write a component it never declared, and the real compiler refuses it with DS0288 in the words a person hand-writing that file would get. Deriving them would make the mistake unreachable and put the effect check in two places. The vocabulary is built from the project's components rather than written down here, so a renamed component fails validation by name. There is no `dt` node: a system's `update` body has none, measured as DS0205 against the real compiler. | Play in editor                        | **Press play, press stop, and the scene is exactly as it was** — the oldest defect an editor has, and the one every engine has shipped at some point. `editor/src/pie/session.ts` captures the world before the first step and restores it on stop, checked by a digest of the whole world rather than a spot check of a few fields. The world reaches it through `Snapshotter`, which is the engine's own seam, so nothing here knows what a world is. | Hierarchical detail, baked            | **A distant block of a city is one coarse mesh, and a distant tree is its own picture.** `assets/src/bake/hlod.ts` builds both offline. The proxy is not a new mesh merger — `coarseLevel.ts` already emits the boundary of an occupancy grid rather than decimating a surface, which is what stops a merge growing triangles through a car's bodywork — so what is new is the grouping and the level schedule. **A proxy can be refused**, and that is the honest half: a grid-based merge cannot promise fewer triangles than its input, because its output scales with surface area rather than with triangle count, so the half-budget is checked and a group already cheap gets `null` instead of something larger than what it replaced. The impostor's hard part is its edges: colour is dilated past the silhouette and every tile carries a two-texel gutter, because a transparent texel left at the clear colour is what makes a distant tree glow at its atlas seams. Measured on a tree at eight directions a side: **1.0000 silhouette agreement on a baked direction and 0.9083 between two**, since the blend carries no parallax correction and the fix costs the square of the direction count. | Terrain that is GPU-driven            | **Which squares of the field to draw, at what detail, as one decision per patch.** `terrain/src/clipmap.ts` takes a camera and a patch index and answers — reading the frame and nothing else, which is what lets it move into a compute pass beside the cluster cut rather than be rewritten there. Each level's block snaps to an **even** patch index, which is the whole of why the levels nest: an even multiple of a level's patch span is a multiple of the next level's, so a finer block's edge always falls on a coarser patch boundary and a coarse patch is covered entirely or not at all. **The hole a finer level leaves is not fixed at the centre**, which looks wrong and is right: levels re-centre at different moments, so culling by coverage rather than by a central hole is what removes the need for the L-shaped strip the usual implementation carries. Asserted by counting: **65,536 field cells drawn, exactly, at every one of thirty-three camera positions across a coarse patch** — an area equal to the footprint with no cell counted twice is no overlap and no hole, together. It builds no geometry; `heightfieldPatch` does, and matches the seam it always did. | Terrain heights as a texture          | **A heightfield is a `DTEX` layer, and collision reads the decoded numbers rather than the source ones.** `terrain/src/terrainTexture.ts` stores heights as a decode program over a latent, so terrain inherits the format's residency, streaming and determinism instead of growing an image path of its own. **The plan had the requirement backwards**: it asked that decoded heights match the source within the format's tolerance, which they do and which is not enough — a renderer reading the layer while a query reads the source differ by exactly that tolerance, everywhere, permanently, and a character floating by a fraction of a millimetre on every surface in the world is a defect nobody attributes. So `terrainFromHeightLayer` builds the `Terrain` from the **decoded** samples and everything reads that one object. The tolerance is half a quantisation step **plus one float32 step of the range**, because the normalised value is itself stored as a float32 and the decode multiplies that error back up: measured 4.6372e-5 against a half-step of 4.6314e-5. Splat weights decode renormalised, since four weights rounded to eight bits sum to between 0.994 and 1.006 and a shader that trusts the sum shades a whole hillside wrong, smoothly enough to read as lighting. | A world bigger than a float           | **The simulation never rebases; rendering does.** `core/src/world/` holds a sparse cell grid, a render origin that follows the camera in whole cells, and the rule that keeps them apart: simulation coordinates stay absolute and double, because a rebase would change floating-point results and therefore the replay fingerprint — only in sessions that crossed an origin boundary, which is a divergence nobody reproduces on demand. The origin moves in **whole cells**, since a continuously-moving one re-quantises every vertex every frame and the world shimmers: measured over a two-hundred-and-twenty-tick walk at the far end of the world, it moves **75 times rather than 220**. A round trip through render space costs an ulp of a number under five hundred and **does not grow with distance**, where the same coordinate put into single precision is wrong by **exactly one metre** at 2²⁴–2²⁵, because single precision counts in twos there and a position on a half-metre is a whole metre from anything it can hold. **Cells stream by where the camera will look, not only by where it will be**: given the projection its predicted views are drawn through, a stream wants the cells round the camera and then every cell those views look into, nearest first. `cellsInFrustum` walks the box round a view's corners in double precision and keeps a cell unless it lies wholly beyond one plane — 33,554 km out, it tells a sliver a tenth of a metre inside the view from one a tenth outside, which planes held in single precision keep both of. | A streamed region that did not drift  | **Freezing is a simulation decision and unloading is a memory one**, and `core/src/world/freeze.ts` keeps them apart on purpose. A cell outside the simulated radius freezes whether or not its contents are resident, and only a frozen cell may be unloaded — so streaming can change where the bytes live and never what the simulation computes. The alternative, unloading causing freezing, makes the simulation depend on how much memory a machine had: a divergence that appears on one player's computer and nowhere else. **A frozen cell still contributes to the fingerprint**, from a digest taken when it froze, because a run that agrees only once everything has thawed is a run that disagreed for a while — and in a rollback session those numbers were already sent. **What it costs is stated rather than discovered**: an agent in an unloaded cell does not walk anywhere, does not age and does not finish what it was doing. `seam.test.ts` walks a world at six magnitudes and asserts the streamed fingerprint against a run holding every cell — and asserts that the forbidden arrangement diverges, so the gate cannot pass vacuously. | A navigation mesh                     | **`@driftengine/nav` ships, 8,401 bytes gzipped, and it reverses a refusal that named its own trigger.** `core/src/nav/navGraph.ts` states that it is a graph rather than a mesh, that this is a decision rather than a first step, and that a mesh is _the row that is still open_ if a world's walkable space is genuinely a region — and a streamed open world is that world. Geometry becomes a walkable voxel field (two layers under an overhang, which is why it is voxels and not a heightfield), a watershed partition, contours checked for self-intersection rather than assumed simple, and convex polygons whose adjacency is symmetric — a one-directional build makes paths work in one direction only and nothing says so. **One A\* in the repository**: the query builds a `NavGraph` and hands it to core's existing `NavSearch`, then funnels, so open ground is a straight line and not a walk along polygon centres. The graph is not replaced; it stays right for roads, corridors and docking lanes. **Two limitations ship with a test pinning each**: a region with a free-standing pillar loses the inner loop, so an agent walks through the pillar, and the funnel gives the shortest path through the corridor A\* chose — 10.75 against an ideal 9.81 on one wall. **Steering is still refused**, which is the line the reversal did not cross: a path is a function of geometry and an engine can own one; how a character moves along it is a game's feel. | Gizmo drags as commands               | **A drag is one undo entry, and an edge-on plane does not fling the object.** `editor/src/viewport/gizmo.ts` turns a handle drag into `Command`s the undo stack merges. The arithmetic is the editor's rather than core's, and the reason is a conditioning number: core translates by the closest point between the ray and the axis line, which is right and refuses only within `1e-6` of parallel — between that cutoff and a comfortable angle the answer divides by the squared sine, so **two degrees off the axis multiplies a pixel of mouse noise by 820**. Here a drag is computed against a plane containing the axis, **chosen per drag as the one whose normal most faces the camera**: the two candidates are orthogonal, so the conditioning is never worse than **√2**, where a fixed choice reaches a billion four times a turn. **What no plane fixes is an axis pointing at the camera** — every plane containing it is edge-on — so the drag is refused rather than invented, and hiding the handle stays the viewport's decision. Commands carry **absolute positions rather than a delta**, which is what makes the `merge` contract's trap harmless here: applying an absorbed command twice writes the same position twice. A delta-based one would move the object twice as far as the pointer and read as a sensitivity bug. | The editor opens                      | **`npm run editor` and it is there**: a menu bar, a viewport, three docked panel slots, selection by picking, delete, undo, redo, select-all and a command palette. Driven in a real browser rather than described — click selects, `Delete` removes and records an entry, `Ctrl+Z` puts it back, `Ctrl+K` opens the palette. **The three panels are empty on purpose**; they are Wave 3C's, and the shell exists first so each panel is written against a command stack that already refuses to let it touch the world. `shell.ts` is the product and `app.ts` stays the general shell, which is a deviation from the plan and the right one: assembling a product into `app.ts` would make the reusable thing depend on a selection model. **What it does not do is in `editor/README.md` rather than left to be found** — the viewport is drawn by a 2D context so the product opens before the engine's pass is wired to it, the gizmo is tested but nothing paints its arms, and nobody who did not write it has used it, which is the one step of Wave 2C a test cannot replace. | `DTEX`, the chunk                     | **A material in the container as a decode program over a latent, rather than as pictures.** `drft/src/dtex.ts` carries the latent grid, the channel specs, the graph's nodes, a small network's shape and weights, and a tile table with a **content hash** per tile so two identical tiles share one payload. **The chunk carries no semantics**: `@driftengine/drft` has no dependencies and does not know what an operation means, so the types are plain arrays that `@driftengine/texture`'s satisfy structurally — the arrangement `Terrain` already has with `Heightfield` across the physics boundary, and the register count is guarded by a test that imports the interpreter's own constant through a devDependency. **It validates containment, not meaning**: a tile whose bytes run past the payload and a result register no node writes are refused, because those hand a reader arbitrary memory or an uninitialised value. Those guards are unreachable through the writer, so the tests corrupt a written chunk to reach them. **No per-chunk version**, which is where it departs from the plan — the file's version covers the format and a second one is a second thing to keep in step. **Additive**, so an older reader skips it by its length and loses only the material it could not have decoded. | A texture cannot move the simulation  | **Asserted rather than left true by construction.** A run sampling an animated `DTEX` every tick fingerprints identically to a run sampling nothing, and the same simulation run twice at different wall-clock times fingerprints identically — because `t` is the caller's, from the simulation's clock. **And a run that reads a wall clock instead is asserted to diverge**, without which the first two pass for a decoder that reads a clock nobody noticed. The clock is injected now and the separation is chosen rather than measured. | The script editor                     | **DriftScript is edited against the language server that already exists, not a second language implementation.** `editor/src/panels/script.ts` is a text view, a diagnostic gutter and a completion popup; every rule about what the language means stays with the compiler, which is the same line the behaviour-graph editor holds and for the same reason. **It works with no client at all** — a headless build has none and a test has none, so it is a text view before it is anything else. **The server's view of the buffer lags it by a message**, so a diagnostic arrives describing text already deleted every time somebody types quickly: ranges are clamped, and one entirely past the end collapses to an empty mark at the end rather than disappearing, because the server has something to say and dropping it loses the only sign that it did. **Nothing awaits the server**: a change notification goes out and the buffer is already updated, and a completion reply that arrives after a dismissal is dropped rather than reopening a popup over text somebody went back to typing. | DriftCapture stage one: geometry      | **A clip becomes a surface, on the device, with no service.** `@driftengine/capture` takes a `FrameSource` — a video element in a browser, ffmpeg on the native host — chooses frames, runs Depth Anything 3 Small for poses, depth, intrinsics and a confidence together, fuses the views into a truncated signed-distance volume, marches it and decimates the result. **Maturity: it reconstructs what a clip saw from where the clip saw it, and nothing more.** Measured 2026-09-20 on an RX 9070 XT, six frames of a 1,401-frame 1080p handheld clip: 7.2 s in the browser and 9.05 s on the native host, of which 3.6 s and 5.5 s are loading the weights. | DriftCapture stage three: materials   | **`delight` separates what a surface reflects from the light it was photographed under**, by the median of several views for a highlight and by chromaticity for a shadow. **Maturity: it recovers colour and says how much it trusts it, and on ordinary footage that is not much.** Measured on the same clips: a mean confidence of **0.276** on a wooden table and **0.249** on a room, which is the stage reporting the case its own header names as where it fails — a grey object on a grey floor, with no chromaticity to tell shading from paint. **It cannot remove a cast shadow**, because a shadowed point is shadowed from every camera and agreement is not evidence of albedo. It is also the most expensive stage in the pipeline by thirty times: **44 s over 16,670 triangles and 179 s over 33,060**, ray-casting each vertex against every triangle with no acceleration structure. Colour is per vertex, so its detail ceiling is the mesh rather than the footage | A compute shader can be tested        | **`packages/core/scripts/gpuCompute.mjs` runs WGSL on a real device and reads the buffers back**, which is what lets the GPU-driven pipeline's arithmetic have a test at all. Every pass there is written twice — once in TypeScript as the reference and once in WGSL — and until this existed the WGSL half had nothing but a generator check that confirms a committed file matches its source, which says nothing about whether the arithmetic is right. **It serves its own page from a loopback server**, because `navigator.gpu` is not exposed on `about:blank` and `http://localhost` is a secure context; there is no dev server to start first. `scripts/gpu-parity.mjs` runs three passes over generated input and requires agreement: **256 spheres with 149 culled, 256 clusters with 58 selected, and a 37×21 depth pyramid reduced to 18×10** — an odd size on purpose, because the extra row and column are what a reduction gets wrong. Both answers must occur in each case, or the agreement is between two constants. The check was audited by breaking the WGSL five ways — the reversed-Z minimum, the conservative direction of the cull, the second half of the cut rule, the plane normalisation, and the odd-row fold — and it caught all five. | **Recorded sessions** | **A timeline lives in memory and dies with the process.** Everything a bug report would need is already there — the keyframes, the input, a fingerprint a frame — and nothing writes them to a file, so a tester who reproduces something cannot hand it over. It is the obvious next thing and Wave 5B deliberately did not build it: a session on disk is a _format_, and this repository's rule for a format is that it is designed once and then frozen. The sentinel is `writeSessionRecording`.
