                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Animation**         | **Clips and skeletons ship in `@driftengine/animation`**, and nothing draws with them yet. `Skeleton` resolves a `Pose` — three flat arrays, not an array of objects — into a skinning palette written in place, and refuses a hierarchy that is not sorted parents-first rather than producing a rig wrong in one limb. **Skinned shadow casting shipped** and is the one capability this row lost without the sentinel noticing; see §5. `sampleClip` is **a pure function of a time the caller supplies**: no clock, no `Math.random`, wrapping rather than clamping and correct for a negative time, holding at a track's ends rather than extrapolating, and taking the shorter arc between two rotations on opposite hemispheres. That last one is asserted by a test that had to be rewritten to assert it — the obvious pair of keys has a dot product of exactly zero, so the hemisphere flip never fires and the first version passed with the correction deleted. **Rigid TRS ships too**: `RigidAnimation` drives `SceneNode`s from a clip, so a door, a lift or a turntable animates with no shader change at all — and it calls `markMoved`, without which a node moves on the first frame and freezes on the second, because a fresh node is dirty already and nothing marks one that was written in place. **The skinned vertex shader is built and generated, and nothing selects it yet.** `MeshData` carries `joints` and `weights` as two more optional attributes at locations 11 and 12, `setSkinPalette` uploads a palette into a vertex data texture on both backends, and `flatVert` is a two-variant permutation whose skinned arm reads that palette with an integer fetch. **A permutation and not a uniform gate, measured: 1,118 bytes gzipped against the 246,925 one more fragment flag costs**, because the vertex shader had no permutation axis at all and two 4.4 KB strings mostly dedupe inside deflate's 32 KB window — so the 2^n rule in `ARCHITECTURE.md` §1 is a fact about the fragment corpus rather than about permutation. **Both backends select it per draw**: a rigged mesh takes the skinned pipeline and an unrigged one does not, so a scene holding characters and walls draws both correctly. WebGL2 compiles a second flat program lazily on the first rigged mesh and feeds it the whole frame's lit state — a uniform location belongs to a program, and an unwritten uniform is zero, which is the failure this engine has recorded twice; WebGPU carries the flag through the pipeline key, the bind group layout and the bind group together, because a skinned module against an unskinned layout validates, draws and is wrong. **Every published scene is 0 pixels of 921,600 on WebGPU, all seven**, against a before-and-after pair captured from two servers in one run. **Driven and compared**: `demo/dev/skinning.html` bends a two-joint bar beside an unrigged control, and rest against bent moves **22,608 pixels of 832,000 on both backends**, which agree **to the pixel** at either phase. The palette takes texture unit 11 and not 0 — `MAX_VERTEX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS` and `MAX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS` bound the two stages separately but do not number their units apart, so a palette at unit 0 lands on the directional shadow map and the driver answers `two textures of different types use the same sampler location`. Found on hardware on the first capture, which is what a capture is for; WebGPU never had it, its bindings being per bind group. **glTF imports a rig**: `readGltfSkins` reads skins and animations, sorts joints parents-first — which only the importer can do, since every index naming a joint has to move with them — and remaps a mesh's `JOINTS_0` and every animation channel onto that order. **Flattening stays the default and a skin is the one exception**: a skinned primitive keeps its vertices in model space, because a palette entry already places them and baking the node's world matrix in as well throws the rig across the scene. A document with no `skins` takes the path it always took. Weights are normalised on the way in, warning per mesh, rather than divided per vertex per frame; a vertex carrying no weight at all is left alone and reported, because inventing an influence would move geometry nobody rigged. **The container carries a rig at 1.6**: `SKIN` holds joints, parents and inverse binds; `ANIM` holds a clip per chunk; and **`NODE` is finally written** — specified in `FORMAT.md` §4.3 since v1, with no writer and no reader for the whole of it, until rigid TRS needed a hierarchy. All three are optional, so a 1.5 reader opens a 1.6 file as the geometry it also holds, which is rule 2 doing its job; §4.4's own example of a free additive change was a file carrying `ANIM`, and it stopped being hypothetical. The skin is written parents-first and the **reader** refuses any other order, because a palette is resolved in index order. **End to end**: `bake` writes the rig a glTF carried, `streamDrft` reports `onNodes`, `onSkin` and `onClip` as their chunks land, and `DrftLoader` hands all three on. That last one is asserted rather than assumed — the normal-map texture index was written, carried and readable for a whole release while the loader was the single layer that discarded it, invisible to every test of either side because both sides were correct. **And it carried half of one until 1.11.** `SKIN` was correct from the day it shipped and the _per-vertex_ half it points at was never written at all: `MeshData` declared `joints` and `weights` and `validateMeshData` checked both — four floats a vertex, and neither without the other — while `buildMesh` listed the optional arrays it had bits for and there were none for these. **The write succeeded in silence**, which is the whole of why it survived four minor versions: a baker handed the writer a correctly-validated skinned mesh, got no error, and produced a file carrying a skeleton, its bind pose and its clips pointing at vertices that recorded no influence on any of them — and `Mesh.isSkinned` reads `data.joints`, so what came back drew in bind pose for ever. A consumer wrote its own binary container for one human body rather than use this, about seventy lines across a baker and a loader. Every other layer was already right: the glTF reader reads `JOINTS_0` and `WEIGHTS_0`, the weld's attribute table carries them, and both backends upload them at attributes 11 and 12. `ATTR_JOINTS` and `ATTR_WEIGHTS` are the next two free bits, appended last, so a 1.10 reader meets the seven arrays it knows in the seven places it expects them and draws the asset in bind pose. **The round-trip test that should have caught it was right and its fixture was not**: it enumerates the keys of the mesh it builds and reports every loss at once — the method `relief` bought — and the mesh it built carried no influences, so there was nothing to enumerate. The fixture carries them now. **And `.fbx` carries a rig too, which is the format most of them arrive in.** `readModel` documented `skins` and `clips` as "glTF does; nothing else here does", and FBX is how characters are _sold_ — it is the only thing Mixamo exports — so the one format a bought character comes in was the one a rig could not be read from. A Renderpeople figure measured through this reader gave a bag of triangles with no skeleton, no weights and no clip; the same file converted to glTF first gave 88 joints and a 64-track take. **The bind pose is the bone's transform undone and the mesh's applied**, and where each half comes from is what 3.40.0 got wrong and a later release corrected. A cluster carries `TransformLink`, where the bone was when the mesh was bound, and `Transform`, which the SDK documents as where the _mesh_ was — so `inverseBind` looks like the inverse of the first times the second. **Exporters do not write that field that way.** `Transform` is a property of the mesh and would be one matrix for the whole skin; measured on a bought character, **sixty-eight of its sixty-nine weight-bearing clusters disagree about it**, each holding something close to the inverse of its own `TransformLink`. Composed as documented, the bone's frame goes in twice: that character's hip came back as a pure translation of `(0, -94.4, +94.4)` where the joint is at `(0, 94.4, 0)`, so inverting it put every joint on a mirror of the skeleton that no geometry occupies, and one hand landed on the origin, which no bind pose contains. The mesh's half is taken from the node graph instead — the one authority this reader already has for where anything is, and the same walk every static mesh goes through. **The check that finds this is worth keeping**: invert a joint's bind matrix, take the translation, and compare it against the centroid of the vertices that joint dominates. On a correct rig they agree within a limb's own length; here they disagreed by up to 1.77 m, and afterwards by at most 0.35 m, which is a femur. **A bone names its cluster and its parent bone, and only one of those is hierarchy**: the transform walk took whichever the exporter wrote first, and a cluster is not a model, so a prop parented to a hand drew as though the hand were a root. Weights are normalised on the way in and a vertex held by more than four joints keeps its four _largest_, both said once per mesh. **Rotations are the chain and not the curve**: FBX composes a joint's local rotation as `PreRotation * R * inverse(PostRotation)`, both of the outer terms fixed per joint and written on the model rather than in the curve, so a reader taking the curve alone plays a take in which every joint carrying one is turned by a constant amount — **twenty-nine of this character's eighty-eight**. Every key still interpolates and the clip still runs, which is why it reads as a bad export rather than as an unread field. A non-default `RotationOrder` is the one part of the chain still refused by name. **And a binary FBX separates a name from its class with `\0\x01`, not with `::`** — the ASCII form's separator is the one a reader tends to be written against, because it is the one the specification's examples show, so every joint came back as `…_spine_01\0\x01Model` and the take as `Take 001\0\x01AnimStack`. Nothing fails on a name: `Joint.name` is what retargeting matches on, so a rig whose every joint carries a class suffix matches nothing, one subsystem away from the reader that wrote it. Both were found on real bytes, which is what real bytes are for. **And the geometry stopped arriving five times over.** The reader wrote `indices[i] = i` across every corner it had fanned, so a bought character came back at 64,518 vertices where its own file describes 12,216 — the baker welds, so a baked asset never showed it and anything calling `readModel` directly carried all of it. Deduplicating on the layer _offsets_ is the cheap answer and shares almost nothing, because an exporter writing `ByPolygonVertex` `Direct` gives every corner its own offset into repeated values: measured on a rigged car, 1,958,002 vertices of 1,958,016 corners, fourteen shared out of two million. Keyed on the values instead, bucketed by control point, the same car is **388,362** and the three FBX files in this repository come down by 4.2 to 5.0 times — and the read is **three and a half times faster**, 827 ms against 2,952 ms, because the allocations went with the duplicates. What is still absent: materials and textures are unchanged, morph channels driven by curves are not read, only the first animation layer of a stack is, and the `Take` records of pre-7000 files are not. **Measured on the character it was written for**, a 24.6 MB Renderpeople figure at version 7300: 12,216 vertices and 21,506 triangles — the same vertex count the file gives through a glTF conversion — 88 joints named and sorted parents-first with no joint naming a parent after it, a 176-track take of 2.267 s, every joint index in range, no vertex left unweighted, and weights summing to one within 4.5e-8. Baked to `.drft` 1.11 and read back it is the same asset, and the engine's own `Skeleton` accepts the rig and resolves an identity palette at the bind pose to 2.7e-5 over the whole 88-joint chain. **That last figure is not evidence of much, and saying so is the point**: it derives the pose from the inverse binds themselves, so it was equally green while those matrices put every joint on a mirror of the skeleton. What caught that was comparing them against the geometry, which is a different question and the only one that could have. **Units are read too**: `GlobalSettings.UnitScaleFactor` counts centimetres per file unit, so `unitScale` is that over a hundred, and a consumer scaling a bought character no longer divides by a measured height, which is a guess dressed as arithmetic and is wrong for anything that is not a standing human. **The two rig-specific exports that ship beside it are not a reader fault**: `_ue4.fbx` and `_u3d.fbx` carry 95 and 88 `LimbNode`s with their curves and **no `Geometry` records at all**, so they are animation-only files and the refusal was correct — it just could not say so, and now it counts what it found and names which of the three shapes of nothing it met. `fbxHarness.ts` writes the binary records a test needs, because the files that would prove this on real bytes are licensed character assets that cannot be committed here. **The graph over clips ships**: `blendPoses` and `addPose` — additive being a _delta_ rather than a target, so translation adds, rotation composes and scale multiplies — `BlendTree` over a two-way lerp and a one-dimensional set, and `AnimationStateMachine` with crossfaded transitions. **Both take a bind pose**, and that is not optional in practice: `sampleClip` leaves a channel no track mentions as it found it, so a rotation-only clip preserves the pose it was given — but `blendPoses` interpolates _every_ channel, so a tree whose scratch poses start at zero translation collapses every joint onto its parent's origin the moment it blends anything. The failure is a figure folded in on itself rather than an error, and it was found by building `demo/character.ts` on the API and looking at the result. Every layer is a pure function of a caller-supplied step: a state machine is where an engine most naturally reaches for a clock, because a fade has a duration, and one here would end the replay story. Parameters are the consumer's own strings throughout. A fade in flight is not re-evaluated against the condition that started it, or a transition would stutter wherever its parameter sat on the threshold. `setJoint` writes a joint directly, which is what Track B's ragdolls need from a pose. **Two-bone IK ships**: `solveTwoBone` is closed form rather than iterative, because two bones and a target are a triangle and a triangle has an answer — and a solver whose result depended on how many iterations were run is a solver a replay cannot use. An unreachable target straightens the chain toward it, which is what a limb does. **The order is the non-obvious part**: the mid joint is bent first, because rotating the root turns its whole subtree and so changes where the chain points and never how long it is — bending the root first leaves the tip on the right ray at the wrong distance, measured as 1.22 units where 1.00 was wanted. The pole hint then decides the one thing the target cannot, which way the elbow faces, and it is applied as a roll about the line to the target after aiming. `Skeleton.world` is public for solvers and attachments, since a palette entry is a world matrix times an inverse bind and is useless to anything asking where a joint _is_. **Morph targets ship on both backends**: deltas belong to the _mesh_ and weights to the _draw_, so two characters sharing one head mesh wear different expressions without a second copy of the geometry. They ride the vertex data texture the joint palette established — which is why the row was affordable, since eleven attribute locations were already spoken for and glTF morph wants up to twenty-four more. **Morph is applied before skinning**, because a target deforms the bind pose and the skeleton then carries that shape; the other order makes an expression drift as a limb moves. Measured on hardware: the bulge moves **16,733 pixels of 832,000 on both backends**, which agree to the pixel with morph on and off. **And they import**: glTF's targets are read and transposed to be interleaved by vertex, which is a transpose of how glTF stores them — one accessor per target there, all of a vertex's targets adjacent here, because the shader fetches them together. A file with more than eight keeps eight and says which it dropped, since a facial rig routinely carries dozens and refusing it serves nobody. The container carries them as **`MORP` at 1.7**, and the mesh ordinal is in the payload rather than the chunk table's `index` — that field is the ordinal _within a FourCC_, so for a file where only the second mesh has targets a reader pairing by it would deform the first. What is absent: **morphed normals** — positions only, so shading lags a strongly morphed surface — **Retargeting ships**: match by name, transfer rotations, and leave the target rig its own bone lengths — two rigs of different proportions share joint _orientations_ and not lengths, so copying a translation puts the taller one's limbs inside its own body. The root is the exception, because that is where locomotion lives. Matching is **exact and there is no name database**, for the reason the gamepad layer ships none: a table of synonyms rots silently and its failure is a limb that does not move. Unmatched joints are _reported_ rather than acted on, since whether one is a broken import or a simpler rig is a product decision. What is absent: **no joint limits, no twist, no chains longer than two bones, and no retargeting between different topologies** — a split spine playing a single-spine clip needs a decision about distributing the rotation, and that belongs to whoever knows what the character is. **Root motion ships**: `extractRootMotion` answers how far the root travelled between two sample times and `stripRootMotion` pins the pose's root to the clip's value at time zero, so the caller moves the character and the pose does not. **Loops are accumulated rather than subtracted**, which is the whole difficulty and the thing a naive version gets wrong invisibly: sampling the root at both times and subtracting answers a full stride _backwards_ every time the clip wraps, because the root snaps from the end of the cycle to the start of it. So the interval is split at every loop boundary it crosses and the pieces composed — asserted by a test whose expected value is +2 where the subtraction answers −2. **The delta is in the root's own frame at the earlier time**, so a caller applies `position += worldRotation * delta` and a character that has turned walks along its own forward axis; the rejected convention is a delta in the clip's space, one subtraction shorter, which drags every turned character sideways. That choice is asserted by a clip whose root faces ninety degrees about Y, where the two conventions answer `(0, 0, 2)` and `(2, 0, 0)` and nothing else in the suite can tell them apart. It stays a pure function of the clip and two times, reads no clock, and writes into a caller-owned target; the interpolation is `sampleTrack`, split out of `sampleClip` in the same commit so root motion reads the same decision rather than a second copy of it. What it gives up: **a vertical bob authored on the root leaves the pose along with everything else**, so a caller whose height is owned by a physics controller ignores the y component and the bob is then in neither the pose nor the position. What would make that wrong is a consumer wanting per-axis control, and the answer then is a mask on the extraction rather than a second convention. Bound to DriftScript as `animation.rootMotion` and `animation.stripRoot` with a `Motion` opaque, and **both descriptions say to pair the two calls**, because a script that extracts without stripping moves its character at exactly double speed with nothing failing. **The clause that once close this row was left standing through four commits that falsified it** — it read "no blending, blend trees or state machine; no IK, morph targets, root motion or retargeting; and the container carries none of it", each of which the paragraphs above now describe shipping, and one of which the same sentence had already contradicted twice. A row long enough to accrete is a row that needs reading end to end before it is added to. `cinematic/` moves cameras and nothing else. |
| **Chemistry**         | **Nothing.** The one gap this row carried — condensed tar — closed: `tar(l)` is a species `library/organic` registers beside the vapour it comes from, a dew point at 523 K condenses one into the other and back, and `aerosolAt` sums it, so **a smouldering fire's smoke is pale and a flaming fire's is black out of the same three reactions** with nothing arbitrating between them. Everything the design specified is built: `§14`'s sleeping, budgets and tiers closed, and the nine refusals below are refusals rather than gaps. Nine things the track **refuses outright** rather than defers, each with what would reverse it recorded in the design's §26: **fluid dynamics** — the field is advection and buoyancy, with no pressure projection, so a plume rises and bends and never curls into a vortex ring, and **its reversal condition was measured and corrected **: the design named a compute-shader budget, and the blocker is neither the budget nor the seam. A twenty-iteration Jacobi in `Float64Array` is 2.89 ms at 32,768 cells against the 59.8 ms that field's transport already costs, so the solve is 5% of what it would join; and the GPU route is shut because `step()` is synchronous and a compute dispatch's only way back is an async map, so a projection there would deliver a velocity from whichever earlier frame the browser happened to finish. What is actually in the way is that the field **stores no velocity at all** — `sweep` derives one per face and throws it away — so the row needs a stored MAC field at +17% of the stride and `sweep` rewritten onto it, which is the redesign that row promised it was not; **detonation** — deflagration is modelled and a supersonic shock front is not, since a shock is a physics problem in a package that owns no solver; **electrochemistry** — corrosion is an Arrhenius surface reaction rather than a half-cell model, so no batteries, no electrolysis, no galvanic couples. **The design's row said "gated on humidity" and that was corrected **: `ReactionGates` is temperature only and `library/metal.ts` records the absence itself, so a bar in a desert corrodes as fast as one in a bog. The refusal holds; what it is refused in favour of is weaker than it was written as; **radiative transfer through participating media** — smoke does not absorb and re-emit the fire's radiation, though **the evidence taken says that overstates it**: the engine draws smoke two ways and the particle path, which is the one `emitSmoke` writes into, already runs a point-light loop and comes back at the fire's own hue where the plume path comes back neutral. Absorption is absent on both — a wall lit through 96 plumes or 900 particles is bit-identical to one lit through clear air — and the refusal rests on a shader constant rather than on physics, since `smoke.ts` caps a quad at an alpha of 0.13 and 96 of them transmit 106% of a flame's brightness; **structural failure** — `structuralIntegrity` is a readout and an event, and nothing breaks, because a breakable joint belongs to whoever owns the solver; **two-way buoyancy on rigid bodies** — the field does not push bodies, for the same reason; **toxicology** — concentrations are reported in ppm and nothing models a dose or an effect, which is a game decision made with numbers this exports; **nuclear** — no fission, no fusion, no decay chains; and **smell and taste**, named because it is the first thing anybody asks of a cooking model and there is no physical quantity to compute. Eight of the nine carry sentinels below; the ninth cannot, since there is no symbol a smell model would have | **Physics**           | `physics/` is **kinematic convex collision**, swept per axis: `boxShape`, `sphereShape` and `hullShape` build a `ConvexShape` — the last from any point set, with an optional radius that rounds it — `colliderFromShape` gives the broad phase its bounds, and `ColliderSet` hashes them spatially. A blocked move reports the normal it was blocked by and whether the contact was worth standing on. **This row once said "no convex or mesh colliders" while `hullShape` was exported from the barrel** — no sentinel guards a clause like that, which is precisely what §5 says sentinels cannot do for you. **Rigid body dynamics ship.** `PhysicsWorld` steps bodies on a fixed clock: structure-of-arrays state in `Float32Array` with doubles for every intermediate, a dynamic AABB tree for the broadphase whose pairs are radix-sorted by body index so tree shape never reaches the solver, contact manifolds in three cases (SAT and clipping between polytopes, exact closest-point for a sphere or capsule against one, closest segments between two round shapes), and **substepped soft constraints** — stiffness stated as a frequency, so raising the substep count buys accuracy without changing behaviour, measured on a ten-box stack and a bouncing ball. Contacts persist across ticks by **feature id** rather than by proximity, which is what makes warm starting correct rather than tolerance-dependent. Islands are connected components over dynamic bodies only, so two towers on one floor are two islands; sleeping is island-gated and tick-counted. An **executor seam** ships with a serial runner and a shuffled one whose only job is a gate proving island order cannot affect the result. `fingerprintBodies` hashes a world the way `fingerprintColliders` hashes its geometry. **Vehicles and cloth ship, which completes Track B's row.** A **raycast vehicle**: a chassis body with wheels that are rays, suspension as a spring-damper impulse at the contact, and a **table-driven tyre curve** — Pacejka's formula is `sin(atan(…))` and both are banned from the tick, which is the one place in this track where the arithmetic contract produced a _better_ API than the closed form it replaced. Every wheel's impulse is gathered before any is applied, because applying them in order let each wheel see a velocity the previous had changed and the asymmetry accumulated into a yaw: 5.49 metres of drift over 155 travelled, against 0.001 after the fix. A raycast wheel cannot wedge in geometry or collide with another wheel, and that is said at the decision. **What is absent here, and sentinelled**: a worker pool behind the executor seam. **Convex decomposition left this list **; see the paragraphs below. **Two-way cloth coupling, cloth self-collision and a concave mesh collider all left this list **; see the paragraphs below. **A cylinder primitive left this list **, and §5 records that its sentinel fired on the commit that landed it. The last five were named in `README.md`'s gap list and in no place a test could read, which is the same shape as the `hullShape` clause above and was caught before it went wrong rather than after. **Cloth** is XPBD: distance and bending constraints with compliance, so stiffness stays meaningful as the iteration count changes — the same property soft constraints were chosen for. It is a separate solver from the rigid bodies deliberately, because thousands of rotationless particles are the wrong data layout for a rigid constraint graph. **Two-way coupled, by an impulse exchange rather than by a merged island** — and the refusal this replaces was right about the price and wrong about the only way to pay it. Putting particles into the rigid solver's constraint graph _would_ merge islands, and merged islands are what the parallel executor is made of, so that stays refused. What ships is the exchange the two solvers can make without either learning the other's structure: the collision pass already moves a particle out of a body, a particle moved by `d` in a tick of `h` has had its momentum changed by `m·d/h`, and the body receives the opposite **at the contact point** through the same `applyImpulse` any consumer would call — so a sheet landing on one end of a plank tips it, which an impulse through the centre of mass could not. **Explicit, so the body answers on the next tick**: it is a spring with a one-tick delay in it, and a very heavy sheet on a very light body rings. `coupling` is a scale from 0 to 1 and **0 is the default**, so no existing world moves until it asks; `particleMass` is in kilograms and is separate from `invMass` on purpose, because that array is a relative weight the compliance is tuned against and redefining it would move every sheet anybody has tuned. Asserted against the same world with no sheet in it, which must agree exactly at zero. **Self-collision ships the same day**, and it is off by default for the reason its own tuning is the hard half: `selfDistance` in metres, a spatial hash rebuilt each tick with one bucket a particle, a 3×3×3 cell scan, and a symmetric push apart split by inverse mass. **Particles a link joins are exempt**, built once as a CSR adjacency — not an optimisation, since a stretch link's rest length _is_ the spacing and a self-collision distance anywhere near it would have every neighbour fighting its own link and the sheet would inflate rather than drape. A projection rather than a compliant constraint, because a contact is an inequality and XPBD's accumulated multiplier is for something that holds all tick. **Measured on a sheet squeezed until it folds**: with it off the closest unlinked pair comes to **58 mm** inside a sheet whose own spacing is 100, and with it on the closest pair is at or above what was asked for at 60, 80 and 90 mm. **Bending resists bowing rather than orientation**, which is a property of a skip-one distance constraint rather than of the tuning: three collinear particles satisfy it at any angle, so it will not hold a cantilever out. Measured, and said where the links are built. **And for a while it could not be drawn**, which is the shape of gap a capability list is worst at showing: cloth shipped in 2.9 and `RendererApi` had `createMesh`, `drawMesh` and `disposeMesh` and no way to rewrite a vertex — so a deforming surface could only be drawn by recreating a mesh every frame, which is a GPU buffer allocation per frame, or by splitting it into rigid quads with a matrix each, which caps the resolution at the number of draw calls a consumer can afford. `updateMesh` closes it: positions and normals only, because colour and emissive describe what a surface _is_ and do not change because it bent; the vertex count is fixed, because the index buffer and the pipeline are sized against it; and a mesh says `{ dynamic: true }` at creation, which decides a buffer hint on WebGL2 and, on WebGPU — where every attribute interleaves into one buffer and a position cannot be patched without the rest of the vertex — whether the interleaved array is kept at all. **Found by a consumer trying to hang a banner**, which is the only way a row like this gets found.

**Six sentinels, four fired and two did not, and the pattern is now legible.** `rigid-body-dynamics`, `joints-constraints`, `world-raycast`, `vehicles` and `cloth` named a class or a symbol the implementation was always going to have. `triggers` named `sensorEvents` and `ragdolls` named `ragdollFromSkeleton`; what shipped was `BODY_SENSOR`, `ContactEvents`, and `ragdollFromBones` — the second forced by the package boundary. **A sentinel naming a plausible class survives the guess; one naming a function is a guess at a name, made before the code exists, which is the worst moment to make it.**

**A character controller and ragdolls ship.** `CharacterController` is a kinematic capsule sweeping the same world every query does: sweep-slide-project at a fixed pass count, step-up under a height limit, slope classification, and a push into dynamic bodies that carries the character's _speed_ rather than its per-tick step. Its feel is on it too — acceleration, air control, variable jump height, slide boost, and **coyote time and jump buffering counted in ticks** rather than accumulated in a float of seconds. `AGENTS.md`'s worked example for the engine/game boundary is corrected to match its own audio rule: the mechanism and its parameters are engine, and which numbers you choose is game. **There is no ground snap**: it was built, measured at a _worse_ foot gap than none — 0.490 metres against 0.457 descending a sharp forty-degree crest — and removed, with the instrument that would justify bringing it back written where it stood. **A ragdoll's joint limits are per joint**: `swingCos` and `twistSin` were one pair applied to every joint a rig has, and a knee is a hinge with no twist where a shoulder is nearly a ball — so a consumer chose which of the two to get wrong. Reported from outside, where the choice was loose (a 78° cone and 74° of twist everywhere) and what it produced was reported from play as _a scrambled ball of things, limbs torso head mixed together_: at 78° nothing stops a knee folding a limb through the torso, so a body that lands knots itself. Either option now takes an array indexed the way `parents` is, with the default standing in past its end and wherever an entry is not a finite number — because the other reading of a missing entry is zero, and zero is a 90° cone at the joint nobody thought about. What it does **not** buy is a real hinge: a narrow cone still bends a little in every direction, and the axis a revolute joint would need is rig data this builder is never handed.

`ragdollFromBones` takes **plain data** — a parent array and a flat array of joint world matrices, which a skeleton already exposes — and writes back through a structural target that an animation `Pose` satisfies exactly, so neither package imports the other. One capsule per bone, cone-twist jointed to its parent's, masses from bone volume, and `drive` steers toward an animated pose rather than replacing it, which is what makes a hit reaction rather than a body going instantly limp. **The joints are anchored at the bone ends they share, and were pinned through the middle of the bone before that**: a knee is not the middle of a shin, and anchored at the child's centre the shin turns about its own middle inside its cone, so the knee end of the shin walks away from the knee end of the thigh. Reported from outside at 56 to 100 cm open in flight; the test that sees it measures the two ends that share a joint, because every body is still exactly one bone from its parent's _centre_ either way. **Bones that share an end no longer collide either**, since two capsules jointed end to end overlap by construction and that contact fights the joint holding them together; `selfCollision: false` switches off all of it, and is measurably worse, because the cones alone do not stop a foot reaching the ribcage.

**The `ragdolls` sentinel did not fire either, which is the sixth.** It named `class Ragdoll|ragdollFromSkeleton`; what shipped is an _interface_ `Ragdoll` and `ragdollFromBones`, because §2 forbids importing the package `Skeleton` lives in. Two guesses in one track, both made before the code existed, both green over capabilities that had arrived.

**Joints, queries and sensors ship.** Six joint types — distance, spherical, revolute, prismatic, fixed and cone-twist — each with its rows unrolled rather than one configurable 6-DOF joint, with motors, one-sided limits and a breaking threshold, solved before contacts in the same substep loop because a joint is structural and a contact is transient. **No angle appears anywhere in them**: a swing limit compares a dot product against a stored cosine and a twist limit compares a quaternion component, which is what the solver wanted anyway since it clamps rather than measures. `raycastWorld`, `shapecastWorld` and `overlapWorld` fill caller-owned buffers and allocate nothing, and a ray starting inside a body reports that body at fraction zero rather than nothing. A **sensor** runs narrowphase and skips the solver, and `ContactEvents` drains enter, stay and exit into a caller-owned buffer _after_ the tick, ordered by pair key — never callbacks during the solve, which would both invalidate the indices the solver holds and break the executor.

**A seventh joint type ships, and it is a refusal narrowed rather than reversed.** `joints.ts` refused a configurable 6-DOF joint in its own header, on the ground that a generic joint is a constraint set decided at runtime — a branch per row in the hottest loop in the engine, and a megamorphic call site above it. That argument still stands and nothing here has changed: the six keep their own arms, their own rows and their own numbers, and **none of them gained a branch**, which the joint tests already there assert by staying green alongside the determinism gate. What the refusal named as its own cost was that "the package has to grow a type", and that is exactly what arrived: `JOINT_SIX_DOF` is a seventh arm above the chain rather than a runtime configuration the other six go through, so the branch a six-DOF joint pays for is paid by six-DOF joints and by nothing else. Three linear and three angular degrees, each **free, limited or locked**, in **body A's own frame** — not a frame of the joint's own, which costs a caller wanting other axes an orientation on A and would be reversed by four more floats per joint. **The mode is explicit rather than inferred from the bounds**: the widespread convention that `lower > upper` means free needs no extra field and turns a caller who swapped two numbers into a joint that silently does nothing, where a mode byte cannot be mistyped into the wrong meaning. Locked is **zero**, so an undescribed joint is rigid rather than one whose bodies fly apart. **It solves six independent scalar rows rather than two coupled 3x3 blocks**, because the blocks would not exist — a caller leaving linear y free and locking x and z has a 2x2, and the next caller has a different one — and the cost is measured: an all-locked six-DOF joint is softer than `JOINT_FIXED`, so the type's own comment says to reach for the fixed one when all six are locked, and a test asserts the two agree to within a millimetre rather than exactly. Angular bounds are **sines of half angles**, this package's own unit, because `Math.acos` and `Math.atan2` are both on the banned list. **It has no motor and says so on the console at `add`**, once per process, rather than accepting one and never driving — a motor asked for and silently not delivered reads as a broken motor rather than an unsupported one. It costs **1,391 gzipped bytes, 4.6% of the package**, which is what an unrolled solver looks like when the thing it unrolls is a configuration rather than a shape. **Not reachable from DriftScript**, and neither are the other six: `drift/physics` binds bodies, contacts, queries and forces and has never bound a joint, though its own header once said "joints" — see §4.

**The `triggers` sentinel never fired, and that is the fifth time this document has recorded that failure.** It was added naming `sensorEvents|class Sensor`; what shipped a commit later was `BODY_SENSOR` and `ContactEvents`, so the guard sat green over a capability that had arrived. A sentinel is a guess at a name, and a guess made before the code exists is a guess made at the worst moment — the two that _did_ fire here, `joints-constraints` and `world-raycast`, were written when the shape of the answer was already known.

**`StallEscape` ships**: a kinematic body that has stopped making progress, and the cheapest way out of it. A character controller resolves a move against geometry and has no opinion about a body that has been asking to move for half a second and going nowhere — which is where players get stuck, and where a consumer meeting it for the first time gets it wrong in the same order everybody does. Progress is a question about **net travel over a window**, never this tick's displacement, because a body jammed under a low ceiling _jitters_ by thirty times any per-tick threshold while sitting at the same coordinates. A body that is **grounded, supported and has headroom is not stuck** — three separate facts, and the first two differ exactly where a fall was arrested on a contact no rule calls support. A direction the world would refuse is not an escape route, so an `EscapeVeto` is taken structurally, the same shape `GroundProbe` is and for the same reason: a consumer with an analytic surface has a second authority about where a body may be, and a deck edge carrying no collider at all reports clear air to a probe that asks only the colliders. Horizontal wins over vertical by a wide margin, because being eased upward reads as levitating and slipping sideways reads as slipping. And **sealed is reported, never acted on** — the engine says there is nowhere to put the body, and what that costs a player belongs to the consumer. Every rule in it was paid for in a shipping game, and the entry point is 322 lines of them.

**A 32-layer mask ships with it** — thirty-two rather than sixty-four because a JavaScript bitwise operator is 32-bit — and a pair interacts only where each side's mask holds the other's layer. **And two named bodies can be excluded outright**: a mask says what a body _is_, so it can express "this kind does not meet that kind" and cannot express "these two in particular", which is the whole of what a ragdoll needs. `world.ignorePair(a, b)`, with `allowPair` and `pairIgnored` beside it, is the second question, and it is followed through a removal because a body index is a slot and not an identity. A world that never calls it pays one integer compare per candidate pair. **An elliptical friction cone ships, and it is off by default.** The two friction rows were each clamped to `mu * N` on their own, which is a **box**: along the diagonal between the two tangent axes the pair reaches `sqrt(2) * mu * N`, forty-one per cent more grip than the same surface offers along an axis — and the tangent basis is built from the contact normal, so _which_ headings are cheap is an artefact of that construction rather than a fact about the world. **Measured**: a box launched at 4 m/s over eight headings travels **1.064 m along the axes and 0.737 m along the diagonals, a ratio of 1.46**; under the ellipse it travels 1.059 to 1.073 m, a ratio of **1.013**, and the longest distance is unchanged, which is the control that says the ellipse did not simply weaken friction. **`frictionModel: 'elliptical'` is a world option and `'box'` is the default**, because every stacking result moves under the ellipse: `fingerprintBodies`, both baselines, and any golden fingerprint or stored replay a consumer has kept. A production engine does not silently invalidate those; _what would reverse it_ is a major version, where the honest thing is to make the ellipse the default and say so in the porting guide. **One coefficient, not two**, so the ellipse is a circle: anisotropic friction is the natural API for an ellipse and it needs a tangent frame anchored to a _material_, where these tangents rotate arbitrarily with the normal — a per-axis coefficient over them would mean something different from one tick to the next, which is a silent wrong answer. _What would reverse it:_ a tangent frame carried by the body, which is a larger change than the cone and which `vehicle.ts` already answers its own way with a grip table. The coupled solve also reads **one** relative velocity for both rows where the box path re-reads it between them, which is a second reason the numbers move and is why there is no version of this that a stored replay survives. **A static concave mesh collider ships.** `meshShape(positions, indices)` builds the triangles, their planes, an edge classification and a `DynamicTree` over them — the tree this package already has, built once and never moved, so no second acceleration structure had to be written or tested. **Static only, and the limit is enforced rather than documented**: `addBody` refuses a mesh on anything but a static body and `colliderFromShape` refuses one outright, because a moving concave mesh needs its tree refitted every tick and a mass tensor a triangle soup does not have, and because a mesh handed to the kinematic sweep would arrive as its own bounding box and turn a hollow level into a solid brick. **Every triangle goes through `collideShapes` unchanged**, as a three-point polytope written into one scratch shape — so the separating-axis test, the clipping, the sphere and capsule paths and the cylinder's own module are all exact against a mesh on the day it lands, and none of them was written twice. What that costs is the moving shape transformed once per candidate triangle rather than once per pair. **A mesh pair fills a _set_ of manifolds where every other pair fills one**, because a body in the corner of a mesh room has two or three contact planes and reducing them to one picks a wall and lets the body through the others. The solver already supported it — `prepareContact` appends — and `storeWarm` now accumulates by pair rather than replacing, with the triangle folded into every feature id so a box on a seam stops handing one triangle's impulse to another. **One-sided**, because a level mesh is a surface rather than a solid and a two-sided triangle fires anything that has sunk below it back out the wrong way. **And the interior-edge filter is the half that decides whether it feels right, measured rather than argued.** A box sliding across coplanar triangles meets their shared edge, where the narrow phase finds an edge normal and shoves it backwards — a character stumbling on a flat floor once a metre. Each edge is classified once at build time as convex or not, and a normal off a non-convex edge is replaced by the face's with the separation recomputed from the face plane. **A box slid at 6 m/s across sixteen quads keeps 80% of its speed with the filter and 1% without it**, which is the number the row's own note predicted and nobody had. Rays are two-sided, by Möller-Trumbore against the same tree, because a sight line that saw through a wall from behind is a worse answer than one that did not. **Convex decomposition ships, and with it the compound body that gives its output somewhere to go.** `decomposeConvex` is offline: it voxelises a triangle soup, floods the outside to find the interior, claims maximal boxes of solid cells, merges them, and returns at most 32 hulls of at most 50 points each — inside `hullShape`'s cap of 64. **A grid rather than the triangles**, because a collision mesh is routinely not watertight and every method that reasons over the source has to decide what its inside is; a flood answers that once, the same way, for any input, at a cost set by the resolution rather than by the triangle count. **The merge is measured two ways and that is the design.** Reaching the part budget takes thousands of merges, ordered by how empty a merged bounding box would be; going below it takes a handful, and each asks how much of the merged hull is not solid. **A box cannot tell a convex solid from a cavity**, and three attempts to make it were each wrong differently: a fixed threshold on box emptiness left a convex prism as **eight parts**, because a cylinder's box is 21.5% empty however it is cut; scoring the change against the sum of the parents gave negative costs that always pass and collapsed a cup to one hull at **403% bloat**; anchoring against the emptier parent let each merge license the next and reached **57%**. A real hull costs 1.09 ms at fifty points and is affordable at that count because a region is always a union of boxes, so its support set is exact from its seeds' corners and needs no walk over cells. **And greedy pairwise merging cannot finish a slanted convex solid either**: a tetrahedron came back as sixteen parts at 20.3% bloat, because every individual merge across a staircase leaves a notch while merging all of them is free — so the whole solid is tested for convexity once, before anything is merged, which is the case a crate, a wedge, a rock and a wheel are all in. **The defect that cost the most to find was in the fill.** A face lying exactly in a cell boundary plane is tangent to the cells on both sides, so the plane test compares two quantities equal in exact arithmetic and differing by a rounding step in this one; when it fell the wrong way _neither_ cell was marked, the flood walked out through the base and the interior came back empty. Measured on a closed 24-sided prism of true volume 3.106, the fill answered **3.57, 0.56, 0.47, 3.37, 3.33, 3.31, 0.20 and 0.17** at resolutions 32 through 96 — correct at four and the bare shell at four, with nothing in the shape to say which. The cell box is grown by one part in a million, which is the safe direction: a spurious cell costs a little accuracy and a missed one is a hole. **It was visible only because the check sweeps resolutions**, since a leak deflates the source volume and the hulls together and every bound held at any single one. Measured by `npm run check:decompose`: a convex prism returns one part, an L-beam two at zero bloat, a cup 12 to 14 with its cavity open, a staircase 4 to 6. **A torus is the honest limit** at 27.0% summed and 16.2% occupied — the gap is overlap counted twice — and the budget is not what binds it, since the same torus measures 26.7% at eight parts and 20.6% at thirty-two and reaches the same figure with the merge's tail switched off; `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` carries what would improve it. **`BodyDesc.shapes` is where the hulls go**, and it had to exist: `BodySet.shape` held one shape per body, so this row's own refusal message — _"convex decomposition into hulls, which the runtime already accepts"_ — was true of the kinematic sweep, which has taken `Body.parts` all along, and false of the dynamics it was written in. A part carries no offset and no rotation, because a `ConvexShape` is already a point cloud in the body's frame. Mass is `combineMassProperties`: volumes added, the centre volume-weighted, each tensor moved by the parallel axis theorem — **overlap is counted twice and that is the decision**, since removing it exactly is a boolean intersection of convex solids correcting a number the caller invented when they chose a density. Contacts are one manifold per touching part in a set sized to `MAX_BODY_PARTS`, so a compound against a single convex shape can never overflow, with the part pair folded into every feature id the way `meshContact` folds a triangle index. **`compound × mesh` shares the manifold budget between the parts that find candidates, never below one each** — a departure from the mesh path's first-come rule, which is defensible when the ninth candidate is a triangle and indefensible when it is a limb. `addBody` refuses a body carrying both `shape` and `shapes` or neither, an empty list, more parts than the cap, and a mesh as a part. **Two of the four mutations run against these claims survived the first version of the tests**: handing the whole mesh budget to the first part passed a settled body's tilt, because the simulation reaches a lopsided equilibrium anyway, and removing the feature-id fold passed everything, because two identical parts carrying identical loads are exactly where swapping their impulses shows nothing — both are asked of the narrow phase directly now. **The container carries the result as `COLL` at 1.12**, a FourCC claimed in v1 with no payload, no reader and no writer until this row decided what a baked hull is: a set of convex hulls, as points, because `@driftengine/drft` depends on nothing. `drft bake --collider hull[:N] | box | none` writes it and prefers a vehicle folder's `collider.kn5` over the model's own geometry. **`physics-only` did not move, and that took a correction**: `MAX_BODY_PARTS` was declared beside `decomposeConvex`, and importing one integer from an offline module put the whole voxeliser into every bundle touching physics — a named import of a `const` is enough to defeat tree shaking across a module boundary, and an A/B on that line is what said so. **What is still absent** is a worker pool behind the island executor's seam. Each names a sentinel or a refusal on record. **The worker pool is measured and still absent, and the seam's own comment named the wrong quantity.** It said "a pool is slower than serial below some body count"; a pool splits _islands_, so a world with one island has nothing to split however many bodies it holds — `islandParallelism.test.ts` pins that with a hundred jointed bodies solving as one island, and `packages/physics/scripts/island-bench.ts` prints the numbers. Measured on a 24-core desktop: the island solve is **58% to 76% of a tick**, so Amdahl caps any speedup at about 2x to 4x before a worker starts; one island of ten boxes is **160 to 185 microseconds** and the hundred-body single island is **1,129**; and a fork-join over a `SharedArrayBuffer` costs **6.8 microseconds at one worker, 11.8 at four, 23.7 at eight** with no work in it — half of one per cent against 2.6 milliseconds of solve at sixteen islands. **So the handshake is not what stops it.** What stops it was measured in a real browser rather than remembered: on a page that is not cross-origin isolated `SharedArrayBuffer` is **not defined at all**, and with `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` set it exists while `Atomics.wait` still answers `TypeError: Atomics.wait cannot be called in this context` **on the main thread**. A synchronous fork-join therefore has to busy-spin, or the whole fixed-step loop has to move into a worker where blocking is allowed — which is a different architecture rather than a pool behind this seam. And `require-corp` lands on the **consumer's whole site**: every cross-origin resource that does not opt into CORP stops loading, which is fonts, CDN images, embedded video and analytics. The row stays open with its sentinel and those numbers attached. **A row this long is a row that has to be read end to end before it is added to**, which the Animation row above says and which this one had stopped doing: it went on listing joints, ragdolls, raycast, triggers, layers, vehicles and cloth as absent for as long as it took to build every one of them. **The kernel moved to `@driftengine/physics` ** and core re-exports every name, so no import changed; the package imports no other engine package, which makes a simulation with no renderer in its module graph. A shape now carries its **faces** as planes and ordered loops beside the deduped separating directions, and `shapeMassProperties` is exact for a hull by tetrahedral decomposition over them — one build-time addition serving both contact clipping and inertia. `capsuleShape` names what the representation already expressed, two points and a rounding radius. **A cylinder ships, and the measurement that closed it is the one that had kept it open.** This row spent a fortnight calling it a refusal while `README.md`'s gap list called it a gap and a sentinel guarded it — three places, two answers — and what settled the disagreement was a number rather than an argument. The workaround `shape.ts` recommended was an n-gon prism through `hullShape`; `hullShape` refuses more than 64 points, a prism spends two a side, so **thirty-two sides is the wall**, and a thirty-two-sided wheel of radius 1 rolling at 6 m/s **bobs 16 mm** against 49 mm at sixteen sides and 119 mm at eight. No side count can improve that. The refusal's own reversal condition named "a wheel rim, a rolling barrel", and a centimetre and a half of bob on a slow, close, rolling subject is plainly visible — so the workaround did not cover the case the refusal pointed at, and the refusal was withdrawn. The same wheel as a `cylinderShape` bobs **under 2 mm**, inside the solver's own 5 mm slop, and `prismRoll.test.ts` now measures both side by side.

**What it is, structurally, is a second kind of rounding rather than a second shape type.** `ConvexShape.sideRadius` grows a point cloud by a _disc_ perpendicular to the segment through its first two points, where `radius` grows it by a ball — two flat caps, a curved side, a sharp rim. The axis is the shape's own two points rather than a stored vector, so a cylinder baked into world space by a collider carries its orientation the way its position is carried. `mass.ts` gains the two textbook moments in closed form, `shapeBounds` grows by the disc's extent down each axis rather than by the radius on all three, `query.ts` answers a ray with a quadratic and two discs instead of the march a capsule needs, `cloth.ts` pushes a particle out through the same four-region closest point, and `collide/sweep.ts`'s projections carry the disc term. **Contacts are a module of their own**, `cylinderContact.ts`: a curved side enumerates no separating axis, so the axis list is built against the _other_ shape — its faces, its edges crossed with the cylinder's axis, and two directions per vertex — and every one of them is answered exactly by the cylinder's own support. The touching feature is then a cap disc, a side line or a rim point, each clipped differently. It costs **5,492 gzipped bytes, 17.3% of the package**, which is the largest single step this entry point has taken and is what a second representation costs rather than what a constructor costs.

**Building it found a solver bug older than it, and the bug was not about cylinders.** The solver stores each contact anchor in its body's frame and turns it forward through the substeps, which is exact for a face or a corner and wrong for anything round: the point where a rolling ball meets the floor stays at the bottom, and an anchor that turns with the body climbs its side and reports a gap. Measured — **a sphere of radius 1 rolling at 6 rad/s sank 28 mm into the floor and stayed there**, and in the solver baseline scene a sphere rested at 0.3916 where its radius is 0.4. A curved anchor is now held in world frame; the sphere rests at exactly 0.4000, and the spurious rolling resistance the drift had been producing is gone, which is why that scene's floor had to grow four hundred metres for the ball to still be on it at tick 600. `Manifold.curvedA` and `curvedB` carry the decision, a cylinder sets them per feature because its cap is flat and its side is not, and the baseline fingerprint was re-frozen in the same commit. And the kernel's determinism claim is now true: ten `Math.hypot` calls are gone and `scripts/determinism.test.mjs` fails on any function ECMAScript declines to specify. |
| **Scene** | **The entity model ships in `@driftengine/entities`** — identity, component storage, queries and systems. An entity is one number carrying a 26-bit index and a 27-bit generation, so a handle to something destroyed is refused rather than silently addressing whatever took its slot; storage is a sparse set per component type with a typed-array column per numeric field; a query walks the smallest set and allocates nothing, per call as well as per step. A system **declares what it reads and writes and is held to it** — an undeclared write is refused naming both, and **a system whose refusal fires no longer takes the rest of the tick with it**: the throw once leave `runSchedule`, so every system scheduled after the failing one never ran, once per tick, for as long as the game was up. Reported from outside, and found from _play_ rather than from a check — the system that stopped was three places later and was the one stepping a vehicle, so the symptom was a car moving in jerks and the only evidence was a console line no headless gate reads. Each failure is caught, said once naming the system and the reason, and the schedule carries on; nothing is disabled, so a transient failure recovers and a declaration error costs a throw a tick until it is fixed. What it gives up is the stack reaching a debugger's uncaught-exception break — and the schedule orders by declaration with explicit `after` edges topologically sorted, reporting which adjacent systems could run together without running them that way. `everyTicks` strides the fixed step and is never a rate in seconds. Destroying from inside a system is deferred, because a removal swaps the last dense entry into the hole and would silently skip whichever entity was last. **Prefabs and scene serialization ship too**: a prefab is a value with no link back to its instances, and a scene addresses every value by a stable field id — so a scene saved before a component gained a field loads with the field at its default, one whose field was removed loads without it, and one whose field changed _type_ is refused naming it rather than coerced. That migration is `driftscript`'s, unchanged: there is one description of a component and one thing that reconciles two versions of it. Entity references are remapped on load rather than preserved, because a saved handle's slot may be live in the world being loaded into. No occlusion culling. **A transform hierarchy exists**: `SceneNode` holds a translation, a quaternion and a scale, derives world matrices only for what moved, and refuses a cycle at attach rather than meeting one in a walk. It does not draw — a traversal yields nodes and the caller issues the verbs, because draw order is semantic. **Frustum culling and LOD selection exist**: every mesh carries bounds measured at upload, `renderer.visible` answers for one, `?cull=1` makes `drawMesh` skip what is outside, and `lodForBounds` picks a level by apparent size. **A node's bounds enclose its whole subtree, so `visitVisible` discards a subtree on one test** — the hierarchy _is_ the acceleration structure and there is no second one. A caller not using nodes gets a linear scan, which is the honest cost of describing a world some other way. **Occlusion culling ships, and it is on the CPU** — which is the decision the whole thing turns on rather than a shortcut. The two obvious answers each fail a rule this engine already holds: a hardware occlusion query answers a frame late, needs a bounding-box draw per candidate, and is spelled differently on the two backends; a GPU depth pyramid over the frame's own depth has to be _read back_ to cull on the CPU, which stalls, or tested in a compute shader, which WebGL2 does not have. Neither can be asserted without a GPU, and this repository's whole culling story — `sphereInFrustum`, `boundsVisible`, `lodForBounds` — is assertions over arithmetic. So **the consumer declares its occluders** through `addOccluder` and `OcclusionBuffer` rasterises them into a buffer a few hundred texels wide, builds a max pyramid over it, and answers `renderer.occluded(bounds, model)` with a rectangle test. _What that gives up_ is that a small object never occludes anything: a crowd does not hide the crowd behind it. _What would reverse it_ is a scene whose occlusion is genuinely made of small things. **Everything about it errs toward drawing**, because a cull that is wrong the other way is a hole in the world and no threshold makes that acceptable. Three constructions keep it so, each asserted: **back faces**, since a box hides what is behind its far surface and rasterising the near one would cull the box's own interior; **eroded by one texel**, because a triangle sampled at texel centres over-covers by half a texel at every silhouette — measured, the cull then runs to two centimetres of the true silhouette instead of twelve, with nothing between it and a hole but the coverage being exact where it is not; and a **maximum** pyramid tested against the object's **nearest** point, which three spheres on one line pin down. **Driven on hardware, both backends**: `demo/dev/occlusion.html` puts seventy-two boxes behind a wall and four that must survive — one in front, two past the edges, one taller than it — and `scripts/occlusion-check.mjs` reads the counts and photographs the frame. **60 of 76 draws removed, all four controls drawn, and zero pixels of 870,400 changed**, with the two backends culling exactly the same objects because it is exactly the same code. The pixel comparison excludes the page's own readout: compared whole, the two frames differ by 1,916 pixels in a band at the bottom-left, every one of them a letter of the count the page prints. **Instanced mesh draws ship.** A mesh already on the device can be given a per-instance placement and colour — `createInstanced`, `uploadInstanced`, `drawInstanced` and its blended twin — so thirty copies of one model are one draw call and, the half that matters more on WebGPU, **one slot of the frame's material ring** where thirty individual draws spend one each. Distinct from `createScatter`, which owns its own base geometry and carries a scale, a yaw and a wind response because it describes a plant; this attaches to a mesh the consumer already uploaded and carries a full transform, because a vehicle pitches and rolls and a yaw cannot say so. **Shadows came with it**: `ShadowCasterSink` grows an `instanced` verb, or a batch casts one shadow from whichever matrix was last bound and the other twenty-nine are missing — a lighting fault to look at rather than a pass anybody would suspect. _What it gives up_ is skinning and morphing, both refused loudly: eleven of WebGL2's guaranteed sixteen attribute locations are the base mesh and the five that remain are exactly the matrix and the tint, so the joint indices and weights have nowhere to go — and a morph weight is per draw, so every instance would wear one expression between them. _What would make it wrong_ is a twelfth base attribute, which cannot coexist with instancing at all. Driven on hardware on both backends by `demo/instancing.ts`: two ranks of thirty, thirty draws against one, and swapping which rank is instanced changes **0 of 704,000 pixels**. **A world is a grid of cells, and an unloaded region is _frozen_.** Frozen means exactly what it says: the region does not simulate. **An agent in an unloaded cell does not walk anywhere**, does not age, and does not finish what it was doing — so a patrol the player has walked away from is exactly where they left it, however long they were gone. That is a decision rather than an accident, and it is written here because a consumer discovering it from behaviour is the failure the decision was made to prevent. **Freezing is a simulation decision and unloading is a memory one**: a frozen cell does not simulate whether or not its contents are resident, and only a frozen cell may be unloaded. The alternative — unloading causes freezing — would make the simulation depend on how much memory a machine had, which is a divergence that appears on one player's computer and nowhere else. **A frozen cell still contributes to the fingerprint**, constant for as long as it is frozen, so a run that streamed a region and one that never did agree at _every_ frame rather than only once everything has thawed — and two runs that froze different state are seen to disagree at the frame they froze rather than twenty frames later at the thaw, by which time a rollback netcode has already sent them. `freeze.ts` and its eleven tests hold that, including the two runs compared frame by frame. **A deterministic surrogate is permitted only inside the fingerprint**: a consumer that wants an unloaded region to appear to have progressed may compute one from the frozen state, and it must be a pure function of that state or the two runs stop agreeing. |

A mesh with no frame gets one from screen-space derivatives, so a normal map works on procedural geometry too. `setMaterial` is the way in; `setSurfaceTexture` is a deprecated wrapper over it. **ORM maps ship**, end to end: occlusion in R, roughness in G and metallic in B, glTF's packing, on unit 6. That last one is **split by metalness**, and the split is what keeps it from being a look change: a dielectric's highlight goes in before the blend, where that blend has always dimmed it by the surface's own reflectance, and only a metal's is added after. Adding the whole term after the blend was tried first and moved the published scenes — gilded-chamber by 2,542 pixels of 750,080 — because a near-black glass lens carrying `specular` 1 took a white blob where it had none. Split, every gating scene is **zero pixels on both backends** against the engine before any of this landed. The R channel is baked occlusion over everything the surface contributes, matching the screen-space AO the composite applies, which double-counts with the shadow maps and is stated rather than hidden. `setMaterial` is the way in; `setSurfaceTexture` is a deprecated wrapper over it. **The container carries a reference to four images** — albedo, normal, ORM and emissive indices in `MATL` at stride 72, beside three glTF factors — of which albedo, ORM and **normal are bound, the last of them**, and emissive is carried and not yet read. The normal index spent a whole minor version written by the baker, read by the reader and dropped by `DrftLoader`, which is the one layer between them that did not pass it on: nothing failed, and a bought model simply drew smoother than its maker shipped it. Measured on an imported figure carrying four of them, binding it moved 47% of the subject's pixels. `gltf.ts` no longer discards a `metallicRoughnessTexture`'s factors, and drops a _separate_ occlusion image with a reason rather than spending a second unit on it. **And it reads both of glTF's material models.** A material stating the archived `KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness` carries **no `pbrMetallicRoughness` object at all**, so a reader that knew only the core model found no base colour map and bound none of the file's images: measured on a 1995 Fiat Punto GT, **20 textures loaded and 0 bound**, with 144 of 144 meshes reporting no albedo map and the whole car painted in one flat fallback colour. The specular colour and the glossiness are now solved for jointly into a metalness and a roughness — the extension's own Appendix B, base-colour derivation included, which is what makes chrome, whose diffuse is black and whose colour is entirely in its specular, arrive as chrome rather than as a black mirror. The map modulates the surface's own emission rather than creating it — glTF's rule, emitted colour being the factor times the texture — so a mesh whose `emissive` attribute is 0 stays dark however bright the image, and that is stated at the field, in the shader and on the demo page because it is the one thing about this map that surprises people. Sampled sRGB, unlike the normal and ORM maps, because it is a colour rather than data. `emissiveScale` is the per-channel factor beside `roughnessScale` and `metallicScale`. **All four of `MATL`'s texture indices are now bound**, the emissive one having waited on a renderer that could take it rather than having been dropped. Measured on both backends, which returned identical figures: a mapped panel's luminance deviation is 30.8 against 0.0 unmapped, the scale multiplies it, and a mesh emitting nothing stays at 0.0. **Still absent: height, clearcoat, sheen and transmission maps.** **Irradiance from spherical harmonics ships, on both backends.** `render/irradianceSh.ts` projects a baked cube onto nine coefficients and the lit pass evaluates them against the normal with **no texture fetch at all**: nine multiply-adds over a bare polynomial, every constant folded in at bake time. Measured on `demo/dev/ibl.html`, a grid of spheres between one emissive wall and one nearly black one: 25 of 25 spheres lit from the bright side at a mean margin of 13.3 of 255 against a control of 1.0, identical on both backends. **And a bake can be asked for the reflection alone.** Projecting the room's diffuse light was not a choice until then: `bakeReflectionProbe` and `setEnvironmentImage` both read the cube back unconditionally, so a consumer who wanted a car and a puddle to mirror the village got, as well, **every diffuse surface in the world taking its ambient from the projection instead of from the values it wrote into `Environment`** — once, mid-session, at whatever moment the bake landed. It correlates with nothing a consumer can see: not the hour, not the weather, not the position, only with when a streamer goes quiet, and it was reported four times over two days as four different bugs. It is also invisible to a consumer's own instrumentation over `Environment`, because the substitution happens past `Environment` and inside the renderer. `ProbeBakeOptions.irradiance: false` declines the second half on either call and on both backends; the reflection is unaffected and the ambient stays whatever the consumer set. **It also stops paying for it** — the readback and the projection are the expensive part of a bake, and `renderer.test.ts` counts exactly that on both backends: six `readPixels`, one a cube face, by default and none at all when declined. **It declines rather than undoes**: a bake that declines leaves an earlier projection in place, so the guarantee is for a consumer that passes it on every bake. **A GGX prefilter ships, on both backends.** The mip chain stops being a box filter and becomes the specular integral: each level is convolved with the GGX lobe for the roughness it stands for, importance-sampled, with the source level of each sample chosen from its own solid angle so a wide lobe does not read a level fine enough to sample a few bright texels and turn them into fireflies. It costs one cube of memory and **no texture unit**, since `uEnvironment` binds the prefilter instead. Declared channel semantics, so a Y-down normal comes back Y-up and gloss comes back as roughness and nothing downstream guesses; the exact sRGB curve rather than the 2.2 approximation, which differ at the midpoint by 0.2140 against 0.2176. Normal mips that add roughness as normals disagree instead of sparkling — possible here because roughness and normals live in one object. A decode graph that is **data walked by one shader, never a permutation**, sentinel `DECODE_OP\|validateDecodeGraph`, with a reference interpreter beside it because a shader cannot be unit-tested at speed. Time is a sampling argument rather than a clock, sentinel `flipbookFrame\|latentLerpWeights`, which makes an animated texture byte-exact under replay. Content-addressed tiles, materials bound as array slices because WebGPU has no bindless, and one network evaluator that reconstruction and capture will share. **Predictive residency ships**, sentinel `predictViews\|runPrediction`: the simulation is saved, advanced, sampled for what those views will want, and restored — no feedback buffer, no readback, and it works for passes that could never write feedback. What a predicted view wants is `tilesForView`, over grids `latentTileGrid` cuts from real latents and addresses by content. **The device-side decode interpreter ships**, sentinel `DECODE_WGSL\|packDecodeTables`, in `@driftengine/core`'s GPU-driven pass and checked against `decodeCpu` on a device — §3. **The writable overlay ships**, sentinel `writeOverlay\|recordOverlayWrite`: sparse tiles over a material, and a journal that replays every mark a session made. The offline joint encoder is a baker, so it is `@driftengine/assets`' `encodeMaterial` and a game that only decodes never carries it |

The two backends differ in **one pixel of 921,600** by more than 8, identically with the grade off, inverting and rotating, so it is the scene's own and the grade does not widen it. | **Reconstruction** | **The learned tier, DriftNeural, was withdrawn by the design's own stop condition**, sentinel `learned-reconstruction`. A network refining the finished frame, trained by `tools/recon-train/` on 54 pairs of the published scenes, averaged +0.01 dB against the native frame on scenes it had not seen — +0.05 for a linear filter, −0.9 on the voxel sandbox — and lost the one clear difference in a blind comparison with the analytic tier, so a request for tier 1 is tier 0 (`recon/tier.ts`). What would bring it back is a network inside the resolve, fed the render's jittered samples and its history: a different network, trained on sequences rather than frames. **Frame generation is a reference, not a pass**, sentinel `frame-generation`: `recon/frameGen.ts` projects, resolves, fills and composites over typed arrays and states the latency it adds, and nothing in the frame calls it — running it needs a device pass and a renderer that draws the world on every k-th display frame and the interface on every one. **WebGL2 is refused**: the tiers are compute dispatches, so `reconstructionSupported` answers false there and WebGL2 draws at the output size, as it always has |
| **Structure** | A package **can** contribute a pass: `registerPass` takes a definition with declared reads, `drawPass` runs it where the caller puts it, and both backends hand it their own context. **A pass may bring its own attachments**, to the design `pass.ts` had been carrying as a plan. `PassDefinition.prepare` is a sibling of `draw` rather than a widening of it — `draw` is handed an open `GPURenderPassEncoder` and a render pass cannot be nested — and its WebGPU arm carries a `GPUCommandEncoder` instead. **The window already existed and the graph learns nothing**: `beginFrame` creates the encoder and `ensurePass` defers the frame's render pass to the first draw, so there is a point with an encoder and no open pass, and commands on one encoder run in recording order — a target filled there completes before any frame pass could sample it, with **no dependency ordering reintroduced**. Gate 1.2 withdrew that with a reason on record and this does not undo it: `prepare` runs at one fixed point for every pass that declares it, in registration order, which is an order and not a graph. **On WebGL2 the contract is a restore**, and that was the decision the row was blocked on: there is no verb-level graph to schedule against, so `prepare` is called with the default framebuffer bound and must leave it bound — the promise `draw` already makes about program, vertex array, blend, depth and viewport, one step stronger because a framebuffer left bound takes the whole frame rather than one draw.
