The asymmetry is real and is stated rather than hidden. `createPassAttachment` builds the target from the `PassDevice` the pass was handed at `init` — colour and optional depth, `rgba8` or `rgba16float`, released by the pass's own `dispose` — and it is **single-sampled on purpose**, because a multisampled one needs a resolve target beside it and a decision nobody has asked for. `prepare` **costs nothing for a pass that does not declare it**: both renderers count the passes that do and skip the step at zero. **What is still absent is any reordering**, and that stays a refusal rather than a gap. **Driven on hardware, both backends**: `demo/dev/passtarget.html` writes red on even frames and green on odd ones into a pass-owned target and samples it across the frame, and `scripts/passtarget-check.mjs` reads the canvas back — the alternation is the instrument, because a target filled one frame late reports the _previous_ frame's colour on every frame, which a still picture cannot see. Perturbed by writing `frame - 1`, and both backends went red. **WebGPU records every drawing verb through a frame graph, on by default**, and the schedule opens the frame's pass and the mirror's, derives their `loadOp` and depth `storeOp`, and drops passes nothing reads; `?graph=0` turns it off in one reload and WebGL2 has no verb-level graph. Turning it on changed **nothing a consumer can see**: all seven published scenes are 0 of 921,600 pixels changed against it forced off, whole frame, with no device errors either way. Two defects had kept it off and both were the same shape — a decision taken at one moment used at another, which only recording can separate: a draw took the pipeline of whichever pass was open rather than the one it would land in, and a probe bake never replayed its records, so it baked an empty cube and leaked six draws into the next pass to open. **A package can dispatch compute on WebGPU**: `registerCompute` takes a definition, `dispatchCompute` runs it on a command encoder of its own so the frame's render pass is never closed for it, and `ComputeDevice` hands over the raw device the way `PassDevice` does. **WebGL2 has no compute and never will**, so `renderer.computeSupported` answers `false` there and `registerCompute` refuses in words rather than returning a handle that would silently do nothing. **The engine dispatches one of its own**: `clusterBinner.ts` bins lights into froxels through a hand-authored WGSL kernel, which is the first compute pipeline here and the reason `AGENTS.md` now exempts compute from the rule that WGSL is generated. **A second dependency representation ships beside the fixed table**, for a frame whose composition is not fixed: `virtual.ts` declares transients by identifier because a thirty-one-bit mask cannot hold hundreds of them, `lifetime.ts` and `alias.ts` let two that are never alive together share memory, `graphSchedule.ts` culls transitively where the mask scheduler can only cull once, and `validateGraph` refuses a read of what nothing wrote. Internal to `render/` and not on the package barrel; `frame/index.ts` says why. **It schedules production frames since 2026-09-17**: the GPU-driven pass's stages every frame, and the forward flush under `quality.identifierGraph` — §3 has the captures. **`indirectSupport` is a backend fact rather than a verb** — a contributed pass already holds the render pass encoder and a compute definition already holds the compute one, so indirect execution needs permission rather than a method. It answers false on WebGL2, which has no compute stage to write an argument buffer and no indirect draw to read one; emulating it through a readback is slower than the draw it would replace, so the refusal is recorded rather than worked around. |
| **2D and interface** | **`@driftengine/ui2d` ships** — sprites, sheets, tilemaps, a retained tree, layout, focus and input routing, as `@driftengine/ui2d`, and it draws through `registerPass` rather than through a verb on the renderer — which is what lets it be a package at all, and what `pass.ts` says the contributed-pass seam exists for. **8.7 KB gzipped on top of core, and nothing for a consumer that never imports it**: the sprite program is authored and generated into WGSL inside the package, so core carries no sampler for it. That places it between Track D's two shader rows — 4 KB for drawn decals, 7.5 KB for screen-space reflection — and well under the 19.8 KB a branch in `flatFrag` costs, which is what a `drawSprite` verb beside `fillPanel` would have been. **Two coordinate systems and they count y opposite ways**: `screenToNdc` is CSS pixels from the top-left, the convention `InsetRect` and `fillPanel` already use, and `worldToNdc` is a 2D world through a `Camera2D`, where y counts up — a caller placing a platform above a floor should not have to subtract, and one shared convention would make every caller wrong half the time. **There is no depth and the order sprites were submitted in is the layering**, which is the same decision gate 1.2 took about pass ordering. A batch is one instance buffer and a list of **runs**: consecutive sprites on one texture are one draw, a slot change starts a run, and going back to the first slot starts a third rather than regrouping — regrouping would reorder the picture. The batch does not grow, and past its capacity `drawSprite` counts into `dropped` rather than allocating under a frame. `drawTilemap` costs the **view rather than the map**: the visible span is arithmetic on four numbers, measured at 25 tiles drawn out of a million-cell map. **`scripts/sprite-check.mjs` is the exit test**, on the card, on both backends, 22 assertions: every sheet in it is two texels by two with four different colours, so a sprite's four quadrants say which corner is which — an assertion a mirror fails and a bounding box cannot. The two backends agree byte for byte on both submission orders and a sprite lands on its CSS rectangle to **0.00 px** on every edge. **It found a real defect on its first run**: a contributed pass inherits whatever cull state the last scene draw left on, and a screen-space quad's winding is not the scene's, so WebGL2 drew nothing at all while WebGPU — whose pipeline states its own cull mode — was pixel-perfect, with no error on either side. **The retained tree is the other half and it touches no GPU at all**: `layoutUiTree` is two passes over an object graph — measure bottom-up, place top-down — and no third, because a `fit` size that depended on the space it was given would need a rule for when to stop. Three size cases (`fit`, `grow`, a number) rather than percentages or flex weights, since a percentage of a `fit` parent is a cycle. It allocates nothing: every number lands in a `UiRect` the node already owns, which is why a node is an object with fields rather than a description that gets resolved into one. `uiHitTest` searches **last-drawn first**, so the hit test agrees with the picture, and a node that is not `interactive` does not block what is behind it — a backdrop that swallowed clicks makes every button under a plate dead, which no screenshot shows. `routeUiPointer` activates on a press and a release **on the same node**, so somebody who pressed the wrong button can slide off it. Focus order is tree order rather than a declared index, and a node hidden since it was focused does not take the keyboard with it. **The pass fills a white slot of its own**, so a solid rectangle needs no sheet — `demo/dev/ui.html` uses none at all. **`scripts/ui-check.mjs` is the exit test**, 17 assertions on the card: it publishes the boxes the layout computed _and_ the bounding boxes of the colours they were drawn in, and asserts they agree — a bar sized by its own contents lands at 530, 660, 220 by 60 on both backends, to **0.0 px**, with the frame byte-identical in all three pointer states. The control is the pointer: the middle button paints itself from its own `hovered` and `pressed` flags, so routing is a colour in the frame rather than the router's own return value read back. **It is an interface framework now, not only a sprite layer.** Clipping that collapses any number of ancestors into one rectangle; scrolling applied at placement so hit testing, focus and clipping need not know it exists; inherited draw layers with a stable order; nine-slice that shrinks both insets together rather than overlapping corners; a pure text model whose caret steps over surrogate pairs; disjoint style runs; virtualised lists; theme tokens flattened at derivation, and unpacked into a node's colour by `themeRgba` rather than by every consumer writing the same four shifts; a retained diff whose vanished node repaints where it was; and pointer capture, without which every slider is wrong in the same way. **Composition and the clipboard are a `TextHost` the caller supplies**, sentinel `TextHost\|createNullTextHost`, because this has to run where there is no document object model. **An accessibility tree is produced and a host publishes it** — and on a host with no accessibility service `createNullA11yHost` publishes to nothing, which is stated here rather than discovered. |
| **Audio** | **The mix is a tree**: `MixConsole` holds buses that nest to any depth, each `input gain → inserts → tap → output gain`, with sends taken from the tap so a fader moves what it sends. Solo silences siblings and leaves ancestors and descendants alone — anything else silences a soloed leaf through its own parent — and a bus born while somebody is soloing arrives already gated, because the gate is a property of the tree rather than an event. Snapshots capture levels, mutes and sends and deliberately **not** insert parameters: the master cutoff is written every frame from a consumer's own state, and a snapshot that captured it would fight that writer. `AudioGraph` keeps the transport and forwards its whole mix surface, and the rewrite is asserted rather than claimed — an offline render through the new layout is **bit-for-bit identical** to one frozen from the code that predates it, both channels, which is what `scripts/audio-baseline.mjs` exists to say. **A listener graph ships**: `AudioListenerGraph` carries position, facing and a **derived** velocity, agreeing with `stereoPan` on yaw 0 facing −Z by construction rather than by coincidence, with `warp` for a teleport so nothing derives a speed from a jump that never happened. It writes the modern `positionX` parameters where a browser has them and the deprecated `setPosition` pair where it does not. **Sources are placed in the world**: `createSpatialSource` builds `buffer → detune → occlusion lowpass → occlusion gain → panner → bus`, panned with `panningModel: 'HRTF'` rather than `equalpower`, which is what puts a sound _behind_ a listener at all. **Doppler is computed here rather than configured**, because the specification removed `dopplerFactor` and `speedOfSound` from `PannerNode`: the ratio is `(c + vListener·d) / (c + vSource·d)`, applied through `detune` in cents with `playbackRate` as the fallback, and clamped — a whole tone each way by default, because past that it stops reading as motion. It is **off per source unless asked for**, since on a looping bed a listener walking past makes the bed's pitch wander. **Occlusion is a curve the engine owns over a number the consumer owns**: a consumer answers "how much wall" through `OcclusionProbe`, closed over its own colliders, and the engine decides what that means — a geometric cutoff from 20 kHz to 500 Hz for the reason `liftFrequencyHz` gives, twelve decibels down, smoothed in time so one rate means one thing at any frame rate. A fully occluded source is **quieter and duller, never silent**: a sound that vanishes behind a wall teaches a player that walls delete things. Probes are throttled and staggered by source index, because a segment test per source per frame is the consumer's cost and the most expensive thing this feature can do. **The spatial layer is standalone functions rather than console methods**, so a consumer who never places a sound does not carry the panner — measured: `core-and-audio` is 457,315 bytes gzipped and `core-audio-spatial` 458,794. **Reverb zones ship, and a zone is a bus** — which is the payoff for having built a tree rather than a fixed set of sends: a room is not a special case in the mixer, so everything true of a bus is true of a room, including solo and mute. A zone is full inside its radius and fades across a blend, because a hard edge is heard as the room switching on. **At most two sound at once**, the space being left and the space being entered; a convolver is the most expensive node in this graph and a third is inaudible under that crossfade while costing everything the second one costs. Every convolver is built at registration and never on entry, since building an impulse allocates and costs milliseconds and a threshold is the worst possible moment to pay it. A zone's return is parented to `master` so its tail goes through the master filter, **unlike the three legacy returns** which join downstream of it: those carry the score, and a score is not in the world, where a room whose tail stayed bright while everything else muffled would read as coming from somewhere else. **Listener-based**, so a sound inside a cave heard from outside does not carry the cave's tail — the alternative is a convolver per source and is priced accordingly. **Source-attached zones ship, and they are a second routing rather than a second convolver** — which is what made the row affordable and what `zones.ts` had been saying since it was written. The return already carries a convolver built at registration, so `SpatialSource.attachZone` costs one `GainNode` and a per-frame amount. It closes the case the listener model names as the one it cannot serve: a sound inside a cave heard from _outside_ it now carries the cave's tail, because the **source's** position decides its own send. **The budget still binds and it binds per source**: at most two zones sound for one source, because the budget was never about the sends — it is about how many convolvers are audible at once, and a source driving four returns makes four of them audible. **The send is taken before the panner and after the occlusion**: a reverb send comes off the channel on any console and the return is itself a stereo space, so a point-panned tail would arrive from the source's direction rather than from the room, and a sound behind a wall has a muffled tail too. **The trap is that both routings reach one return.** The listener's zones send from a whole bus, so a source on that bus — or on a descendant of it, which is the case a consumer with its own tree actually builds — is already reaching the return whenever the listener is in the same space, and its own send is then a second copy that is inaudible as a fault and merely wrong. `attachZone` walks the parent chain and says so, once per misconfigured bus rather than once per source. **Ambisonics ships**: `createAmbisonicSoundfield` takes a four-channel first-order field in **ACN order with SN3D normalisation**, which is what a B-format recording carries and what every capture tool emits — a private ordering would be one shuffle nobody could see, in a file this engine did not make. The ambisonic frame is x-forward, y-left, z-up and is **not** this engine's; `ambisonicFromWorld` is the single place that conversion happens, and a wrong handedness there plays every direction mirrored while sounding like a working renderer. It decodes through **six virtual speakers on an octahedron** — the world axes — each panned through the same head model a placed source uses, so a whole recorded scene costs **six convolutions however much is in it**, where placing its contents as sources would cost six per sound. The decode is the projection cardioid `(W + d · (X, Y, Z)) / speakers`: unity where a speaker faces the source, zero on the antipode, and **summing to exactly one over the octahedron**, so a field is neither louder nor quieter for having been decoded — which is the number a hand-rolled decoder gets wrong first, and it is asserted for four directions. **The matrix is constant, and the rotation is deliberately not here**: the speakers are fixed in the world and the head's rotation is applied once, by the `AudioListener` the panners already answer to. A decoder that rotated the field as well would apply it twice, and the symptom — a field counter-rotating at double speed as a player turns — reads as a broken recording rather than as a double transform. _Cost:_ a **head-locked** field, which is what a music bed wants, cannot be had this way, and the answer then is a second decode with the speakers in the head's frame rather than a rotation added to this one. Six rather than four because the field carries height and a horizontal ring throws it away, which would make the third channel decoration. A buffer that is not four channels is **refused at construction**, because taking the first four channels of a stereo file is a plausible result silent in two thirds of the field. `positional.ts` is `distanceGain` and `stereoPan`, and both stay — a diffuse bed is what they are for, and a panner per brazier is the expensive way to get the same two numbers. **Not reachable from DriftScript**, and neither is the rest of the spatial layer — see §4. |
| **Input** | **Gamepad ships**, and it needs no wiring: `InputSource` polls the Standard Gamepad once on an animation frame of its own, so a consumer that linked nothing still gets a working controller. A consumer reads **positions** rather than anybody's lettering — index 0 is A on an Xbox pad, Cross on a PlayStation pad and **B** on a Nintendo pad, which swaps the two physically, so any lettering the engine picked would be false about somebody's hardware. `identity` answers what the pad in hand calls that position, across four families with a generic fallback and **no device database**: a per-device table rots silently and its failure is a wrong glyph a player sees and no test can. Glyph keys are identifiers a consumer maps to its own art; the engine ships none. `lastDevice` flips on **use rather than presence**, so a pad plugged in for something else does not take the prompts from a player still on the keyboard, and `onDeviceChange` fires only on a change so prompts are redrawn once rather than every frame. The mouse alone carries a movement threshold, because a keydown and a touchstart are intentional and a mousemove is not necessarily anything. Edges are latched at the poll rather than derived at read, so a slow frame that runs the fixed-step loop twice cannot turn one press into two — `pressed` is readable by anything and `consumePress` claims it. `getGamepads` allocates an array and the objects behind it, which is the browser's cost and cannot be pooled, so it is called exactly once a frame and never from a read. A pad the browser will not vouch for is **served rather than refused** — reachable by raw index, answering `mapping: 'unknown'`, and saying so once per device rather than once per frame. Any source can be switched off, and a disabled gamepad stops the browser being asked for pads at all — the poll itself still runs, because it advances the _input_ frame rather than only sampling pads: the keyboard answers `keyPressed` and `consumeKeyPress` on the same latch a button does, so one action can read either device without either being a special case. `autoPoll: false` hands the sampling point to a consumer that wants it pinned to its own fixed tick, which is what a recorded replay needs. **Action maps and rebinding ship**, which completes Track H. A game asks whether _jump_ happened rather than which device said so, so the device branch stops being written by hand at every site that reads input. An action is the consumer's own string, never an engine enumeration: a game's verbs are a game's business. Digital actions answer the same three verbs a pad does; analog ones answer a direction, and take **the larger of stick and keys rather than the sum**, because a player holding a key while pushing the stick the same way is asking to go that way once, not at twice the speed. A keyboard diagonal is normalised so it is not faster than a straight line. `rebind` **reports the actions it displaced rather than deciding about them**, since stealing, warning or refusing is a product decision. Persistence is **a diff from the defaults, not a snapshot**: a snapshot freezes the map at the version that saved it, so a game adding an action later would find every returning player without it and no way to tell a deliberate choice from a stale record. It goes through `KeyValueStore`, so bindings can live in a browser, a native shell, on a server or nowhere, and an unreadable record is the defaults reported once rather than a broken game. **Rumble ships**, and **the refusal is half of it**: `GamepadView.canRumble` answers whether this pad has motors this browser can drive, and `rumble(durationMs, strong, weak)` and `stopRumble()` each answer whether the platform took the call rather than accepting it and doing nothing quietly — so a settings screen greys the control out instead of offering a slider a player's hardware ignores. That is the same rule the host seam keeps for a window mode a shell cannot enter, and it is the half of this row a player could never have discovered. The engine takes **durations and magnitudes and nothing else**: no pattern language, no named effect and no curve, each of which would be a decision about what a game does with the hardware. `strong` is the low-frequency motor and `weak` the high-frequency one, which is what a standard pad has two of; magnitudes are clamped into [0, 1] and a duration is clamped to the specification's ceiling of **5,000 ms**, because a longer request is not an error a caller can see — the promise resolves with a word nobody reads and browsers differ on whether they clamp it or drop it. **The actuator is re-read at every poll** rather than kept from the first: a `Gamepad` is a fresh snapshot each `getGamepads` call and a pad unplugged and plugged back in is a different device behind the same slot. A `playEffect` that rejects — which is what a pad unplugged mid-effect does — is swallowed and reported **once per pad**, the shape the unvouched-layout refusal established, because an unhandled rejection is a stack trace nobody can act on and silence leaves a player with nothing to read. Reachable from DriftScript as `input.canRumble`, `input.rumble` and `input.stopRumble`, all three carrying `host` and none deterministic — a replay must not be able to tell whether the player's pad was plugged in. What is absent inside this: **`hapticActuators[].pulse` is not used on purpose**, because it carries one magnitude where this has two, so serving it would mean dropping the weak motor or averaging the pair and both are a silent lie about what the caller asked for — a platform with only `pulse` answers false and is greyed out, which is true rather than convenient, and what would make that wrong is a measurement on a browser a consumer actually ships to. And **trigger rumble is not reached**: `'trigger-rumble'` drives two more motors only some pads have, so it needs its own capability answer beside `canRumble` rather than riding this one. |
| **Assistive technology on the native host** | **A screen reader cannot read the native host.** The editor builds its accessibility tree on every host and hands it to an `A11yHost`; in a browser that becomes nodes an assistive technology walks, and on the native host it is published to nothing (`createNullA11yHost`), because SDL gives a window no platform accessibility service and reaching AT-SPI, UI Automation or `NSAccessibility` is work of its own. Sentinel `native-accessibility`, which scans `packages/` — where the host is, as `packages/native-host` — and `editor/`. |
| **Terrain** | **`@driftengine/terrain` ships**, and it imports no renderer: a `Terrain` is a heightfield and `heightfieldPatch` hands back `MeshData`, drawn by the pass that already exists. That is why it is a package — a world with no terrain pays nothing — and it is **1.4 KB gzipped on top of core**, which is the floor of the scale Track D priced a capability on. **The query answers the surface that is drawn**, and that is the whole design: a heightfield is stored as a lattice and drawn as triangles, and a bilinear patch through four corners is _not_ the pair of triangles that spans them — they agree only at the corners and along their shared diagonal. Interpolating bilinearly because it is the obvious thing puts a character above the ground over half of every cell and below it over the other half, by up to a quarter of that cell's height range, everywhere, for ever, with no screenshot that shows it and no test that fails. So `heightAt` reads the triangle, `heightfieldPatch` emits that same triangulation, and a test asserts **every vertex of a patch** against the query rather than a sample of them. **The normal is the other way round on purpose**: a central difference over the samples, continuous across every cell boundary, because a face normal jumps at every edge and makes two patches shade differently along the edge they share — a crack that is not there. **The seam between two levels of detail is matched rather than hidden.** Where a patch drawn at full detail meets one that skips every fourth sample, the fine edge has vertices the coarse edge does not, and those sit on the field while the coarse edge cuts the chord beneath them: the gap is a hole through to the sky. The usual remedy is a skirt — a vertical curtain dropped from every patch edge, the wrong colour, lit the wrong way, and paid for along every boundary in the world for ever. `neighbours` moves the fine edge's odd vertices onto the coarse edge's own straight segment instead, so the two are one polyline and there is nothing to fill; it costs one interpolation per boundary vertex at build time and no geometry at all. **Measured on an AMD card at 1280x720, both backends**: an unmatched seam lets **15,401 pixels** of the world through, counted per column below that column's own horizon so sky is never mistaken for a hole, and a matched one lets through **exactly zero** — with the two backends agreeing on both figures and byte for byte on both frames, the geometry being built once on the CPU and handed to each. **What matching costs, stated because it is real**: along a matched edge the drawn surface is the coarse chord rather than the field, so the query and the picture differ there by up to the sag of one coarse cell — the same error the coarse patch carries over its whole area, arriving one cell early. **Several materials blend across one field, as vertex colour.** `TerrainMaterials` takes a weight map and `heightfieldPatch` bakes the blend into the vertices — which is the idiomatic answer here rather than a compromise, this engine's colour _being_ vertex data. A splat map read by a shader would mean a texture bound on every terrain draw and a branch in `flatFrag`, which Track D measured at 19.8 KB gzipped generated into sixteen fragment permutations; this costs nothing at runtime, the blend happening once where the patch is built. **What it gives up is sharpness**: the blend is only as fine as the mesh, so a boundary inside a cell is a gradient across it and a patch at a quarter detail blends four times as coarsely — a consumer wanting a road edge draws that patch at full detail, which is the dial the geometry already has. **And the weights are read bilinearly, which is the opposite of how a height is read**: a height is read as the triangle because the surface is _drawn_ as triangles and the query must agree with the picture, and a weight is not drawn at all, so reading it as triangles would put a crease along every cell diagonal for nothing. Weights are normalised and an unpainted sample falls back to the first material, because black is not a colour terrain should be by accident. **It collides, through the mesh the picture is made of**: `meshShape` takes exactly the two arrays a patch hands back, so the geometry drawn is the geometry collided with and nothing is authored twice — asserted rather than claimed, a ray cast against that body landing where `heightAt` says the ground is at forty points off the lattice. **That assertion found a real defect**: the mesh was split along one diagonal while the query read the other, and every per-vertex test passed it because a vertex lies on both triangulations — and every test field was of the form `f(x) + g(z)`, which is _separable_, and for a separable field both diagonals give the identical surface. The fields carry a cross term now. **`drift/terrain` is bound**: `heightAt`, three normal components, `slopeAt`, `covers` and the two extents, all deterministic reads. They are declared under `physics.read` and **that is a description rather than a borrowing** — the terrain _is_ the collision surface, which this package's own tests assert — but the honest reason is that the language names no `terrain.*` effect at all: `drift/terrain` is in `SPECIFIED_MODULES` and was missed when the effects were named, where `drift/behavior` was given `behavior.read` and `behavior.write` ahead of any provider precisely so a track would not need a language release first. `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` carries it. **And it collides as a heightfield, not only as a mesh**: `heightfieldShape` in `@driftengine/physics` indexes the cell under a body straight from its x and z, carrying the heights it was handed and **no geometry at all** — no vertex buffer, no index buffer, no tree. Measured at a 129-square field, a mesh collider's positions and indices alone are more than five times the bytes of the heights, before the tree over them is counted. **It is not a second narrow phase**, which is the design decision that matters: `meshContact.ts` still owns every contact rule — many manifolds rather than one, one-sided triangles, the interior-edge filter that stops a box stumbling on a flat seam — and a field only changes _where triangles come from_, an index range instead of a tree query and four samples instead of an index buffer. **The proof is differential rather than descriptive**: both colliders are built over one field and a box is walked across it, and the normals, counts and separations must be _identical_ at every pose; splitting the field's cells the other way turns that red. And the flat-floor case is asserted directly too, since a heightfield collider that reproduced the mesh path's own bug would pass a comparison against it. **The triangulation rule exists in two packages and is guarded rather than trusted**: `@driftengine/physics` imports no other engine package, so it cannot see a `Terrain` — but a `Terrain` _is_ a `Heightfield` structurally, which is how `heightfieldShape(terrain)` type-checks with no import in either direction, and `terrainCollision.test.ts` casts sixty rays at both colliders and at the query and requires all three to agree. That is the arrangement `glDepthFunc` has with `DEPTH_COMPARE`, for the same reason. `Terrain`, `heightfieldPatch`, `TerrainMaterials`, `demo/dev/terrain.html`, `scripts/terrain-check.mjs` |
| **Splats** | **The package ships** — see §1. **`.sog` ships**, sentinel `readSplatSog\|unbundleSog`: the PlayCanvas container, version 2, a ZIP of lossless WebP images and a manifest naming what each channel is. **Two formats share the name** — the self-organising-Gaussians paper is a technique whose released scenes decompress to `.ply` and which documents no on-disk structure, and what capture tools emit is the container. The WebP decoder is a **parameter**, because Node has none and this package will not vendor a thousand lines of VP8L; `browserWebpDecoder` forwards to `createImageTexelDecoder` in core, which reads texels back through a texture upload rather than a canvas. **That is not fastidiousness and it was measured**: a 2D canvas stores colour premultiplied and WebCodecs decodes a WebP with alpha to a premultiplied `BGRA` frame, so every RGB value returns through `round(round(c*a/255)*255/a)` — 3 of 255 out on `sh0.webp`, whose RGB are codebook _indices_ beside an opacity in alpha, against 0 through the texture. Checked against a bundle `@playcanvas/splat-transform` produced from sixty-four Gaussians chosen in this repository: every field inside the quantiser's own resolution, and matched one to one because the container is free to reorder. **View-dependent colour ships**, and the costing that had been sitting in this row is what chose its shape rather than being replaced by it. `readSplatPly` keeps the **l=1 band** — nine coefficients, transposed out of the file's channel-major order into `SplatSource.sh1` — and `packSplats` writes them as **one extra `RGBA32UI` texel**: nine 8-bit values and a **per-splat scale** in the fourth word. Bytes rather than halves because nine halves is eighteen bytes and would not fit a texel; a per-splat scale rather than a capture-wide one because it costs the sixteenth byte and gives every splat the whole range for its own coefficients. The shader evaluates `−C1·y·c0 + C1·z·c1 − C1·x·c2` in the reference sign convention, against a direction taken in the **capture's own space** — `cameraInCaptureSpace` inverts `view · model` once a frame, because the coefficients were trained in that frame and a world-space direction leaves the sheen behind when the capture turns. **The arithmetic that stopped at degree 1**: a splat with no harmonics is two texels, **32 bytes**, and the vertex stage runs **six times a splat** because the quad is two unindexed triangles — so the data texture is read at **192 bytes a splat a frame** before any cache. A degree-`n` expansion is `((n+1)² − 1) × 3` coefficients: one extra texel at degree 1, three at degree 2, six at degree 3, read at 288, 480 and 768 bytes a splat a frame. **Against `SPLAT_BUDGET_DEFAULT`, 400,000 splats**: 76.8 MB a frame at degree 0, **115.2 at degree 1**, 192 at degree 2 and **307.2 at degree 3** — and this document's own mobile figure is **388.7 MB a frame of attachment traffic**, so degree 3 would very nearly double the memory traffic of a frame on the one device that is already the constraint, and the texture would grow from 12.8 MB to 51. Degrees 2 and 3 are declined with those numbers on record rather than left unnamed. **Opt-in by construction, not by a flag**: a capture without an l=1 band is eight words a splat and two texels exactly as before, and the shader's gate is a uniform, so it performs no third fetch. The record width travels through `SplatData.wordsPerSplat` and through the `SPLT` block's own header — which `FORMAT.md` §4.7 had already designed for this, saying a capture carrying harmonics later "fits by raising `wordsPerSplat` and nothing else". **Driven on hardware, both backends.** `demo/dev/splats.html?sh=1&turn=` gives every splat a synthetic band with only `Y(1,0)` set, so the shift is proportional to the z component of the view direction and its **sign flips** between a camera at +z and one at −z — which a view-_independent_ bug cannot do. Measured over the cloud's own pixels: at turn 0 the red channel moves **−57.20** on WebGPU and **−57.23** on WebGL2; at turn π it moves **+70.38** and **+70.43**. Two backends, one answer, to under a tenth of an 8-bit level. |
| **Networking** | **Track J ships** as `@driftengine/network`, 2.3 KB gzipped standalone and 6,901 bytes raw — no renderer in its module graph, which is the property that lets an authoritative host run it, asserted against the manifest rather than described. **One rewind core under both models, because prediction and rollback are the same operation**: put the state back to tick _T_, correct what was wrong about _T_, step forward to where we were. A lockstep peer does it when a guessed input turns out wrong; a predicting client does it when its authority disagrees. A `WorldSnapshot` is the state that goes back — **not** `SerializedScene`, which carries schemas, keys values by stable field id and _creates_ entities on load, all of which are right for a save and fatal for a rewind, since an input recorded against entity 4,194,307 has to still mean that entity. `Transport` is a caller's, per `AGENTS.md`; three arrive — a loopback whose latency, jitter, loss, reordering and duplication come from a seed, a WebSocket, and a WebRTC data channel configured `ordered: false` and `maxRetransmits: 0`, because either alone is half the fix. **Three roles rather than two**: a relay written in another language can carry for this engine and cannot run its simulation, so relay, authority and participant are separate. Two findings came from tests going red rather than from the design: **a fingerprint is only comparable at a confirmed tick**, since the newest tick is speculative and each peer has predicted what the other knows — comparing live worlds halted a healthy session at tick 32; and **an input message carries a run of consecutive ticks**, because at 15% loss a single-input packet loses that input for good and the control with one per packet does not converge. `Sim` is opt-in 48.16 fixed point whose multiply is exact wherever its result is representable, checked against BigInt on products the naive form gets wrong; its consumer is the conformance fixture, which runs in the unit tests, in `scripts/exactness-cross.mjs` and in the browser check, because a feature nothing turns on is written rather than ported. `drift/network` and `drift/rollback` are bound — and Track J answered the effect question the language deferred to it: **`network.write` stays outside `DETERMINISTIC_EFFECTS`, and the reason is the rewind loop rather than the send**, since a `@deterministic` function is precisely the kind that gets re-run and a send is not idempotent. `scripts/network-check.mjs` is the exit test: 31 assertions, both backends, pixel-identical, and two of them were checked by breaking what they cover |
| **XR** | **Track I ships** as `@driftengine/xr`: sessions, stereo views, controller input and hand joints, over both backends. **The camera had to learn to be supplied rather than configured**, and `camera.ts` had already written the reason down for an unrelated purpose — _only a centred crop of a symmetric frustum is itself a symmetric frustum; an off-centre one is sheared, which `perspective` cannot produce_ — which is exactly what a headset's eye projection is, off-axis by the distance from pupil to display centre. So `adoptView` takes the runtime's matrices, recomputes the combined and inverse ones so culling and picking keep working, and decomposes `position` and `forward` back out, because a listener placed at `camera.position` would otherwise follow the last flat frame; `yaw`, `pitch` and `roll` are deliberately left alone, since a supplied rotation may be one no Euler triple describes. The loop gained an optional `frameSource`, so a session drives frames on the headset's clock and the `XRFrame` reaches `render` as a fourth argument typed `unknown`, because core has no business naming one. **Both layer paths are built**: `XRGPUBinding` with a projection layer where a runtime has one, `XRWebGLLayer` otherwise, and a WebGPU layer that fails to build falls through to WebGL2 with a sentence rather than refusing, because a game on WebGPU meeting a WebGL-only WebXR should still enter a session. **`support.ts` asks by doing**, which is `probeDevice`'s rule applied to a runtime: measured 2026-09-05 in Chrome 151 with no headset, `inline` reports supported, the session starts, the reference space is granted, and then `makeXRCompatible` throws `InvalidStateError` — and without it there is no base layer and therefore no frame at all, which is the step no support flag reports on. **A hand joint that stops being tracked keeps its last pose**, because a tracker loses joints constantly as fingers occlude each other and zeroing one collapses that finger onto the wrist for a frame; the flag says the pose is stale and what to do about it is the game's. **`drift/xr` is bound with twelve capabilities and it was the last surface the linker refused**, so every module the language specifies is now described here. None of them is deterministic, on `drift/ui`'s own argument about a pointer, and none is a matrix, on `drift/render`'s about reading a dial back. **What has not been measured is written down rather than implied**: `npm run check:xr` covers what a machine with no headset reaches, the unit tests cover everything past the first frame against a synthetic runtime, and a real immersive session, stereo on hardware, controller input, hand tracking, device performance and the compositor's reprojection are carried as an open row |
| **Sky clock** | `celestialStateAt` samples a sun, a moon, a lunar phase and a day factor from a timestamp the caller supplies, allocating nothing. **It knew no latitude for a time**, and the gap was reported by a consumer who had worked it out for themselves and written a note beside their workaround — which is the shape of report this document exists to make unnecessary. The simplified model swung the sun through a fixed arc peaking at 66° wherever the world was meant to be, had no season, swept a whole turn of azimuth in a day, and pinned the moon exactly opposite the sun — which contradicted the phase reported beside it, so a crescent rose at midnight. **A `CelestialSite` fixes all four**: a declination from the day of the year by Cooper's equation, an hour angle from the clock, and the two spherical formulas over them and the latitude; the moon then takes its phase as its elongation, so a new moon shares the sun's place and a full one is half a turn from it. `obliquityDeg` is a parameter because a stylised world may want no seasons at all or sharper ones. **The simplified model is kept rather than replaced**, and a caller that names no site gets the same numbers bit for bit — asserted against hand-derived literals rather than against a second call, because every world authored here is tuned against that arc and a model that silently moved the sun would move every shadow in every consumer at once. **Nor could it name an hour**, which is the second thing a consumer worked out before this document did. The hour came off the timestamp through `Date#getHours` — the _host machine's_ wall clock — so one build, one instant and a pinned day put solar noon at **12:00** under `TZ=UTC`, **10:00** in Rome, **16:00** in New York and **03:00** in Tokyo, and the only way to say an hour was to build a timestamp whose host offset cancelled the one being added. **That trick steadies the sun and cannot reach the moon**, whose phase is read off the timestamp's absolute value and so drifted with the host — a fiftieth of a cycle, five per cent of illumination on a disc nine thousandths of a radian across: invisible, and still not a fact about the world. **`CelestialSite.longitudeDeg` and `utcOffsetHours` are the way to say it**: either one makes the timestamp a plain UTC instant and the engine derives the site's own hour, the offset naming its calendar day and the meridian placing its sun — up to half an hour off the centre of its zone, which is a correction this row once hand back to the caller. A site naming neither, and a caller passing no site at all, keeps the host reading exactly, because that is the model every world here was authored against; `celestialClock.test.ts` walks four time zones inside one process and asserts both halves of that, the four numbers above included. Found by a player in Italy watching the sun set before six. **What it still gives up**: the equation of time, a quarter of an hour either way across the year, which stays the caller's because it is a property of the planet's orbit rather than of the place — a world with an obliquity of its own has an equation of time of its own; and the moon's five-degree orbital inclination, worth up to five degrees of its altitude. **Driven through the sky**: `?scene=6&lat=&day=` on the day-clock scene moves 141,717 pixels of 921,600 at the equator in June, 377,612 at Tromsø in June, and 743,377 in December — where the mean luminance falls from 124.9 to 50.9, which is a polar night. |
| **Saves** | **An asynchronous backend ships**, and the decision it records is the interesting half. `KeyValueStore` is synchronous because preferences are read during _boot_, before the first frame — an await there is a frame drawn on the wrong settings and then corrected, a visible flicker on every load. So the choice was to widen the seam to an asynchronous twin every consumer and every store integration would have to learn, or to hydrate a cache once and drain writes behind it. **Both shipped implementations that are already asynchronous underneath chose the second, independently** — the file store the desktop shell owns and `SteamCloudStore` — and neither needed the interface widened, which is the strongest evidence about the shape there was. `RemoteSaveStore` is that arrangement written once, with the three things a hand-rolled copy leaves out. **Coalescing**: a settings slider writes on every drag frame, so one request per write is sixty requests for one decision, and writes accumulate into a batch with one entry per key. **Retry**: a growing backoff, and giving up on the _attempt_ is never giving up on the _data_ — a failed batch is merged back **under** anything written while it was away, because a merge that overwrote would resend the slider's first value and silently undo the drag, which is asserted by a test that fails a batch mid-flight. **A status**: `status`, `pending`, `lastError` and `onStatusChange`, because a game showing "saved" over a queue that has been failing for ten minutes is worse than either a crash or an honest indicator, and it is what fire-and-forget produces by construction. Nothing throws and nothing rejects: `load` answers a boolean, `flush` resolves either way, and a backend that throws synchronously reads exactly as one that rejects. The timer is **taken as a capability**, on `KeyValueStore`'s own rule about not assuming a browser origin — and a platform with no timer at all still saves, on `flush`, rather than being refused at construction. `SaveBackend.save` takes a **batch** rather than one key, because a consumer with a per-key API can loop inside it and a consumer with a document API cannot build a batch out of per-key calls. What it costs: **a write is durable later, not now**, so a player closing the tab inside the flush delay loses it — `flush()` is the answer, called from whatever the consumer's platform gives it, and the engine registers no `visibilitychange` listener itself because a DOM listener is a decision about the page. What would make it wrong is a consumer needing a write acknowledged before acting on it, and the answer then is `await flush()` at that one site rather than an asynchronous surface everywhere. Reachable from DriftScript as `persistence.saveStatus` and `persistence.pendingSaves`, both of which answer honestly for a synchronous store — idle, and zero. **`flush` is not bound**, and that is the language rather than the engine: it answers a promise and DriftScript has no await. |
| **Drift AI's two bridges** | **Both shipped, and this row formerly refused them for reasons that had stopped being true.** It said there was no navigation bridge because _"nothing pathfinds — `drift/navigation` is refused by the linker on no track at all"_, and no network authority because _"Track J is not built"_. Navigation shipped, and so did Track J; the sentinels below stayed armed and correct while the prose above them went stale, which is the same failure `drift/render` carried for five releases. **The navigation bridge is a factory over a three-function adapter**, because the engine owns the graph and the search and the consumer owns what an agent is. Its one tool, `navigate@1`, **runs the search in `admits`** — the first guard in this package that says something stronger than "the entity still exists", and the answer to a buffered intent being a proposal authored against one snapshot and executed later. A destination stranded between the proposal and the act is discarded and the floor covers. It costs three searches for an intent that is accepted and applied: `take` guards the buffered intent, `applyCommand` guards it again on the way in because a snapshot is never authority, and `execute` runs a third. **The authority bridge got smaller by reading what was already here.** Its design proposed replicating a `u16` intent id on Track J's input path, since `inputLog.ts` is fixed-width per participant per tick and refuses variable-length payloads in writing. But `CommandLog` already records what a model decided and when it crossed, and `ReplaySession` already reads that log, recomputes floor intents and **calls no provider, ever** — so a participant is a replay whose log arrives over a network instead of from a recording, and a rewind is a replay of the same log. One mechanism, two reasons for reaching it. What is left is which side decides, getting decisions onto the wire, and reporting when one lands for a tick already run; performing the rewind is the consumer's, who owns the `RewindLoop`. **Four capabilities reach a script through `drift/ai`** and not one duplicates the twelve `drift/navigation` already binds, because every one of those takes a `NavPath` or a `NavGraph` and none can be aimed at an `Agent`: `reachable` (`navigation.read`, the guard as a question, since `route` computes _and_ writes), `navigate` (`navigation.write`, deterministic on 1.12.0's own argument and therefore safe on every peer — the authority rule is about _model_-authored intents, and a script's command is a function of the simulation that replicates itself by being re-run), `path` (`navigation.read`, the join, so all twelve work on an agent instead of any being bound twice) and `deciding` (`network.read`, on the narrowing `drift/network.authority` already uses). **Nothing hands a script the tools or arguments a model chose**, which is the refusal this row is most able to get wrong: `intentId` is safe because the floor put it there and a replay recomputes it, and a capability returning the model's action would let a `@deterministic` system branch on a provider's answer and take the other branch on replay. `npm run check:ai-bridges` is the exit test: twelve assertions over a page running an authority, a participant, a cut graph and a rewind, and the first two establish that decisions were taken and moved the world before any of the rest is claimed |
| **A script asking what is near it** | **`ecs.findNearest` and `ecs.nearest` ship**, closing a gap a consumer reported as the reason a rule they wanted to hot-reload was living in TypeScript: a script could act only on entities it was handed or a query yielded, so "react to whatever is close" had nowhere to be written. The search takes the component and its three position fields **as names**, so nothing here knows what a transform is called. **Two capabilities rather than one, and the split is what the type cost.** The result is an `Entity`, and a handle is not a number a script can compare to −1 — that is the point of it having its own type — so there is no value left to mean "nothing found". An option would say it and allocates one object per call, on a path written to run every frame for every agent that looks around, which is the allocation `next` refuses. So the search answers a `bool` and `nearest` reads what it found, valid until the next search on that world: the shape `raycast` and `hitBody` already have here, with the same documented lifetime. **A linear scan and it says so**: the entity model keeps no spatial structure, so this costs one pass over everything carrying the component, compared squared so nothing takes a square root. Two things were found by writing it. It walks a **cursor** rather than the store's dense array, because inside a system the value a script passes as `world` is the `SystemView` the schedule handed it and that carries no `store` — a first version worked from a bare world and threw the moment a system called it. And a component named only in a _string_ is invisible to DriftScript's access inference, so the metadata never mentioned it and the system was refused at runtime for undeclared access, with no way for the author to grant it — writing `reads Position` was checked and then dropped. **DriftScript 1.6.0 makes a declaration add**, so declared and inferred access are unioned; under-declaring is still an error, and over-declaring only costs a scheduler that serialises two systems it could have run together |
| **`drift/ecs` speaks `Entity`** | **The whole surface moved off `f64`**, and the paragraph explaining why it could not is gone with it. A handle carries a 26-bit index and a 27-bit generation — the entire 53-bit budget a double holds — so the width was never negotiable, and until DriftScript 1.6.0 the language had no way to _name_ it in a capability signature. It does now, and `Entity` is a type of its own rather than an alias: a handle is assignable **to** an `f64` and not **from** one, so a number a script computed cannot arrive where a handle is wanted, and `e.Health` is legal on a handle and on nothing else. `create`, `at`, `next`, `nearest` and `prefab.spawn` return one; every entity parameter takes one. **`read` still answers `f64`**, because it reads a component _field_, which is a number — typing that as a handle would be the same mistake pointing the other way. **What it breaks**: a script holding a handle in an `f64` can no longer pass it back, which is the refusal working rather than a cost — `docs/corpus/EcsCoroutines.drs` declared `self: f64` and now declares `self: Entity` |
| **DriftScript's unwired surfaces** | **Every surface the language specifies is now described, and this row is a history rather than a gap.** `drift/xr` was the last one the linker refused and **it left that list with Track I**, bound with twelve capabilities; the sentence that stood here — that one surface parses and does not link — has been false since that release and no gate covers prose. **`drift/render` left that list, having been free to leave since 3.43.0.** Its refusal named Track D, Track D completed with refraction, and the surface sat refused for five releases because nothing re-read the mapping when the track closed — while `host.test.ts` had already been corrected to say it waited on a row of its own. What is bound is **seven** per-frame presentation dials — `medium` joined them with the global medium — and **none of the fifty fields of `RenderQuality`**, on the ceiling-and-dial split `renderQuality.ts` already argues for depth of field: a profile is chosen once from what a device can afford and is clamped against what the adapter reports, so a script writing to one would overrule a decision made about hardware it cannot see. Nothing reads a dial back either, because every one is clamped against that ceiling and a read would answer a fact about the machine wearing the costume of a fact about the frame — the argument the language wrote for `network.read` and a confirmed-input watermark. The effect is `scene.write`, which is outside `DETERMINISTIC_EFFECTS`, so a `@deterministic` system may not dim the screen. **Three left that list.** `drift/editor` went with Track K. `drift/network` and `drift/rollback` went with Track J, together, because they are one mechanism: a rewind loop is what lockstep corrects a guess with and what a predicting client corrects a mispredicted world with, so a session and the rewind under it arrive at the same moment or neither is usable. **Track J answered the question the language had deferred to it.** `capability.ts` left `network.write` outside `DETERMINISTIC_EFFECTS` saying the exclusion was _"a deferral rather than a judgement: the track that builds one is the one that can say whether its writes are the simulation or a consequence of it"_. The answer is that it stays outside, and the reason is the rewind loop rather than the send: publishing changes no simulation state, which reads like an argument for admitting it and is backwards once rollback exists, because a `@deterministic` function is precisely the kind that gets re-run and a send is not idempotent. `network.read` stays inside, narrowed to what cannot vary with packet timing — which participant this is, and whether it is the authority. `drift/rollback` is `nondeterministic` throughout, because a system branching on "am I replaying" takes one path live and the other on replay. **DS-8 closed with it**, in DriftScript 1.13.0: `@replicated` is checked rather than merely lexed, and the fixed clock turned out to have survived a rewind all along — it is a step count, so a deadline is an absolute step number and means the same thing after the clock moves either way. **`drift/behavior` landed** and the requirement it was built against is one a hand-written routine cannot meet: a preempted branch is _suspended_ rather than reset, so an agent that stops its errand because it started raining resumes at the step it had reached. **`drift/navigation` was the other**: a graph, an A* whose ties break on the node index so a replay walks the road it walked before, and a follower; its reads are deterministic and its writes became so in 1.12.0. `drift/ecs` and `drift/prefab` were here until Track M shipped, and the sentinels that guarded them are gone with the refusal, which is the mechanism working rather than an edit somebody remembered. **Mock capability providers were withdrawn deliberately**: a mock is a second implementation of a contract with no first implementation to check it against, so anything it agrees with is itself. `docs/corpus/NetworkReplicatedActor.drs` was the file written against a surface that did not exist; it now describes the real one and is compiled against a description of it. **The island worker pool has no `drift/*` surface and that is a decision, recorded here so it is not read later as an oversight.** A pool needs `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` on the consumer's document, so whether one can exist is settled before any script runs and is a property of a deployment. A capability like `physics.workers(4)` would do what it says on an isolated page and silently nothing everywhere else, which is the blind surface the audit removed fifty-seven of. The honest script-visible thing would be a _reading_ of how fast physics happened to be, and a script that branches on that is not deterministic. `parallelism` is where a host reads it instead |

## 2a. The native host and the browser, both ways

**The engine runs on two hosts from one codebase**: a browser, and `@driftengine/native-host` —
Node, Dawn and SDL, with no browser between. Neither is a superset of the other, so the record goes
both ways or it is marketing. Measured 2026-09-19 on an RX 9070 XT under COSMIC, Chrome 151 against
the binding's Dawn, `@kmamal/gpu` 0.2.0. **What the native host has** is guarded by §5's `present`
block, which fails when a capability goes or when the binding under a measured row moves; **what it
lacks** is guarded by sentinels, like every row in §2.

**What the native host has that a page does not:**

| Capability                             | On the native host                                                                                                                                                                                                  | In a page                                                                                                                | Guard                  |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| Threads with shared memory, no headers | `SharedArrayBuffer` and a `Worker` exist whatever serves the game, and the physics island pool runs on threads by its own default (`threads.test.ts`)                                                               | only in a cross-origin isolated page, which takes two headers from the server; otherwise the pool refuses and names them | `native-threads`       |
| The adapter's own limits               | 3D textures 16,384 a side, 8,192 array layers, 1D textures 32,768, a uniform binding up to 4 GiB, offsets aligned to 4 bytes, a workgroup 1,024 deep                                                                | 2,048, 2,048, 16,384, 64 KiB, 256 and 64: the browser reports a tier rather than the adapter                             | `native-device-limits` |
| Tiles from disk                        | `tileFiles(dir)` hands the texture streamer tiles read from a directory, for a game's native entry to use                                                                                                           | over HTTP, from a server                                                                                                 | `native-tile-files`    |
| A game as an archive, WebGPU included  | `native-linux-x64`: 61.3 MB with its own Node, a WebGPU frame 750 ms after launch — where the Electron build of the same program did not start under this machine's Wayland session and offered no WebGPU under X11 | nothing to install, which is the other table's first row                                                                 | `native-target`        |
| Haptics                                | the standard's `dual-rumble` effect through SDL — **parity rather than advantage**                                                                                                                                  | the same effect, which Chrome gives a page on Linux                                                                      | `native-rumble`        |

**What a page has that the native host does not:**

| Capability                      | In a page                                                                                                                                                                          | On the native host                                                                                                                                                                | Sentinel                |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Instant distribution            | a URL, with nothing installed                                                                                                                                                      | an archive a player downloads and unpacks. **No sentinel**: a native host is installed by definition, so this row cannot become false                                             | —                       |
| Windows and macOS               | every browser                                                                                                                                                                      | Linux x64 alone. **After 4.0.0**, by the maintainer's word; the three bindings publish binaries for both, and each platform needs a launcher, its signing and its own measurement | `native-windows-macos`  |
| The newer device                | Chrome's Dawn: 48 sampled textures a stage, 16 storage buffers, 128 colour-attachment bytes a sample, both texture-format tiers, `primitive-index` and `texture-component-swizzle` | the binding's older Dawn: 16, 10 and 32, and none of those features — and 0.2.1, the next binding, refuses every `createView`                                                     | `native-device-limits`  |
| WebGL2                          | beneath WebGPU wherever there is no usable device                                                                                                                                  | WebGPU only: a machine with no Vulkan device cannot run it                                                                                                                        | `native-webgl2`         |
| Assistive technology            | a tree an assistive technology walks                                                                                                                                               | published to nothing — §2's row                                                                                                                                                   | `native-accessibility`  |
| A document beyond the canvas    | the game's own HTML interface                                                                                                                                                      | `document.createElement` refuses by name                                                                                                                                          | `native-dom`            |
| The engine's badge              | drawn as markup (`ui/splash.ts`), or by the desktop shell in a window of its own                                                                                                   | not drawn, and `drift-package doctor` says so                                                                                                                                     | `native-badge`          |
| A store                         | the desktop shell carries Steam                                                                                                                                                    | `steam.appId` does nothing, and `doctor` says so                                                                                                                                  | `native-store`          |
| Pipelines kept between launches | Chrome builds the starter's renderer in 75 ms warm                                                                                                                                 | compiled on every start, 355 ms of 750: Dawn has a blob cache and the binding exposes none of it                                                                                  | `native-pipeline-cache` |
| Clip export, sharing, WebXR     | `VideoEncoder`, `navigator.share`, `navigator.xr`                                                                                                                                  | absent, and the engine says so where it asks                                                                                                                                      | `native-media`          |

## 3. Three limits that are measured rather than assumed

**The lit pass uses ten of WebGL2's guaranteed sixteen texture units.** Three
directional cascades at 0–2, the point-shadow array at 3, then the four material maps together —
surface at 4, normal at 5, ORM at 6, emissive at 7 — the environment probe at 8, the froxel table
at 9, and **six free**. The probe was always there and this paragraph did not count it, which is
corrected rather than quietly restated; `textureUnitBudget.test.ts` derives the total from the
highest unit now rather than counting it, because counting it is what got it wrong. It once fill all sixteen exactly — the twelve point-shadow cubemaps were twelve separate
`samplerCube` declarations, because GLSL ES cannot index a sampler array — and that was found from
a phone, on a scene lit almost entirely by point lights, rendering 0.7% of the frame above black.
`textureUnitBudget.test.ts` holds the arithmetic, including that a light now costs a _layer_ rather
than a unit, which is the property most easily undone by accident.

**They are what the material maps come out of, and all three have now been spent.** The normal map
took the first, the ORM map the second and the emissive map the third, each named in
`textureUnitBudget.test.ts` before it was taken so that the change spending one had to read what it
was spending. **Phase 1.3 is complete**: the material core is tangents, `ATTR_TANGENT`, and normal,
ORM and emissive maps, end to end from glTF through the container to both backends.

**The froxel table spends one unconditionally, and that is what a runtime branch costs.** Clustered
lighting is a branch on a uniform rather than a permutation — see the Lights row — so its sampler is
declared in every profile, and a declared sampler needs a complete texture bound whether or not the
branch reads it. With clustering off the binding is a single texel rather than 292 KB.

**`MAX_POINT_LIGHTS` is 16, and it was 10 because ten was where the units ran out.** Sixteen lights
is twenty pool layers plus two live ones at 1024², 92.3 MB, against the 100.7 MB the sixteen cubes
it replaces cost — fewer bytes and six more shadowed lights. Eighteen is where the memory exactly
equals the old cost.

**Sixteen is what the engine declares and not always what a part will link.** Twenty of the lit
shader's uniform arrays are sized by that budget and fourteen by the four area lights, and GLSL ES
spends a whole row of the fragment uniform grid per array _element_ whatever its base type: the full
budget is **440 rows**, an Adreno 740 offers **256**, and WebGL2 guarantees only **224**. So the
WebGL2 renderer counts the shader it is about to compile and builds at the largest budget that fits
— 8 lights and 2 rectangles is 252 rows with point shadows still compiled in, and 4 and 1 is 158.
`renderer.shadedLights` reports what was resolved; `maxLights` and `maxAreaLights` are the ceiling
for a consumer who wants to choose one. WebGPU has no such ceiling and reports all sixteen.

**On WebGPU the widest permutation asks for seven sampled textures and four samplers**, against an
adapter offering forty-eight and sixteen. It asked for seventeen and three before, and the
seventeen was why `select.ts` has to request a raised limit at all.

**The point-shadow filter cap is `MAX_FILTER_RADIUS = 0.25`, up from 0.07.** Four attempts went
into widening it and none worked, for one reason: a wide angular filter on a cube map crosses face
seams, which draws as straight lines radiating from beneath the light. Seven separate reports
pointed at those lines. An octahedral map is one projection over the whole sphere and has no faces
to cross, so the cap came off the floor the seams had pinned it to.

**0.25 rather than further, and the ceiling is arithmetic.** The filter width and the strength fade
are driven by the same quantity, so a shadow at `sourceRadius * spread` of 0.625 has faded to
nothing and there is no blur left to apply; at 0.25 it is still at 84% strength and plainly a
shadow. A sweep at 0.07, 0.15, 0.25, 0.40 and 0.625 was captured on both point-lit scenes and none
of them drew a line, a band or a speckle — **and the GPU timings were too noisy to choose on**, two
runs of one build differing by more than two runs of two builds. `scripts/docs.test.mjs` asserts
the number above is the number in `lobes.ts`, because this was prose and prose is what drifted.

**The GPU-driven pipeline is opt-in, WebGPU only, and refuses rather than falls back.**
`createRenderer({ pipeline: 'gpu-driven' })` on a backend without indirect draws throws with the
reason in words, checked against the backend that will _draw_ rather than the one that was asked
for — three of the paths into that decision arrive having fallen back from WebGPU. Verified on
hardware, because nothing in a test environment resolves a renderer:
`/ibl.html?backend=webgl2&pipeline=gpu-driven` fails and draws nothing, `?backend=webgpu&…` draws.

**It draws, on a device, and here is what it costs.** `scripts/gpu-parity.mjs` runs twenty checks
— instance culling, the level cut, the depth reduction, cluster culling, the near-plane refusal, the
compaction into one draw, the visibility buffer's packing, material binning, the surface
reconstruction, the lit expression, the shadow lookup, the gradient a compute invocation has to
assemble for itself, the octahedral probe mapping, the DriftTexture decode interpreter and the
surface frame a textured pixel is read with, and the network evaluator in single and half precision
— and `GpuDrivenPass` is the encoder that runs them in order. **Until 2026-09-17 that was one short**: the instance cull was checked on the device and never dispatched by the pass, and every cluster of a mesh wholly outside the view was cut and tested one by one. It is a stage of the frame now, before the cut: the cut leaves a hidden mesh's clusters unselected, and the cluster cull skips whatever the cut did not select, which also stops it testing every cluster at a level the cut did not choose. The eighteen scenes are 0 of 921,600 against the build before it, and so are the three rigs photographed at three turned yaws, where up to 56 of the wall rig's 197 meshes are behind or beside the eye; the culling stages read below the device clock's 0.066 ms on both builds. **The run prints the count**, because a written one drifted: three documents here
said nine, thirteen and fourteen on 2026-09-17, and the script's own comment called its last check
the fourteenth.

Measured 2026-09-17 on an RX 9070 XT through radv at 1280×510, from the device's own timestamps
rather than from a frame clock — a `requestAnimationFrame` delta reports half a millisecond for the
densest of these with vsync off, because the device is still working when the callback returns.

**A range rather than a number, because the clock is quantised.** Four captures of each rig land on
multiples of about 0.065 ms and nothing between them, so a single frame's figure is a bucket and
quoting one is quoting the low end of a distribution. The figures before 2026-09-17 did exactly
that, and they also predate the shadow map. **Since 2026-09-17 a rig renders the map only where the
frame reads it**, which is the second pipeline's frame graph at work — below the table.

| Rig                | Triangles | Clusters | Device ms     | Where it goes                                      |
| ------------------ | --------- | -------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `gpu-driven-dense` | 1,002,528 | 7,843    | **0.98–1.05** | about half of it the shadow map: 0.46–0.59 without |
| `gpu-driven-occl`  | 2,364     | 1,182    | **0.39–0.52** | two phases, the second drawing what the wall hid   |
| `gpu-driven-mats`  | 780       | 390      | **0.52**      | sixteen bins, three textured; shading 0.26–0.33    |

**Re-measured 2026-09-18, four captures each, after the occlusion history and the light's own cull
below.** The wall rig fell a step, because its history now lets go of what the wall hides; the dense
rig rose one, which is the fixed cost of the light's pyramid over half a 2048 map.

**The wall rig rose one step of the clock on 2026-09-17, from 0.46–0.52**, and that is the phase-one
fix below: phase one now draws everything the history holds instead of trimming it against a pyramid
from the frame before, which is what the two-phase design asks it to do.

**Both pipelines are scheduled by one graph representation, 2026-09-17, which is Wave 1A's exit
criterion.** `GpuDrivenPass` records its twelve stages into a `Deps` table every frame —
`gpudriven/pipeline.ts` holds the edges — and `scheduleGraph` keeps what something reads: the frame
it encodes is the frame it encoded before, command for command in `gpuDrivenPass.test.ts`, except
that **an unshadowed frame no longer draws a map nothing samples**. With `?dirshadows=0` the three
rigs are 0 of 921,600 against the build that still drew it, and the million-triangle rig's device time
falls from 0.92 to 0.46–0.59 ms; with the shadow on it reads what it did. The forward renderer's flush
takes the same scheduler under `quality.identifierGraph` (`?idgraph=1`, off by default), through
`frame/flushGraph.ts`, which records a mask bit as an identifier and derives the passes, clears and
discards the mask scheduler does — a seeded corpus of the renderer's own node shapes agrees exactly,
and every frame-graph test in `webgpu/renderer.test.ts` runs under both. **The eighteen scenes the
harness walks are pixel-identical with it on.** `scheduleGraph` allocates nothing once warm, which
it did not before: a `Set` and a flag array per call. `core-only` grows 1,456 bytes gzipped, because
the renderer reaches the second scheduler whether or not the flag is set.

**`showroom` is not repeatable between runs of one build, whatever the flag says**, and a delta-0
comparison of it has to be read with that in mind. Thirteen captures on 2026-09-17 produced three
distinct images, all differing only at the wheel rims — 33 pixels in three blocks, or 692 in 106 at
worst delta 6 — and both settings produced the same two common ones, six captures a side. The held
clock holds the frame count; it does not appear to hold whatever the wheels' detail settles on while
the model streams in. Every other scene has been identical in every capture taken.

**The six published scenes are pixel-identical with it in the tree**: 0 of 750,080 pixels at
`--delta=16` on WebGPU against the commit before, all eight of them, and `core-only` is
byte-identical — 678,305 gzipped — with and without the barrel exports that reach it.

**What it draws is the standard material's subset, and the subset is complete as of 2026-09-17**:
vertex colour times a material tint, one directional term **with its specular highlight and its
shadow**, the forward path's hemispheric ambient or a baked probe's irradiance, a glow scaled by the
frame's clock, **the room a surface reflects**, **metalness**, and **DriftTexture materials** —
base colour, a normal map and an ORM map, each a decode program run per shaded pixel on the device
— **and since 2026-09-18 an emissive map**, flat/main.ts's `emissiveTint * emissiveMapped`: the
glow is the albedo times the map times the material's emissive, so a black texel glows nowhere.
The city at dusk needed it — lit windows in walls that do not glow — and it took the fourth program
lane the table had reserved, so nothing grew. `vertex-glow-check.mjs` draws a ramp through it on
both of this pipeline's shaders and on the forward path's own map: the three agree to one level of
255, and through a black map all three stay black while every vertex glows. Eleven scenes are 0 of
921,600 against the build before it.
The three rigs stay in `DRAFT_SCENES` until the maintainer says to publish them.

**The scene is no longer fixed, 2026-09-18.** `GpuDrivenPass` uploaded its geometry in a method
called `buildStatic` and its constructor said why: this pipeline's geometry does not move. A voxel
world streams chunks as a player walks and remeshes one on every block they break, so it has to.
`StreamingScene` is four free lists over what the pass binds — vertices, indices, clusters and
meshes — and **it keeps the cluster and mesh records and none of the geometry**: a mesh's vertices
and indices go through a `GeometrySink` straight into the pass's two buffers when it is placed, and
a frame uploads the records that changed rather than the scene. So a scene goes to one pass, and a
