second is refused by name (the old dirty journal already made a changing scene one pass's, silently:
a second pass drew stale geometry). And while a pass holds the scene, a range a removal frees
waits for the next upload before it is reused, because a queue write lands before the frame it was
made during runs; `heldBytes` says what the scene holds on the CPU, which is a scene filled before
its pass mounts until the pass takes it, and one mesh's scratch after.
**There is one constructor and the static case is a scene filled once**, which is what keeps the
three rigs on the path every published scene uses; a second signature would mean the rigs exercise a
path nothing else does, which is how a control stops being a control. A quiet frame issues no upload
at all, and `add` refuses with `null` rather than throwing, because a streaming consumer calls it
from a frame loop where an exception is a crashed demo and a refusal is a chunk that arrives a frame
later. **A removed mesh's cull record is zeroed as well as its index count**, or the light's
bounding sphere stays stretched over geometry that is not there — a shadow map spread across empty
space rather than anything that fails.

**Best fit does not fragment on a voxel workload, and that is measured rather than argued.**
`scripts/stream-fragmentation.mjs` walks a ring of 121 chunks in an outward spiral over 20,000
operations, chunk meshes from 128 to 2,048 quads drawn toward the small end, one operation in twenty
a remesh to a different size. The number that names fragmentation is **an add refused while the
total free exceeds what it asked for** — the room is there, in pieces, and no piece is long enough
— and at a headroom of 1.25 that count is **zero**. It stays zero at 1.15; at **1.05 it is 47**,
every one of them a refusal with room and none for exhaustion. So the free list does fragment, and
it takes a budget with five per cent spare to see it. **Fixed-size pages stay shut**: they bound the
worst case by construction and put an indirection in the vertex fetch, which is four shaders changed
for a problem this says nobody has. The remesh is _not_ what causes it — with remeshing off the 1.05
rung refuses 74 rather than 47 — so streaming varying sizes in and out is the whole effect.

**An alpha cutout ships, in the raster.** `GpuDrivenMaterial.alphaCutoff` discards a fragment whose
base-colour alpha is below it, and the test is in the visibility raster rather than in the shading
pass because that is where a pixel learns which triangle owns it: a discard in `shade` comes after
the buffer already holds the leaf, and what stood behind it was never rastered. That gives the
raster the material table and the whole decode machinery for one question, and **a material whose
cutoff is zero asks none of it** — eleven scenes are 0 of 921,600 against the build before it, which
is the measurement that the branch costs an opaque scene nothing. `gpudriven/alphaTest.ts` is the
rule and `gpu-parity.mjs` checks the shader against it over 80 pairs across eight cutoffs, nine of
them exactly on one. **A device settled the one case the reference had wrong**: WGSL does not
require an implementation to support NaN, so written `cutoff <= 0` the guard let a cutoff that is
not a number fall through to a comparison false for every alpha — this engine discarded the whole
surface and the device drew all of it. Both keep it now. **What is absent**: the depth-only shadow
pass shares the raster's vertex stage and has no fragment stage, so a cutout surface casts the
shadow of its whole quad.

**Transparency ships, through the pipeline's front half.** A visibility buffer stores one surface a
pixel and therefore cannot hold a blend at all — that is architecture rather than an omission, since
the whole saving of the opaque path is that shading happens once per pixel after the frame knows
which triangle won, and a pane of glass has no winner. What is reusable is `instanceCull` and the
cut: "which clusters, at which level of detail" is the same question for a pane as for a wall, so
they **run a second time** over the other half of the scene, filtered by `GpuDrivenMaterial.blend`,
and a blended raster shades in its own fragment stage into two weighted-transparency targets. **The
two halves are exclusive**, asserted cluster by cluster on a device: no cluster is drawn twice and
none is dropped. The blended raster **includes `SHADE_LIGHTING_WGSL` rather than restating it**, so
a pane is lit by the expression a wall is lit by, character for character; the weight and the
resolve are `render/orderIndependent.ts`'s, shared as one WGSL declaration between the raster, the
resolve and the parity entry point, and checked against the reference over 54 fragments with ten of
them against a clamp. **It costs 0.066 ms on the materials rig and exactly nothing on the other
two**, from the device's own timestamps: a scene with no blended material schedules all three stages
away and encodes the frame it encoded before they existed, twenty-one lines of the fixed-frame
fixture having moved by a bind group's serial number and nothing else. The targets are the pass's
own rather than the renderer's, because a contributed pass is handed a device and no attachments;
the resolve is a premultiplied _over_ rather than the forward path's lerp, because this pipeline's
colour target carries a coverage mask in its alpha that the blit reads. **What is absent**: a
transparent surface is not shadowed — `shadowFactor` wants a receiver plane, the shading pass
derives one from barycentric gradients because a compute invocation has no neighbours, and a
fragment stage would need a second derivation for a term whose whole point is that there is one.
**Nor does it cast one**, since 2026-09-18: the map is drawn from the light's own run of the cut,
which takes the opaque half as the camera's first run does — water should not shadow the lake bed,
and a pane that must cast gives it an opaque frame. There is no per-pixel sort and no refraction;
neither exists on the forward path either.

**An ordinary image needs no second texture kind, and that was a reading confirmed rather than a
thing built.** `SAMPLE_BLOCK` is the DriftTexture vocabulary's passthrough — the slot a program
reaches for when a network does not help — and a block is raw bytes, so a program whose only
instruction is one of these _is_ an image sampler. Four places in the code said so and none had ever
been run; `gpu-parity.mjs` now runs it over 256 points on a 64 by 64 picture, corners and texel
centres alike, worst error **1.5e-8**, and it passed the first time it was run.

**All three are in one frame**: `gpu-driven-mats` gained a ring-shaped cutout you can see the scene
through, a pane at 0.45 with a glowing box behind it, and a picture. The pane's blend was verified
by turning the flag off rather than by looking — **5,622 pixels of 921,600 differ**, and with it off
the pane is a solid slab hiding the boxes the blend shows through.

**The voxel sandbox runs on the second pipeline, 2026-09-18, and what that buys is a frame that
stops growing with the world.** `?pipeline=gpu-driven` on scene 0 streams every chunk into one
`StreamingScene`, clustered by position as it arrives, and draws the terrain, its leaves and its
water through one `GpuDrivenPass` whose blit hands the frame its depth — so the mobs, which stay on
the forward path and draw after it, stand behind a hill rather than in front of it. Flying forward
at 5 m/s, 32 m above the spawn's ground, `scripts/sandbox-bench.mjs` times 300 frames a run: `cpu`
is the scene's whole frame on the main thread and `gpu` its device timestamps. Median / ninety-fifth
percentile in milliseconds, RX 9070 XT through radv, re-measured 2026-09-18 once the streaming scene
stopped keeping a copy, and again on 2026-09-19 once a WebGPU mesh stopped keeping one. `buffers` is
what the page holds in ArrayBuffers once the run is over (the backing stores `Runtime.getHeapUsage`
reports, the one figure of that call that moves when a buffer is allocated — `sandbox-bench.mjs
--calibrate` checks it); `held` is what the port reserves on the device for vertices and indices,
sized to the worst chunk the world makes over the ring it keeps.

| Radius | Forward cpu | Forward gpu | Forward draws | Forward buffers | Port cpu    | Port gpu    | Port clusters | Port buffers |     Held |
| -----: | ----------- | ----------- | ------------: | --------------: | ----------- | ----------- | ------------: | -----------: | -------: |
|      6 | 1.10 / 8.70 | 0.39 / 0.46 |           113 |           59 MB | 0.80 / 11.3 | 0.79 / 0.92 |         3,645 |       128 MB |   126 MB |
|     12 | 2.30 / 11.2 | 0.52 / 0.59 |           443 |           89 MB | 1.10 / 14.5 | 1.05 / 1.18 |        12,221 |       138 MB |   407 MB |
|     16 | 3.60 / 14.5 | 0.72 / 0.79 |           769 |          110 MB | 1.20 / 16.1 | 1.25 / 1.38 |        20,728 |       165 MB |   685 MB |
|     20 | 6.00 / 17.2 | 0.85 / 0.98 |         1,182 |          143 MB | 1.50 / 16.5 | 1.38 / 1.51 |        31,916 |       205 MB | 1,033 MB |
|     24 | 7.90 / 21.3 | 1.05 / 1.11 |         1,658 |          184 MB | 1.50 / 20.1 | 1.51 / 1.64 |        45,230 |       252 MB | 1,454 MB |
|     28 | 11.8 / 27.2 | 1.25 / 1.31 |         2,225 |          240 MB | 2.20 / 27.7 | 1.64 / 1.77 |        61,528 |       306 MB | 1,946 MB |
|     31 | 12.6 / 24.5 | 1.38 / 1.51 |         2,709 |          277 MB | 2.30 / 23.0 | 1.77 / 1.90 |        75,048 |       348 MB | 2,361 MB |
|     32 | 13.7 / 23.6 | 1.44 / 1.51 |         2,887 |          290 MB | 2.10 / 18.1 | 1.77 / 2.36 |        79,788 |       365 MB | 2,509 MB |

**The forward path's median frame grows with what it submits, 1.1 ms to 13.7; the port's stays
between 0.8 and 2.3.** That is the whole of the port's claim and it holds: at radius 28 the forward
path spends 11.8 ms of every frame encoding 2,225 draws and the port spends 2.2 ms on everything.
**The port's device time is about twice the forward path's at every radius** — a fixed half a
millisecond of stages the forward path does not have: binning, shading in a compute pass, two culls,
the pyramid, the blended half. A voxel world is the forward path's best case, large quads under one
material with little overdraw, so a visibility buffer has little to save there and its overhead is
what shows. **Neither pipeline holds sixty at the ninety-fifth percentile past radius 20 (this run: the
forward path to 16, the port to 20), and on both the frame that breaks it is a chunk being built** — generation, the light flood and the mesher on the
main thread, which the port does not change and to which it adds its clustering, a ninth of a build.
At a walking pace the ceiling is the world's generation rather than either renderer, and a sandbox
that built its chunks off the main thread would move it.

**The port reaches the sandbox's cap, radius 32, since the streaming scene stopped keeping a copy of
its geometry.** It held every array it uploaded, and at 32 the vertices alone were 2,230,135,200
bytes — an ArrayBuffer Chrome will not allocate (1.99 GiB allocates and 2.0 does not) while this
adapter binds 4 GiB, so the port mounted to 31 and was refused by name at 32. Now the vertices and
indices go straight into the pass's buffers when a chunk is placed and the scene keeps neither. **At
radius 16 the page's buffers went from 851 MB to 168 MB, 683 MB less**, against the 684.7 the
capacity predicts (608.6 MB of vertices and 76.1 of indices); at 32 the port holds 365 MB. What is
left in the port's column is the rest of the page, which this change does not touch. The device's two limits,
read by `scripts/adapter-limits.mjs`, are both 4,294,967,292 bytes, so the device would hold the
vertices of every radius to 44 — past the sandbox's cap — and 45 is where its own refusal would be.
The reservation is still the worst chunk the world makes, about twice the median one, times the
ring, with a quarter over for fragmentation — sizing, which is a separate question from copies.

**The forward path held a second copy too, and it was the engine's.** Its column held more than the
port's at every radius and 2,103 MB at 32, because a live WebGPU mesh kept its whole `MeshData` and
its interleaved rows: the mesh's `complete` getter was made in the same scope as the upload
generator and a `filter`, both of which read `data`, and V8 gives every closure in a scope one
shared context. The handle, the upload and a dynamic mesh's `update` are made by functions of their
own now, a finished upload lets go of its source, and `render/meshRetention.test.ts` forces a
collection and holds it on both backends (WebGL2's `Mesh` was already clean). **Measured against
`main` the same evening: 582 MB to 110 at radius 16, and 2,103 MB to 290 at 32**, with the same
chunks and draws and every published scene 0 px on both backends. The table above is after both
fixes. The port now holds more than the forward path at every radius, by 49 to 75 MB —
what that difference is has not been measured.

**Photographed at matched radius 6, the two differ in 18,969 pixels of 921,600 at `--delta=16`**,
and the port is repeatable to 0 of 921,600 between runs. Where it goes: 5,592 pixels are sky on one
and something solid on the other — 5,305 of them sky seen through a leaf on the forward path where
the port draws the leaf, and 287 the other way, because a cutout read from a coverage-weighted chain
keeps more coverage at a distance than level 0 does, so the port's canopy is denser; 3,684 lie in the
rows of the far horizon, where the forward path's atlas has no chain and aliases; 1,983 are the
readout's own text; 1,733 are sand, whose ripples speckle on the forward path; and 5,977 are texels
of leaves, bark and the sides of grass at a distance. 44% of it sits in islands of four pixels or
fewer and the largest island is 678 pixels, an eight-row strip of distant horizon. No region is a
surface one pipeline draws and the other does not.

**The port does not cast the sun's shadow unless asked, because the forward sandbox casts none** —
nothing in it calls `beginShadowPass`; its shade is baked into vertex colours — so the comparison is
matched. **Asking found the second pipeline's shadow stage unfit for a world, and it is fixed.** It
drew every cluster _slot_ of the scene's capacity, live or not, at every level at once, into one map
fitted to the whole scene's sphere: 2.10 ms at radius 6 and 9.04 ms at radius 14, and texels a
quarter of a metre wide. Now the front half runs a fourth time over the light's own buffers — the
camera's cut with no mesh hidden, a cull against the light's box, a compaction into a list of its
own — and the map draws that list indirectly (and since, in two halves against a pyramid of its own,
below); and past
`GpuDrivenShadowOptions.followRadius` the map is a sphere of that radius around the eye, snapped to
whole texels of a fixed light space so its edges do not crawl, reaching toward the sun as far as the
scene does. With `?portshadow=1`, flying, the stage is 0.07 to 0.20 ms at every radius from 6 to 31 and adds 0.07 to
0.19 ms to the port's whole device frame.
**Under the radius, or with none, the fit is the scene's as it always was**: the three rigs and the
eight published scenes are 0 of 921,600 either side of the change, except the materials rig's
44 pixels, which are its pane's shadow — a blended surface casts none now, above. **The rigs time
as they did** — 0.92–0.98, 0.46–0.59 and 0.46–0.52 ms re-measured the same way — because a rig's
clusters are all live and all inside the light's box, so the list the light culls to is the list it
drew; what the change buys is a world's. **What one sphere
gives up against a cascade**: nothing past the radius is shadowed at all, faded out over the map's
outer quarter rather than cut.

**The second pipeline draws the forward path's haze and hands the frame its depth, 2026-09-18.**
`render/fog.ts` is the medium as arithmetic — `atmosphereFog` fills a `FogTarget` from an
`Environment`, and `GpuDrivenView.fog` takes it — and `FOG_WGSL` applies it on the shading pass and
on the blended raster alike, so a pane at the edge of the view sits in the haze rather than standing
out of it; `gpu-parity` agrees over 392 samples in 56 media, worst 7.8e-5. `presentDepth` makes the
blit write the frame's depth as it lays its colour, so forward-path geometry drawn after the pass
depth-tests against it: `depth-share-check.mjs` hides a box behind the pass's wall, 3,468 pixels to
none, and keeps every pixel of the one in front. The blit lays premultiplied colour **over** the
frame now — it had never composited transparency over anything, and found that out the first time
it was asked.

**A city at dusk is the second pipeline's own published scene, 2026-09-18** — `demo/city.ts`, the
last of `SCENES`. Manhattan at blue hour, generated from one seed with no asset: the 1811 grid of
240 × 61 m blocks, a street wall of walk-ups and prewar blocks with cornices and water tanks,
setback towers on the 1916 rule with floodlit crowns, glass boxes whose curtain walls show lit
office floors, supertalls, neon over the shopfronts. **1,844,094 triangles over 144 blocks**,
streamed a block at a time as the camera flies a 3.27 km loop down the avenues and cross streets
and over the roofs, 1.25–1.84 M held; `?at=seconds` holds a place on it and two captures of one are
identical. Its readout says what each list drew, and at six held places, with the occlusion cull on
and then off:

| Place (`?at=`)        | Drawn on / off | Hidden | Sun's map on / off | Hidden | Frame ms on / off |
| --------------------- | -------------- | ------ | ------------------ | ------ | ----------------- |
| avenue, 12 m (0)      | 1,575 / 12,462 | 87%    | 9,286 / 27,913     | 67%    | 2.82 / 3.34       |
| cross street (7.7)    | 1,105 / 7,863  | 86%    | 8,998 / 27,542     | 67%    | 2.69 / 3.01       |
| climbing (16.3)       | 1,340 / 2,259  | 41%    | 9,129 / 27,349     | 67%    | 2.16 / 2.75       |
| midtown, 200 m (29.7) | 719 / 1,086    | 34%    | 6,870 / 25,769     | 73%    | 1.70 / 2.82       |
| skyline, 195 m (63)   | 4,652 / 13,023 | 64%    | 6,282 / 24,068     | 74%    | 2.03 / 2.82       |
| descent (73)          | 7,219 / 15,253 | 53%    | 7,083 / 26,307     | 73%    | 2.62 / 3.21       |

**In a street the camera's occlusion cull leaves five clusters in six of what its frustum kept, and
above the roofs about half** — the number the demo is a city for. The frame is 1.7–2.8 ms on the
device. `GpuDrivenPass.countDrawn` is what reads those counts back, a frame behind as the stage
times are, through `drawnClusters(list)`; `occlusion = false` switches both views' pyramid tests off
so the same frame can be counted without them.

**Three engine defects the city found, each fixed where it lived:**

- **The occlusion history never forgot a hidden cluster.** `twoPhase.ts` replaces the history with
  what phase two's cull keeps; the device kept the union of what both phases drew, and phase one
  has no pyramid, so a cluster once seen was drawn for as long as it stayed in the frustum. A held
  place drew 1,283 clusters after a flight and 1,386 after standing still, the same picture. Now
  both draw the same 1,105.
- **The light's cone test was off**, although the map's raster already culls the faces turned from
  the sun. It stands its eye 10⁸ m toward the sun now (`LIGHT_CONE_DISTANCE`), where the perspective
  test answers the directional one: the sun's map 46,874 clusters to 27,913.
- **The light had no occlusion**, and a three-degree sun sees a strip of city a kilometre deep,
  every building behind the first row in that row's shadow. It runs the camera's two phases over
  its own history and a pyramid from half its map, turned over into the camera's depth convention;
  27,913 to 9,286. **The sun's map was 2.5–3.0 ms of a 3.2–3.9 ms frame and is 0.8–1.3 of 1.7–2.8.**
  The rigs and the sandbox's port are identical to the pixel either side; and the same build with the
  light's depth left unturned moves the materials rig 203 pixels and the port 915, so that gate can
  fail — the city cannot tell, because at blue hour every receiver is behind many casters.

**The published list says which pipeline each scene draws on.** `DemoScene.pipelines` — absent is
the forward path alone — is `['forward', 'gpu-driven']` for the sandbox and `['gpu-driven']` for the
city, and `DemoSceneOptions.pipeline` lets a host choose; so a page that cannot run the second
pipeline asks the list rather than a mount that refuses. On WebGL2 the city refuses by name, and
`shots.mjs` skips it there.

**What the two demos do not have**, as their design records: skinning on the second pipeline — the
sandbox's mobs stay on the forward path; shadows from transparent or cutout surfaces; a second scale
demo; and the three rigs, which stay drafts and stay controls. **The city grades its light in the
scene** because the renderer has no colour grade or vignette, and its wet street reflects a probe and
not the frame; both are noted for a later release. The maintainer's word on the city's look is
deferred to a later pass.

**Metalness is one number a material where `flat/main.ts` reads one texel of an ORM map**, and that
is the whole of the difference: every expression it enters is the forward path's with a constant
standing in for a fetch. It removes the direct diffuse, gives the highlight the surface's own colour
and whitens it at a grazing angle, raises `f0` from 0.04 to 1 and makes the environment amount
`max(reflectivity, metal)` rather than the product, and tints what the surface reflects by its
albedo. At metalness 0 each is exactly the expression that shipped, asserted over a corpus rather
than at a point. Four of the materials rig's sixteen are metal with a **reflectivity of zero**,
which is the repair: a metal reflects whether or not the pass asked for reflections, and gating that
on `reflectivity` alone is what `flat/main.ts` records as a chromed subject coming out near black
with a baked probe sitting unread.

The one thing still collapsed is the environment gain. `PassEnvironment` carries no such control, so
`mix(1, gain, metal)` is exactly 1 at every metalness — exact rather than approximate, which is the
standard every term here is held to.

**The image-based term landed 2026-09-17, and the seam is the part worth reading.**
`PrepareContext.environment` is new: a contributed pass is handed no frame attachments, so there was
nothing of the renderer's to sample even where a probe existed, and this offers the frame's baked
one per frame rather than at registration — a scene bakes when it likes, and a value captured at
`init` would be null for the life of a pass that registered first. `gpudriven/ibl.ts` is the split
sum's second half in TypeScript, `gpu-parity.mjs`'s **tenth** check runs it against the device
inside the lit expression over 512 surfaces with a third down each branch of the weight, and its
**thirteenth** runs the octahedral mapping — now written three times — against
`shaders/octahedral.ts` over 512 directions with a twelfth of them on the seam where the fold
happens.

**Measured on the materials rig, which grew a room to reflect**: 54,753 pixels at mean delta 12 with
the probe baked, and **swapping two of the room's walls moves 18,092 of them**, which is what says
the reflection carries the room rather than lifting the brightness.

**And looking at that rig found a defect three waves old.** Box tops were missing, and they moved
with the camera: the occlusion cull was reading the depth pyramid at the **mirror** of the region it
was testing, because `sphereScreenBounds` reports clip-up coordinates and the pyramid is seeded from
the depth texture, whose row 0 is where clip `y` is +1. Both copies did it, so `gpu-parity.mjs`
agreed about it — a parity check compares two implementations and neither of them is the truth. The
million-triangle rig had lost an entire ridge of its terrain, in every figure ever measured on it.
Flipped, the frame is **byte-identical to the frame with occlusion culling switched off**, which is
the strongest available statement that the cull now rejects only what is hidden. The other two rigs declare no
room, so no cube is allocated at all and both are 0 of 921,600. The eight published scenes are 0 of
921,600 beside the whole of it.

**And reading that one found its sibling: the cull tested clusters where they were modelled.**
`buildStatic` uploaded `ClusterBuffers.bounds` and `.cones` exactly as the bake wrote them, while
the raster and the shading both multiplied by `transforms[mesh]` — so a mesh placed anywhere but the
origin was frustum-culled against the wrong region, cone-culled with the wrong orientation, LOD-cut
on a misprojected error and occlusion-tested on the wrong rectangle, and drew in the right place
regardless. **All three rigs stood at the origin**, which is why nothing said so. `clusterWorld.ts`
transforms them once at upload, and `occlusionRig` now models every box at its own origin and places
it with a matrix, turning the wall a quarter turn so a rotation reaches the cone axis as well.

Re-expressing a placed box as a modelled box and a transform moves no vertex, so the capture is a
control: **eleven scenes at 0 of 750,080**, the eight published ones and all three rigs. Put the old
upload back under the placed rig and scene 16 loses **1,108 pixels in 23 islands, the largest 489**
— black bites out of the boxes beside the wall. It is mild at this size because a rig a few metres
across keeps its clusters inside the frustum wherever they are said to be; the cost is a consumer
who places a mesh a hundred metres from the origin and loses all of it.

**Both defects were the same shape, so the checks were audited.** A parity check runs a TypeScript
reference and its WGSL twin over generated input and proves the pair agrees; neither of them is the
truth. **Twelve of the thirteen carry an assertion about what their arithmetic means now**, anchored
on something outside the expression: the frustum cull on the clip volume the matrix defines and on
each face found by bisecting along a ray; the level cut on the pixel separation of two points
actually projected; the depth reduction on brute force over each coarse texel's own footprint; the
cone on a populated cone of normals over a populated sphere, every one of which must face away
before a cull is allowed; the screen rectangle on covering the sphere it is built from. `compact`,
`materialBin`, `shadeBins`, `visbuffer`, `receiverPlane` and `environment` already had one.

**A third defect had no picture at all until the camera moved.** Phase one is meant to cull without
the pyramid, because the one it would read is last frame's; the pass wrote the switch as 0 and then
as 1 into one buffer through the queue, and a queue write lands when it is made while the frame's
commands run at submit — so phase one read 1. A cluster last frame's pyramid wrongly hid was then
drawn by neither phase, since phase two judges only what the history does not hold, and was back
the next frame. Every capture was of a camera at rest, and all of them were right. Found 2026-09-17
while reading the pass for Wave 1A's graph, and **each phase has its own settings buffer now**.
`gpuDrivenPass.test.ts` reads every dispatch's settings as the device would, and
**`scripts/motion-check.mjs`** draws each position of a turn twice, arriving and settled, on
`demo/dev/motion.html`: on the occlusion rig at four degrees a frame the old pass lost **4, 8, 10, 6
and 75 pixels at five of 48 steps**, and the fixed one loses none on any of the three rigs. Held
captures of the three are 0 of 921,600 either side of the fix.

**`litColour` is the exception, and what it has instead is a photograph.** Its terms are a hand
transcription of `flat/main.ts`, and every unit test beside it is either a collapse — specular,
shade or reflectivity at zero, each arithmetically the frame that shipped before the term existed —
or a second reading of the same GLSL. So the anchor is `?pipeline=forward`, and it was taken on
2026-09-17 at `--delta=0`: the occlusion rig with the directional shadow off is **0 of 750,080
against the forward path, exactly**, and the million-triangle rig is **117 pixels of worst delta 1,
all of it in islands of four or fewer**. The lit expression, the interpolation, the tint, the
ambient are the forward path's to the bit; the occlusion rig's remaining 256 pixels are its shadow.
**Two things that paragraph said were wrong, and the textured rig is what showed it.** The emissive
was never in that photograph — neither rig in it glows — and the materials rig's 49,222 were not only
a bound: `drawMesh` does carry roughness and specular, per vertex, and reflectivity, per draw, and
that rig's forward path glowed nowhere, because the forward path scales every glow by the frame's
clock and the second pipeline did not. See the textures paragraph below.

**The device has one network evaluator, in two precisions, 2026-09-17.** `render/shaders/network.wgsl.ts`
is the text; the DriftTexture interpreter reads its weights through it from the uniform tables, and a
storage-buffer network through it in half precision where the device has `shader-f16`.
`@driftengine/texture` carries the references: `evalNetwork`, `evalNetworkHalf` — which rounds every
input, product and sum to binary16, written out because Node 22 has no `Float16Array` — and
`halfPrecisionErrorBound`, a bound per network rather than a tolerance: a sampled tolerance reached
0.00213 on 2,400 networks, 0.0039 on the device's corpus and 0.0066 on 40,000. **This machine's driver
contracts each multiply-add into one rounding**, which WGSL permits, so `evalNetworkHalf` computes
either form and the check requires every network to match one of them exactly: over 256 networks up to
four hidden layers of sixteen, 203 matched only the contracted form, 53 both and none neither, and the
worst output reached 52% of its bound. `activationBound` is what a consumer asks before choosing half
precision, since past 65,504 the format has no finite value. The weights travel in the **`NNET`
chunk at container 1.14**, found by role and refused when the count disagrees with the shape.
**`scripts/wgsl-handwritten.test.mjs`** has `naga` validate every hand-written WGSL module — twenty-five
— without a device, which nothing did before.

**Textures landed 2026-09-17, and the forward path is their reference.** `decodeCpu` learned
texel-centre addressing beside the lattice terrain rests on, and mip levels. `packDecodeTables`
flattens every material's programs into two uniform tables — the shading pass was already at eight
storage buffers — and one `rgba8unorm` array, refusing a set past any capacity with the number in the
message; `DECODE_WGSL` interprets them per pixel, centre-addressed latents through the hardware's own
trilinear filter and lattice ones by hand from `textureLoad`. The UV, its screen gradients, the mip
level and the tangent frame all come from the barycentric gradients the shadow's receiver plane
already built. Two device checks joined: `decode`, 768 cases over all nine operations and all four
address modes, worst **3.6e-7**, with an anchor that decodes the reference at the four texel centres
and filters by hand — broken the same way in both copies, the pair agreed at level 0 and the anchor
failed 30 cases there; and `surfaceFrame`, 512 cases, whose unit test asserts the frame is the
surface's own two axes under a screen map of either handedness.

**The materials rig carries three**: a checker with an ORM map on the floor, glazed bricks with a
normal map, a speckle. `?pipeline=forward` decodes each program to an image at every texel centre
and binds it isotropically — the second pipeline takes one level for both axes, where a forward
surface texture takes four anisotropic samples by default, and that difference is real — and
`?plain=1` strips the metal scalar and reflectivity from both pipelines, the one input the forward
mesh cannot carry and the reflection whose forward footprint term this pipeline lacks. **Plain and
unshadowed, the two frames differ by nothing past a delta of 3**: 9,063 pixels at delta 0, all on
textured surfaces, worst 3 of 255. Broken one line at a time on the device, occlusion taken whole
moves 2,881 pixels past delta 4, roughness scaled the wrong way round 344, the normal map's roughness
widening left out 1,666 past delta 16, a flipped bitangent 363 past delta 4 and metal read from the
table rather than the map 7,654 — **and the first two are invisible at delta 16** on that dark floor,
which is why the comparison is held at 4. Texturing three of sixteen materials moved the shading
stage by nothing a clock quantised to 0.065 ms can see: 0.20–0.26 ms before, 0.20–0.26 ms after.

**What that comparison found in the pipeline, before it found anything in the textures.** The
second pipeline added `albedo * emissive` and nothing else, where `flat/main.ts` scales every glow
by `uEmissiveGain * uNightFactor` and lets a shadow take 55% of it — so a rig whose clock said day
glowed on one pipeline and not the other, and no comparison had included a glowing material. It
follows the forward path now, with the share interpolated from one constant into both shaders. And
the forward path widens a normal-mapped surface's roughness by `RELIEF_ROUGHNESS` times the map's
strength everywhere it reads roughness; the plan's shader did not, and it does now.

**Two of the eight anchors written were too weak, and that is the transferable part.** "A culled
sphere has no point the camera could see" passed 500 trials against a near plane extracted the
OpenGL way, which on a 0-to-1 depth matrix sits at half the near distance: a conservative claim
permits a plane pushed outward as far as you like. And the shadow's two corrections turned out not
to be pinned by their difference at all — a map stored upside down and read upside down is a correct
shadow, so the pair is self-consistent either way round. What decides it is that the raster
correction **mirrors**, reversing every triangle's winding, which `gpuDrivenPass` answers with
`frontFace: 'cw'` in another file. The claim is a determinant.

Two of the transform's decisions are not the obvious ones. **The radius takes the longest basis
vector**, which is exactly the largest singular value for `T · R · S` and is stated rather than
assumed, because a sheared matrix has a larger one than its longest column and a bound that is too
small culls what is visible. And **the cone is refused rather than rotated** wherever the transform
is not a similarity: a normal goes through the inverse transpose and a position through the matrix,
and under a squash of ten those point 78.6 degrees apart, so what goes in the buffer is a cutoff of
one — a cone `cullClusters` can never satisfy. Refusing costs the draws the cone would have saved;
getting it wrong deletes surfaces that face the camera.

**What the level selection does not have** is the forward path's footprint term: that widens the
level where the mirror direction swings fast across a pixel, from `fwidth`, which a compute
invocation cannot take. Without it a crease sparkles at a grazing angle. The derivative is
recoverable from the barycentric gradients the way the shadow's receiver plane is, and that is a
term with its own reference rather than one to guess at.

**The highlight landed 2026-09-16, and what landed with it matters more.** The lit expression had
**no reference at all**: `shadeBins.ts` is the reference for the _reconstruction_, and the shading
pass's header argued — correctly, for an expression of four lines — that the interpolation is the
only part that can differ between the pipelines. That stops being true the moment the expression
grows a term, and nothing in the tree computed what the shader computed, so nothing could disagree
with it. `gpudriven/lit.ts` is the twin now, the expression is shared WGSL text rather than inlined,
and `gpu-parity.mjs`'s **tenth** device check runs both over 512 generated surfaces — a fifth of
them sitting exactly on the lobe's peak, because without those the corpus never reaches the
`max(d * d, 1e-8)` floor and the check passed a shader with it deleted.

**The directional shadow's lookup landed next, written reference-first.** `gpudriven/shadow.ts` is
`flat/directionalShadow.ts` in TypeScript for one depth layer — the receiver fade at the
terminator, the border fade, the elevation fade, the twelve Poisson taps, the receiver-plane
compensation and its clamp, and the reach fade that stops one map shadowing the world.
`shaders/gpudriven/shadow.wgsl.ts` is the same arithmetic for the device, and `gpu-parity.mjs`'s
**eleventh** check runs both over 1,024 receivers — 92 of them off the map, 144 in the terminator
band and 147 receiver planes refused as ill-conditioned, because every guard in a shadow lookup
answers _fully lit_ and a guard that fires when it should not removes a shadow rather than drawing
one. A **twelfth** covers the step before the solve: turning three light-space corners and two
barycentric gradients into the two derivative vectors it takes, which is the one piece of the
shadow that exists only because a compute invocation has no neighbours to difference against.

**One layer where the forward path has three**, and that is stated rather than approximated: that
path keeps a static map, a peeled one holding the second static occluder and a dynamic one for
movers, because its shadow _pool_ is shared between lights and rationed across frames. The second
pipeline owns its geometry and a pass owns whatever it renders in `prepare`, so there is one caster
set and one map.

**The map landed the same day, and it is this pipeline's own.** `PassDevice` hands a contributed
pass the device, the formats and the sample count and **no frame attachments** — so there is nothing
of the renderer's to sample even where a map exists, and `prepare` is where a pass renders its own.
It is the visibility raster with a different matrix and an **identity** cluster list: every cluster,
no culling, because the frame's cull is against the camera and a caster standing behind the viewer
still throws a shadow across what is in front of them. **Two matrices, differing by one negated
row**: a generated vertex stage ends with naga's `gl_Position.y = -gl_Position.y` and a hand-written
one does not, so the raster takes the flipped matrix — with `frontFace: 'cw'` travelling beside it —
and the lookup takes the unflipped one.

**Measured, with the strength at zero as the control.** The two rigs that did not otherwise change
are **0 of 921,600 pixels** against the build before the map existed. With it up, the terrain is
still 0 — a gentle slope under a 51-degree sun shadows nothing — the occlusion rig is 256 pixels,
and the materials rig is **17,287, of which 15,427 are one island**: sixty-four shadows laid across
its floor. It costs **0.46 ms** on a million triangles, 0.46 to 0.92 total, which is the price of a
2048 map drawn with no culling at all.

**What the rigs needed is the part worth repeating.** Sixty-four boxes standing in the air have
nothing to cast onto, so the finished term first measured 1,184 pixels of 921,600 — a picture nobody
could tell from a bug. They have a floor now, and the materials rig carries its own sun on the far
side, because the shared one stood behind the camera and put every shadow behind the box casting
it.

**It moves nothing that was drawn before it**: `specular` defaults to zero, so the term is
multiplied by zero, and all three rigs are **0 of 921,600 pixels** against the build without it.
The materials rig sets it on every other material, which is 14,197 pixels at a mean delta of 11.6.

**And it found something in the forward path's own lobe.** `specularLobe` peaks at one until
`roughness` falls under **0.1**, where `max(d * d, 1e-8)` takes over and the peak falls with the
roughness — 0.0039 at 0.05, so a polished surface has a fainter highlight than a satin one. It is
matched here rather than fixed, because the published scenes are calibrated against the shader that
has it; `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` carries the row and `lit.test.ts` pins the numbers.
**Where the two pipelines compute the same lighting they agree to the pixel**: the occlusion rig,
whose materials are white with no emissive and whose environment has neither shadow map nor probe,
is **0 of 563,200 pixels** different from the same geometry through `drawMesh`. The dense rig is
11,353 and the materials rig 10,144, both where the subset shows.
`gpudriven/parity.test.ts` carries the table and the date.

**Indirect light has three levels, and the architecture is the fallback rather than any one of
them.** `ROADMAP.md` refuses screen-space global illumination because it is the one screen-space
effect whose error is not bounded by a fade — a reflection that runs out of screen fades to
nothing, and indirect light that runs out of screen changes the brightness of the room.
`render/gi/` does not reverse that refusal, it **bounds the error with something that is not a
fade**: `traceScreen` is exact wherever the frame has the answer and reports a miss where it does
not, `traceField` marches the world's own signed distance field with an error bounded by that
field's resolution, and `visibleProbes` is behind both — never wrong, only ever coarse, and unable
to fail, so there are exactly three cases and no fourth. The levels **blend** rather than switch,
because every boundary between them moves with the camera: the frame's edge by definition, and the
cascades because they are centred on it.

**A sealed dark room next to a lit one stays dark**, which is the defect every implementation of
this has shipped and the reason probe visibility exists. `gi/leak.test.ts` asserts a maximum
radiance below **0.02** where the lit room is 1, and — the half that makes it a test — asserts the
same scene leaks **above 0.1** with the visibility term turned off. **A white furnace converges**:
`gi/energy.test.ts` runs thirty bounces at albedo one and holds every probe within a thousandth of
the radiance it emits, and a grey furnace at albedo 0.6 arrives at `e / (1 - a)` from dark rather
than starting there. A white object in a white furnace disappears, which is what exercises the
share arithmetic between the three levels — an empty furnace never asks the world-space level
anything.

**The interpolation scheme was chosen by measurement**, as the design required.
`scripts/gi-schemes.mjs` runs a visibility-weighted probe volume and a radiance cascade arrangement
over the same rooms: worst leak **0.000** against **0.172 to 0.224**, at 90.5 KB against 15.6 to
62.5. Cascades leak because the merge carries occlusion along a ray and cannot correct the
interpolation _between_ probes at the end — and more directions makes it worse, which is the
clearest evidence that their angular resolution is orthogonal to the problem.
`notes/2026-09-16-gi-interpolation.md` has the table.

**What it costs, measured 2026-09-16 by `scripts/gi-schemes.mjs`.** A room-sized volume: **0.09 MB
of probes** — 45 at two-metre spacing, each carrying one irradiance value and a 16×16 map of depth
moments — and **4.19 MB of field**, four cascades of 65 cubed with a finest step of 12.5 cm. The
probe bake is **20 ms once** for all 45. A ray down the whole chain is **5.75 µs**.

**And composing the field is 707 ms a frame, which is the number that matters most.** Thirty-two
instances over four cascades is 35 million inverse transforms and trilinear reads, because the
reference visits every sample of every cascade for every instance it cannot cull outright — it says
so in its own header, and it is deliberate: a CPU implementation that was already accelerated would
be a second thing to be wrong rather than the thing the first is checked by. **What the figure
settles is that the compute shader is not an optimisation of this path, it is the only version of
it that can run in a frame.** The brick culling belongs there, with `scripts/gpu-parity.mjs` as the
pattern for checking it against this.

**The composition has a compute shader, and it agrees with the reference exactly.**
`shaders/gi/composeField.wgsl.ts` is one invocation a sample — the inverse transform, the box bound
outside a source, the eight-corner blend and the minimum that makes a union — and
`scripts/gi-parity.mjs` runs it against `composeGlobalField` over 24 rotated and scaled instances of
two different shapes: **107,811 samples across three cascades, 0 disagreements**. It carries no
instance culling, unlike the reference, and does not need one: what the cull saves on a serial loop
is a branch per thread here, and a culled instance is by definition one the minimum would have
discarded.

**What that harness cannot do is time it**, which is worth knowing before reaching for it:
`gpuCompute.mjs` recompiles the shader and re-uploads the source fields on every call, so a
dispatch's marginal cost comes out at about what the whole reference costs and none of it is
compute. A frame time needs the pass wired into the renderer with timestamp queries, which
`GpuDrivenPass` is the pattern for.

**And it runs in a frame.** `backend/webgpu/giFieldPass.ts` is a contributed pass on
`GpuDrivenPass`'s pattern: it dispatches from `prepare`, in the window where an encoder exists and
no render pass is open, so the field is composed before anything could sample it with the graph
learning nothing. Six instances over three cascades of 49 cubed cost **0.07 ms** on an RX 9070 XT,
from the pass's own `timestamp-query` pair — against 707 ms for the processor on a comparable scene.
`draw` sphere-traces the field into the frame, which is what `demo/giField.ts` shows; it is a
`DRAFT_SCENES` entry because a marched distance field is a diagnostic, not a material.

**Moving through it showed a clone of every object that no held frame could, 2026-09-18.** The
maintainer saw it at 120 frames a second: a copy popping in beside each object and trailing it. The
composition moved to the renderer that morning, at `endFrame`, while the march stayed in the pass's
`prepare` — so the march is encoded ahead of the dispatches that rewrite the samples and reads the
samples the previous frame composed, which is right, since the field is anchored to the world. But
the cascades' bounds were written with `queue.writeBuffer`, which lands when it is made rather than
when the command buffer runs: on every frame a cascade stepped, the march read last frame's samples
through this frame's bounds, and the field sat one voxel off — 16.7 cm at the finest cascade and 67
at the coarsest — for exactly one frame. The bounds are staged now and reach the buffer readers bind
by a copy encoded after the composition, so a reader before it sees the old pair and a reader after
it the new one. **A held capture of the scene is 0 of 921,600 either side**, which is the point: a
held frame redraws until the two agree, so the defect lived only in frames nothing photographed.
`fieldCompose.test.ts` holds the ordering with a stub that runs encoded commands at submit, as a
device does; `gi-parity.mjs` and `bounce-check.mjs` read what they read before.

**Drawing it found a defect that every number had passed.** Outside a source's own bounding box the
field returned the distance _to that box_ — a true bound, and just outside the box it is nearly
zero, while the distance to the object inside is most of a metre. `globalField.test.ts`'s "never
overestimates" was happy, zero being an underestimate of everything, and `gi-parity.mjs` was happy
because both sides agreed. What it did was put a **phantom surface** around every instance: a sphere
trace stops where the field falls under its epsilon, and it drew as dark fins radiating from every
object. The bound is taken against the field's own value at the nearest point of the box as well
now — `d(q) >= d(c) - |q - c|` — which is tight against the box and decays to the box distance far
away. **That is what a visualisation is for**, and it is the argument for `DRAFT_SCENES` in one
example. The eight published scenes are **0 of 921,600 pixels** against the
build before this wave, and `core-only` is **byte-identical at 688,564 gzipped** with the barrel
exports that reach it and without them. **The denoiser ships with it**, and takes the reprojection and the
disocclusion flag as _parameters_ rather than computing them: `clipToNeighbourhood` is the one
piece of Wave 3A's temporal machinery that already exists and is reused, and the other two plug
into two arguments when that wave lands. Its weights are renormalised by their own sum, its depth
tolerance is relative, and a disocclusion resets rather than blends. **What is still absent is the
shader**, and the 707 ms above is why that is the next piece of work rather than a nicety.

**Indirect light ships, WebGPU only, off by default behind `quality.indirectLight`.** A consumer
declares what may be traced against with `addDistanceField(field, model, albedo)` and the renderer
composes those into the world field at `endFrame`; `PROBES_PER_FRAME` probes are then traced down
the GI chain and convolved into the irradiance level of the probe array the shading already samples,
so **the light arrives through `gridIrradiance` and the lit pass changes not at all**. There is no
second per-pixel buffer and no new binding.

**What it buys over the rasterised bake beside it is that it follows.** Six face draws a probe is a
hitch, so a scene whose light changes either pays it or keeps the light it had; a traced refresh is
one compute dispatch. Measured on `demo/dev/bounce.html`, a room whose red wall is repainted blue
halfway through: **blue over red on the far wall is 4.909 traced against 0.660 rasterised**, and the
wall makes nine tenths of its change **in 15 frames** — a quarter of a second at 60 Hz, which is
four rounds of an eighteen-probe grid refreshed five a frame. The rasterised grid's latency is not
larger, it is unbounded: it never changes at all.

**What it costs: 0.129 ms a frame** on an RX 9070 XT for one refresh of five probes, from the bake's
own `timestamp-query` pair — beside 0.07 ms for the composition, so indirect light is about two
tenths of a millisecond a frame on that device. `?gputiming=1` is what asks the adapter for the
feature; without it every figure is `null` rather than zero.

**And a scene with no baked lighting**, which is Wave 4's exit criterion in its own words. The trace
evaluates the sun at what it hits — albedo from the composed field, the normal from its gradient, a
shadow march for the rest — so nothing in the chain reads a rasterised capture and a grid starting
at black climbs away from black. `scripts/bounce-check.mjs` runs the page with `?seed=0`, no capture
anywhere, and asserts it measures the same room: **66.0/11.7/11.5 either way**.

**What it does not do.** No specular bounce: the trace writes the irradiance level and the roughness
chain is whatever a rasterised bake left. Nothing for the GPU-driven pipeline. The grid's spacing is
what decides how local the light can be, and a consumer that declares none gets one fitted to the
declared fields at two metres inside `MAX_ENV_PROBES` of 64 — which for a four-metre room widens to
three and stands its probes outside the walls, so a scene that cares says where they go. It is
**not converged**: the far wall never stops moving by a level of 255 over 240 frames, which a
stochastic estimator refreshing five probes a frame with a turning direction set would not be. And
it puts **0.666 of the light** the rasterised bake puts on the same wall — a gap that is not
attributed, though the rasterised bake lights a room the sun does not reach, since this profile has
directional shadows off and it draws the sun on every face whose normal points at it.

**Two defects it cost to find, both of the same shape: something silently read where nothing was.**
A `FieldSource`'s voxels have to be cubic — `bakeObjectSdf` takes one step from the object's longest
axis and varies `dims` instead, and both readers rely on it — and nothing said so, so the demo's
five slabs, sampled 17 cubed over boxes that are not cubes, were each read at their own corner. The
composed field held almost no room: `scripts/bake-census.mjs` counted **98.9% of every probe's rays
leaving a closed room**, and the bounce delivered a thirty-fifth of its light with every gate green.
`assertCubicVoxels` refuses that shape now. And `flatTextures` resolves `uEnvironment` to a one-texel
**white** stand-in until the grid is baked, while a bind group holds whatever texture existed when it
was built — so a grid filled by tracing rather than by `bakeProbeGrid`, which runs before any frame,
left every flat group reading white for the life of the renderer. Every surface came back at exactly
its own albedo times 255, which had been recorded twice as undefined memory. `markProbeFilled`
rebuilds the groups when the last layer lands. The eight published scenes are **0 of 921,600 pixels**
against the build before all of it.

**`CLIP_CORRECTION`'s Y negation cancels one the generator writes, and the comment on it said
otherwise for months.** Every module under `shaders/generated/` ends its vertex entry point with
`gl_Position.y = -gl_Position.y`, which is how `naga` adapts a GLSL shader to WebGPU; the matrix
negates it back, and the net effect on a generated shader is the depth remap alone. The old reading
— that the flip corrects a difference between the framebuffer origins — is not what either viewport
transform does: OpenGL measures upward from the bottom-left and WebGPU downward from the top-left,
so clip `y = +1` is the top of the image on both. **The explanation was wrong while the code was
right**, which held for every generated shader and broke the first hand-written one: the GPU-driven
raster came out an exact vertical mirror of the forward path's, with its winding reversed to match,
so it presented as a culling problem. `PassDevice.depthCorrection` is the matrix a hand-written
shader wants and `shaders/generatedFlip.test.ts` pins the generator's half, per vertex stage, so
the two halves cannot drift apart.

**The software rasteriser is refused, and the measurement is why.** Wave 2A task 11 exists to make
micro-triangles cheaper than the hardware rasteriser can, and WGSL has atomics on 32-bit integers
only — so the published single-pass technique is unreachable and the two-pass one re-traverses
every cluster to resolve the payload. The hardware path rasterises **1,002,528 triangles in
0.197 ms** at 1280×510, averaging well under a pixel each. Pass B alone would have to cost less
than that, on top of pass A. There is nothing to win, the plan's §9 says the decision is already
made, and nothing was built: what stands instead is this figure and the date on it.

**What the two backends now differ by, and what is left of it.** Measured 2026-09-16 on an RX
9070 XT through radv, all eight published scenes at 1280×720, the readout band excluded. The
column that settles what a number means is the last one: a difference spread over thousands of
one-and-two-pixel islands is two shader compilers disagreeing in the last bits on sub-pixel
geometry, and one that arrives as a solid region is a defect.

| Scene            | Pixels past 16 | Mean delta | Islands | In islands ≤4 px | Largest island |
| ---------------- | -------------: | ---------: | ------: | ---------------: | -------------: |
| `storm-sea`      |             35 |      18.68 |      33 |             100% |              2 |
| `night-court`    |            161 |      31.56 |     118 |              93% |             11 |
| `collapse`       |            579 |      21.61 |     401 |             100% |              3 |
| `gilded-chamber` |            748 |      26.08 |     525 |              92% |             12 |
| `voxel-sandbox`  |          2,172 |      25.31 |   1,381 |              78% |            119 |
| `showroom`       |          2,880 |      29.89 |   2,151 |              98% |             12 |
| `day-clock`      |         10,876 |      22.36 |   6,026 |              83% |             19 |
| `wind-field`     |         13,977 |      21.13 |   8,729 |              83% |             42 |

Reproduce it with `node scripts/shots.mjs diff <a> <b> --delta=16 --region=0,92,1280,678 --islands`.

**All eight are that noise floor now** — between 78% and 100% of every scene's change sits in
islands of four pixels or fewer, and **no connected region anywhere exceeds 119 pixels**, on a
frame of 750,080. Cross-correlating each pair at every integer offset confirms they are not
displaced either: the best alignment is zero by a wide margin, which is the other thing a large
count suggests.

**`wind-field` was the one that was not, and it was a scatter batch casting no shadow at all on
WebGPU.** The scatter shadow pipeline took the _frame's_ depth compare, which under `REVERSED_DEPTH`
is `greater`, against a shadow map cleared to 1 — so a fragment at depth 0.3 failed `0.3 > 1` and
**nothing was ever written**. `depthPass.ts` has had `'less'` for the mesh path all along, which is
why meshes cast and scatter did not, and why it took a scene whose only caster is a scatter batch to
show it. The measurement that named it is per backend rather than between them: turning directional
shadows off changed 2,628 pixels on WebGL2 and **0** on WebGPU, and removing the canopy caster on
WebGL2 left a frame pixel-identical to the shadows-off one. It changes 2,631 on WebGPU now, in the
same region, and the scene's largest differing island fell from **6,176 pixels to 62**.

**And a second defect the same sweep found, now fixed: an instanced batch put out the light on
every plain draw of its mesh.** `attachInstances` claims vertex attribute locations 11 to 14 for
the model matrix and 15 for the tint, and a `Mesh` owns one vertex array — so those bindings stayed
live for a _plain_ `drawMesh` through the same array. **Location 13 is also the channel**, whose `y`
lane is `vSkyDirect`, the scale on the directional term. A placement with no rotation has
`(0, 0, 1, 0)` in the matrix's third column, so `aChannel.y` read **zero** and the mesh rendered lit
by the hemispheric ambient alone — correct normals, correct albedo, no error and no warning.
`demo/instancing.ts` draws two ranks of one box the two ways precisely so they can be compared:
before, its top faces read (51, 30, 21) against (218, 110, 59) and the two backends differed by
**14,691 pixels**; after, **0**. The instance columns are disabled for a plain draw and put back for
an instanced one, and `mesh.test.ts` holds both halves. WebGPU has no vertex array to share and was
never affected, which is what made it visible at all.

**The two backends did not draw the same picture, and the reason was that WebGL2's reflection
probe was upside down.** Measured 2026-09-16 on an RX 9070 XT through radv, all eight published
scenes at 1280×720, `--delta=16`, with the readout band excluded, before the correction and after
it:

| Scene            | Pixels changed of 750,080 | After `cubeFaceProjection` | Mean delta |
| ---------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------- |
| `showroom`       | 136,377                   | **2,836**                  | 23.30      |
| `wind-field`     | 15,442                    | 15,442                     | 21.88      |
| `day-clock`      | 10,253                    | 10,253                     | 22.37      |
| `voxel-sandbox`  | 6,635                     | 6,635                      | 82.33      |
| `collapse`       | 498                       | 498                        | 21.46      |
| `gilded-chamber` | 745                       | 745                        | 26.12      |
| `night-court`    | 161                       | 161                        | 31.56      |
| `storm-sea`      | 35                        | 35                         | 18.68      |

**`showroom` is the only one that moved, and it is the only one that bakes a probe into a room with
a vertical structure.** What is left on the other seven is a second question with a different
answer, and `voxel-sandbox`'s mean delta of 82 against everyone else's 20-odd is probably a third.
Showroom's remaining 2,836 is the silhouette noise every page in `demo/dev/` carries — between 100
and 7,000 pixels on all fourteen of them, 0.3% to 0.5% of every luminance band, none of it a
surface.

**A cubemap face's texel rows run downward and a GL framebuffer's run upward.**
`framebufferTexture2D` on `TEXTURE_CUBE_MAP_POSITIVE_X + face` makes framebuffer row 0 the face's
texel row 0, and the face's own direction mapping — the specification's `sc`, `tc`, `ma` table —
says texel row 0 is the +Y end. A camera aimed along the face with its up at +Y puts +Y at the top
of the render area, which in GL is the _last_ row. So every face was stored mirrored, and every
reflection and every irradiance sample taken from it had up and down the wrong way round.
`cubeFaceProjection` negates clip y for the six faces and `bakeProbe` winds them clockwise for the
duration, because negating one axis mirrors every triangle.

**Two things confirm it independently of the parity figure.** The equirectangular loader builds its
faces _by direction_ — `equirectToCubeFaces` walks each texel, reconstructs the direction from the
face basis and samples the sky — so an uploaded environment was always the right way up, and a
baked one was not: two paths into the same cube that disagreed. And `demo/dev/ibl.html?band=1`
shows it directly, with four side walls bright above and dark below: before the correction the
spheres in that room read **26 to 55 of 255 across their tops against 67 to 73 across their
bottoms**, lit from underneath, while WebGPU had them the right way round. After it, both backends
give the same numbers to the level.

**Two controls are what make those numbers mean anything.** WebGL2 captured twice and diffed
against itself is **identical on all eight scenes, zero pixels changed**; WebGPU captured twice is
**identical on all eight too**. Each backend is deterministic run to run, so the difference between
them is a reproducible rendering difference and not capture noise, streaming state, or a temporal
accumulator that had not settled.

**What the difference was not, which is most of what finding it cost.** Not a transfer curve:
bucketing WebGL2's value against WebGPU's mean gives a shift that oscillates with level rather than
a monotone offset. Not a channel swap or a colour cast: the mean signed shift is 1.107, 1.118 and
1.135 on red, green and blue. Not a constant exposure: converted to linear, the median ratio
between the two is **exactly 1.0000** while the fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles are 0.82 and
1.47. And inside the probe path: not the probe's size (32, 64, 128 and 256 all diverged by the same
174,000 pixels), not multisampling (`?samples=1`), not the frame graph (`?graph=0`), not either
shadow permutation or both together, not clustered lighting, not the HDR target, and not the
convolution's sample count.

**What it looks like.** An amplified difference mask of `showroom` is black on the car body, the
dark wall panels and the light housings, and grey over every lit surface, with faint concentric
rings across the platform and ripples along the walls. Zero where the picture is black, growing
with how lit a surface is, and carrying contour structure where banding would be.

**It is uniform within a surface and changes sign between surfaces**, which is the most useful
thing known about it. Sampled along three rows of `showroom`, WebGPU against WebGL2: the ceiling is
**+22** across its whole width, the walls are **0**, and the floor is **−7** across its whole
width. A difference constant over a flat surface that reverses between one facing up and one facing
down is a term depending on the normal, not on geometry, coverage or filtering.

**Four things it is not, each a capture rather than an argument.** Screen effects off (`?fx=0`),
ambient occlusion at 0.0001 and at 2, and the HDR scene target off all leave the count within 370
pixels of the 136,377 it starts at. And it is not an accumulator: it is already **159,032 pixels at
frame 2** and _shrinks_ to 136,377 by frame 420, so it is there in the first frames and settles
slightly rather than building up.

**It is the reflection probe, and that is a control rather than a suspicion.** `?probesize=0`
builds `showroom` with no probe and changes nothing else; the two backends then differ on **3,037**
pixels of 750,080 against the 136,377 they differ on with one, and twelve points sampled across the
ceiling, three walls, two floor tiles, the platform and the car body are **byte-identical on all
three channels**. What is left at 3,037 is the silhouette noise every page in `demo/dev/` shows —
between 100 and 7,000 pixels on all fourteen of them, none of it a surface.

**What the probe does differently, per direction.** Reading the lift each backend takes when the
probe is turned on, against the hemispheric term it replaces:

| Surface                     | normal     | WebGL2 lift  | WebGPU lift                |
| --------------------------- | ---------- | ------------ | -------------------------- |
| ceiling, roughness 0.85     | down       | +59/255      | **+81/255**                |
| three walls, roughness 0.85 | horizontal | +26, +25, +5 | **the same, to the level** |
| floor tiles, roughness 0.12 | up         | +6 to +8     | **0**                      |
| turntable, roughness 0.03   | up         | +12          | **0**                      |

**The ceiling and the walls are the same material** — `ROUGH_WALL`, specular 0.05 and 0.04 — so a
reflection cannot be what separates them, and the term that moves is the probe's _diffuse_
irradiance. Horizontal directions agree exactly; up and down do not, and they move in opposite
directions. That is a probe with its rows the wrong way up, read from a lit surface rather than
from the map — and it is the shape of the answer before the answer was found.

**`ibl-check.mjs` reported both backends agreeing, and it was measuring the wrong axis.**
`demo/dev/ibl.html` builds a room whose only asymmetry is a bright wall at +X and a dark one at
−X, and the check samples each sphere's left and right halves. Every up direction and every down
direction in that room reads the same neutral ceiling and floor, so a probe that differs _only_
vertically produces an identical picture and identical figures. So do `?axis=y`, `?roomlit=1`,
`?detail=` and `?fog=`, all added while looking for this: a whole bright wall, a chequer, an
ambient-lit room and an atmosphere are every one of them symmetric under a vertical flip. **The
room that is not is `?band=1`** — four side walls bright above and dark below — and it found the
defect in one capture. `ibl-check.mjs` drives it now, and deleting `cubeFaceProjection` turns that
check from 25 of 25 spheres at a margin of +13.4 into 0 of 25 at −8.4 while the four older checks
stay green, which is the measure of what they could see.

**A warning for whoever picks this up.** `shots.mjs capture --urls=` does not drive the pages under
`demo/dev/` without a readiness predicate they do not all expose, and a `diff` whose captures are
all missing still prints **"identical"** as its summary. A bisection across those pages was run
that way and reported six features agreeing when it had compared nothing. Check that the PNGs
exist before believing a green diff.

**Where the difference sat.** In `showroom`, 47.8% of bright pixels changed and 0.4% of dark ones,
with mean luminance moving 109.8 to 110.9. That was read here as "an output transform or a specular
term"; it was neither. It was the probe's diffuse irradiance, confined to the bright end because
the surfaces a probe lifts most are the ones that were already lit — a lead written down as a lead,
and wrong.

**Two pages in one dev server were running two different engines.** `demo/dev/ibl.ts` imports
`@driftengine/core` and `demo/showroom.ts` imports `../packages/core/src/index`; the packages
export `./src/index.ts` under the `drift-source` condition and `./dist/index.js` by default, and
vite set neither. So the fix changed `showroom` and left `ibl.html` byte-identical, which reads
exactly like a fix that does nothing. `demo/dev/vite.config.ts` now sets the condition, and the
demo pages are instruments before they are consumer examples: an instrument has to measure the
thing being edited. `scripts/consumerEntries.test.mjs` is what covers the other claim.

**This was reachable the whole time.** The working record had five plans down as blocked on
hardware; the card is present, `requireHardwareGpu` accepts it, `navigator.gpu` resolves to an
`amd`/`rdna-4` adapter, and `scripts/browser.mjs`'s own header had already written down the two
things that make it work — the Vulkan flags, and that WebGPU needs a secure context so `about:blank`
reports no adapter on a machine that has one. Nobody ran the gate, so nobody found out.

## 4. What the record got wrong

The document this file replaces was written eight days and one major version earlier, and three of
its claims are worth stating as corrections rather than quietly dropping.

**The sampler gate is not absolute, and it was named as the reason several features were
impossible in their obvious form.** §2.1 of that document counted sixteen units of sixteen with
nine wanted and none available. On WebGPU that stopped being true when the shadow bindings were
collapsed into one sampler declaration, and nobody reconciled the document with it. See §3 above
for the arithmetic on both backends. The gate is a WebGL2 debt.

**The frame-graph deferral has come due.** §2.5 quoted `renderer.ts` at 3,574 lines and deferred
the decision about a pass graph to whatever the WebGPU work concluded about that file. What it
concluded was a second hand-ordered renderer. `renderer.ts` is now **7686 lines** and
`webgpu/renderer.ts` is **14,409**, for 22,095 lines of pass order held by hand across two files.
The WebGPU figure is rising rather than falling because every verb now carries both paths: the
recording the graph replays and the direct calls `?graph=0` still uses. Both exist until the
switch stops being reversible, which is an open decision in the design rather than an oversight.
Those two numbers are asserted by `scripts/docs.test.mjs` rather than typed, because the first one
was 556 lines wrong within a week and nothing noticed.

**Gaussian splats left `README.md`'s gap list without it being edited, which is the failure the sentinels exist to catch and the reason this section is kept.** `@driftengine/splats` shipped the readers, the off-frame sort and the pass, and the guard stayed green throughout because it named `evaluateSh` — a symbol for the one part that genuinely did not land. A sentinel that is narrower than the row it stands behind reports the row as absent long after most of it arrived, so the sentinel now names view-dependent colour, which is what is left of it, and the row says the same. Recorded here rather than in `README.md`: that document lists gaps, and how a gap list went wrong is this one's business.

**`drift/physics` said it bound joints and never has, found 2026-08-27.** Its own header in
`packages/script/src/bindings/core.ts` read "Track B, complete: bodies, joints, queries, sensors, a
controller and ragdolls", and the capabilities under it are bodies, contacts, queries and
forces — no joint verb, no controller, no ragdoll, and no way for a script to make one. The
sentence was written from the _track's_ deliverables rather than from the list beneath it, which is
the same failure as a binding written from memory of what a camera ought to have: the first version
of `drift/camera` described `lookAt` and `setPosition`, which `CinematicCamera` does not have.

The header is corrected and **the gap is left open on purpose**, with the reason recorded there:
`JointDesc` carries twenty optional fields, so a script-side constructor is either an enormous
signature or a builder this language has no shape for. That is a decision somebody has to take
deliberately, and taking it badly would put a wrong-by-construction surface in front of every script
author. **§1's "Scripting reach" row counts thirteen modules and is still right** — the module is
reachable; what it reaches is narrower than its own comment claimed.

**`drift/audio` said it bound the mix and the rhythm and binds neither, found 2026-08-27.** Its
header called itself "the richest surface available, because Track G is complete: playback,
placement, the mix, and the rhythm the music is doing", over five capabilities: a slot, two ways to
play it, and `distanceGain` and `stereoPan`. No mix verb, no rhythm verb, no HRTF-panned source, no
listener, no reverb zone. **That is the same failure as `drift/physics` above and the same failure
as the first `drift/camera` binding**, three times in three files, and the shape is identical every
time: a header written from what a _track_ delivered rather than from the array beneath it.

Corrected, and **left open on purpose** for the same reason as joints: `MixConsole`,
`AudioListenerGraph`, `SpatialSource` and `ReverbZone` are stateful objects with lifetimes, and a
script surface for them is a design about handles and ownership — who disposes a source, what
happens to its probe slot, whether a zone outlives the script that made it — rather than a table
entry.

**The pattern is worth naming, because a fourth is likely.** Every binding file's header is prose
about a subsystem, and nothing asserts that it describes the capabilities in its own file. A guard
that read the `define` calls and checked the header mentioned no verb the array lacks would have
caught all three; that is a test somebody should write, and it is not written.

**None of its running order was built.** Not splats, rigid node animation, spot lights, general
per-instance transforms, the sampler filter mode, octahedral shadows, PBR inputs, image
environments, clustered lights, depth of field or area lights. The time went to the WebGPU port,
which was the right call and was never reconciled with the plan it displaced. That is the failure
this document's sentinels exist to prevent repeating.

## 5. The sentinels

**Three of these are DriftCapture's, added 2026-09-20 with the capability rows they belong to**,
because a capture that is honest about what it does needs to be equally honest about what it does
not. `capture-texture-atlas`: a capture's colour is one value a vertex, so its detail ceiling is
the mesh rather than the footage, and nothing bakes a texture from the frames. `capture-delight-prior`:
the weights proposal found no licence-clean learned model for delighting and proposed a small one
the project would train itself; it is not trained. `capture-metric-anchor`: a monocular
reconstruction has no scale of its own, and nothing reads a known-size object out of a clip to give
it one — **the metres in the rows above are the depth model's claim and not a measurement.**

Each row names a symbol that would exist if the capability did. `scripts/docs.test.mjs` asserts
every one is still absent from `src/`, so the commit that builds spot lights is the commit that has
to correct this document. Patterns are matched against source with comments stripped, because prose
in a comment mentioning a spotlight is not a spot light.

**A second sentinel retired the same day, and it would not have fired.** `clustered-lights` named
`uClusterGrid`, and the uniforms that actually landed are `uClusterTable`, `uClusterFrustum` and
`uClustered` — so clustered lighting arrived with the guard green, exactly as frustum culling and
LOD did under names the rows had guessed wrong. **That is the third time**, which is
enough to stop calling it a near miss: a sentinel is a reminder to correct this document, not a
detector, and the habit that keeps it honest is correcting the row in the commit that lands the
capability rather than waiting for a red suite to ask.

**A fourth miss, and this one is recorded before it could be discovered.**
`image-based-lighting` named `irradianceSh`, and what landed is a _file_ called `irradianceSh.ts`
whose exported symbols are `projectIrradiance` and `evaluateIrradiance`. Patterns are matched
against source with comments stripped, and a filename is neither — so the guard stayed green
through the commit that built half the capability. It was corrected because the plan said to,
which is the only reason it was corrected at all.

**That is the fourth, and the row above is narrowed rather than deleted for that reason.** What was
left of it, `prefilterEnvMap`, was a name for a thing that did not exist yet and would be written by
somebody who had not read this document — so it was as likely to miss as the other four.

**It did not miss, 2026-08-25.** The guard fired on the commit that built the prefilter, naming
`packages/core/src/render/backend/webgpu/renderer.ts`, and it fired on an _import statement_ rather
than on a definition — which is the first time one of these has been caught by the mechanism rather
than by somebody remembering. A file name is not source; a path in an `import` is. The sentinel is
replaced with `environment-loader`, which names the piece still absent, and the habit is unchanged:
correct the row in the commit that lands the capability, because a green suite is not evidence that
nothing landed.

**A sentinel retired on purpose, 2026-08-24.** `compute-pipelines` named `createComputePipeline`
and is gone from the block below, because the engine now builds one: the froxel binner in
`webgpu/clusterBinner.ts`. The row it guarded is corrected above rather than deleted, since what a
reader wants to know is not that a symbol appeared but which backend can do what.

**A sentinel narrowed on purpose, 2026-08-24.** `clustered-lights` named
`buildLightClusters|uClusterGrid` and the first of those now exists, in a file nothing draws with.
The row was narrowed to `uClusterGrid` rather than corrected away, because that uniform is the
moment the _lit pass_ reads a froxel table — which is when a consumer's scene is lit differently
and when the capability becomes real. A sentinel that fires on groundwork reports a capability
that does not exist, and the failure that costs is a green row nobody trusts. **Narrowing is only
honest when the remaining symbol is strictly later than the one dropped**; here it is, and the
Lights row above says exactly what was built in the meantime.

**Two sentinels added as Track A closed, 2026-08-25.** Four were dropped as the row landed —
`skeletal-animation`, `animation-clips`, `inverse-kinematics` and `morph-targets` — which left
`README.md` naming an animation gap no sentinel backed, and `docs.test.mjs` said so. The two that
replace them name what the row genuinely leaves: **root motion**, which is a decomposition of the
root track and belongs beside `sampleClip`, and **skinned shadow casting**, where the depth pass
has its own vertex shader and its own permutation question. Both are strictly later than anything
Track A built, which is what makes them honest rather than a guard being kept alive for its own
sake.

**And one of those two closed without a word, which is the splats failure in its
second and worse form.** `ce91c4c` built skinned shadow casting end to end: `DEPTH_SKINNED_VERT`
and its WGSL twin, `depthSkinnedProgram` and `shadowSkinnedLayout` on the two backends, and
`ShadowCasterSink.skinnedMesh` carrying the palette so a running figure stops throwing the shadow
of a statue. The sentinel stayed green throughout, because it named `uSkinnedDepth` and
`skinnedDepthVariant` — two symbols nobody wrote and nobody was ever going to. Both documents went
